summary: This Japanese multicenter double-blind randomized trial tested donepezil hydrochloride (3 mg/day for one week, then 5 mg/day for two weeks) against placebo in 110 adults with long COVID who reported significant fatigue within 52 weeks of COVID-19 onset. Donepezil produced no meaningful improvement in fatigue as measured by the Chalder Fatigue Scale at 3 weeks, with a baseline-adjusted mean difference of 0.34 points (95% CI: -2.23 to 2.91, p=0.79). All secondary outcomes — including anxiety, depression, PTSD symptoms, and quality of life — were also negative at both 3 and 8 weeks, and no serious adverse events occurred in either group.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome (Chalder Fatigue Scale at 3 weeks): baseline-adjusted mean difference 0.34 (95% CI -2.23 to 2.91), p=0.79.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. Primary outcome was analyzed via proportional odds model with permutation test; no single numeric effect size (OR or test statistic) for the pooled primary endpoint is reported in the main text or tables — only stated as not statistically significant. Individual symptom severity data at each timepoint are presented only in figures (stacked bar charts, eFigures 3-8 in supplement) without numeric values in text/tables. The change from baseline in moderate/severe symptom percentages in Table 2 are percentage-point changes, not means with SDs. Enrollment stopped early for futility (conditional power <10%). Total AE counts: 771 events in NMV/r, 313 in PBO/r. 784 individuals expressed interest, 168 consented/screened.

summary: The STOP-PASC trial tested a 15-day course of nirmatrelvir-ritonavir (Paxlovid) against placebo-ritonavir in 155 adults with long COVID symptoms lasting at least 3 months, most of whom were vaccinated and had been ill for an average of 17.5 months. The primary outcome — pooled severity of six core symptoms (fatigue, brain fog, body aches, cardiovascular symptoms, shortness of breath, and gastrointestinal symptoms) at 10 weeks — showed no statistically significant difference between the treatment and placebo groups; the trial was stopped early for futility when conditional power fell below 10%. Both groups improved over time, and adverse event rates were similar, with dysgeusia more common in the nirmatrelvir-ritonavir group (62% vs 8%) but no serious safety signals attributed to the drug.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary pooled symptom severity outcome at 10 weeks showed no statistically significant difference between NMV/r and PBO/r groups; trial stopped early for futility (conditional power <10%). For the most bothersome symptom, NMV/r was associated with worse odds at 10 weeks (OR 1.99, 95% CI 1.06–3.72, p=0.03).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Baseline values in Table 1 are reported for n=24 (lithium, after exclusion of 2 LTFU) and n=26 (placebo) based on the n values given in Table 2 change-from-baseline columns, though Table 1 header states n=26 for lithium (randomized). The Body Pain Bother CI lower bound is reported as -5.3 in Table 2, which appears to be a typographic error in the original paper. The BFSS was a novel unvalidated instrument created for this study. Some secondary outcomes (ISI, GAD-2, Headache Bother, Body Pain Bother, Smell/Taste) were analyzed only in subsets with baseline scores above threshold; exact n per arm for these subsets not reported. The paper also reports a subsequent open-label dose-finding study (n=5 enrolled, n=3 completed) with individual patient data in Tables 3-4, but this was not a randomized comparison and is not extracted as RCT outcome data.

summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial tested lithium aspartate (10–15 mg/day for 3 weeks) against placebo in 52 adults with long COVID fatigue and cognitive dysfunction, recruited at a neurology clinic. The primary outcome—combined Fatigue Severity Scale and Brain Fog Severity Scale scores—showed no significant difference between groups (mean intergroup difference: −3.6 points, 95% CI −16.6 to 9.5, p=0.59), meaning the low-dose treatment had no detectable benefit over placebo. A small, unblinded follow-up dose-finding study in 3 participants suggested that higher doses (40–45 mg/day) achieving serum lithium levels of 0.18–0.49 mEq/L may produce larger symptom reductions, but this finding is exploratory only and requires a new randomized trial to confirm.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome (sum of FSS-7 and BFSS scores): intergroup difference −3.6 points, 95% CI −16.6 to 9.5, p=0.59—no significant effect.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested a 3-month personalized resistance exercise program against usual care in 233 adults with persistent symptoms after COVID-19 infection in Scotland, including both community patients and those previously hospitalized. The primary outcome was walking distance on the Incremental Shuttle Walk Test: the exercise group improved by 83 meters versus 47 meters in the control group, an adjusted difference of 36.5 meters (95% CI, 6.6–66.3 m; p=0.02). The intervention also produced statistically significant improvements in quality of life, anxiety and depression scores, and grip strength, with no increase in adverse events or post-exertional malaise.

trial_rating.result_basis: Incremental Shuttle Walk Test adjusted mean difference 36.5 m (95% CI 6.6–66.3 m; p=0.02), against a baseline mean of 328 m, representing an approximately 11% relative improvement over control.

Paper reports 11 treatment-emergent serious adverse events in mITT population (n=320) but does not break them down by arm in the main text (referenced eTable 9 in supplement). PROMIS Sleep 8b and PROMIS distress (raw) outcomes, AVLT delayed recall, AVLT recognition, and digit vigilance errors were also extracted in the tables but omitted from outcome objects to manage output size — all showed no differential treatment benefit. summary: This phase 2 randomized trial (RECOVER-NEURO) tested three remotely delivered cognitive interventions — adaptive computerized training (BrainHQ), a structured cognitive rehabilitation program (PASC-CoRE) combined with BrainHQ, and transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) combined with BrainHQ — in 328 adults with cognitive symptoms persisting at least 12 weeks after COVID-19 infection, across 22 US sites. None of the three active interventions improved self-reported cognitive function (modified ECog2 scale) compared to an active comparator of unstructured computer puzzles over 10 weeks: adjusted mean differences were 0.0 (95% CI −0.2 to 0.2) for BrainHQ vs comparator and 0.1 (95% CI −0.1 to 0.3) for PASC-CoRE+BrainHQ vs comparator. All five arms, including the control, showed roughly equivalent improvement of approximately half a rating point on the 5-point ECog2 scale, and no treatment differences emerged on neuropsychological tests or secondary patient-reported outcomes.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome adjusted mean difference: BrainHQ vs active comparator 0.0 (95% CI −0.2 to 0.2); PASC-CoRE+BrainHQ vs active comparator 0.1 (95% CI −0.1 to 0.3); tDCS-active+BrainHQ vs tDCS-sham+BrainHQ 0.0 (95% CI −0.2 to 0.2) — all null results.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a letter-format secondary analysis of a parent RCT (Méndez-Flores et al. 2022, doi:10.1002/ctm2.763). No per-arm means, SDs, or individual numeric outcome values are reported in the text — only p-value thresholds (p<0.01, p<0.05) for between-group differences. All quantitative biomarker data appear only in supplementary figures (Figures S2-S5) and supplementary tables (Tables S2-S4) which are not included in this text. The network correlation values (rho=0.17, rho=0.36) are reported for male vs female PTIC subgroups only, not as between-arm comparisons. No primary outcome is explicitly designated; all outcomes are biomarker-based (cytokines, chemokines, blood count ratios, physiological network properties). No patient-reported outcomes, clinical outcomes, or adverse events are reported. The analysis focuses on 37 completers (20 PTIC, 17 placebo) from the original 89 randomized, representing very high attrition (~58%). This paper is very poorly suited for quantitative meta-analysis due to absence of extractable numeric effect sizes.

summary: This randomised controlled trial tested polymerised type I collagen (PTIC), an immunomodulatory drug given intramuscularly for 7 days, in 89 unvaccinated adult outpatients with PCR-confirmed COVID-19, with follow-up to 12 weeks to assess post-acute sequelae. The primary analysis focused on physiological network dynamics and inflammatory biomarkers; PTIC-treated patients showed faster reduction in inflammatory markers including IP-10, IL-8, CRP, and eosinophil counts compared to placebo, with sex-dependent effects: women on PTIC showed a larger disruption from baseline network state (network correlation rho=0.17 vs 0.36 in men), indicating stronger early immune remodelling. The analysis was limited to 37 completers (20 PTIC, 17 placebo) out of 89 enrolled, and the primary endpoint was a novel physiological network metric rather than a validated clinical outcome, substantially limiting interpretability.

trial_rating.result_basis: Significant between-group differences in inflammatory markers including IP-10, IL-8, CRP (p<0.01) and IL-1Ra, eosinophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (p<0.05) on day 1 post-treatment; network correlation rho=0.17 (female PTIC) vs 0.36 (male PTIC) at first post-treatment day, but no validated clinical primary endpoint was reported.

CRITICAL LIMITATION: All quantitative outcome data (means, SDs for ΔHR, NPY, Holter HR, HRV parameters) are presented ONLY in figures (Figures 2-5) with no corresponding data tables or numeric values in text. Baseline demographics are referenced as being in 'Supplementary Table 1' which was not included in the full text provided. The paper states 'no side effects related to the device were observed' but provides no structured AE reporting. summary: This randomized controlled trial tested low-level tragus stimulation (LL-TS) — a non-invasive electrical stimulation of the outer ear that activates the vagus nerve — in 57 adults (mean age 32, 61% female) with POTS following COVID-19 infection. Compared to sham stimulation, one month of twice-daily LL-TS (1 hour per session) significantly reduced the heart rate rise on standing, lowered average and maximum 24-hour heart rates, improved autonomic balance (increased parasympathetic HF power, decreased sympathetic LF power and LF/HF ratio), and reduced plasma neuropeptide Y levels, with effects persisting at one-year follow-up. No device-related side effects were observed, though the study was small (n=31 active, n=26 sham), did not assess broader POTS symptoms such as fatigue or cognition, and lacked a non-POTS control group.

trial_rating.result_basis: Heart rate increase on standing significantly attenuated in LL-TS vs sham at 1 month and 1 year (all p<0.05); HRV parameters (LF, HF, LF/HF ratio) significantly improved during postural test (all p<0.001); NPY levels significantly reduced (p<0.05).

Additional isokinetic outcomes for knee flexion (60° and 180°, both legs) were extracted in the tables but omitted from outcomes array to manage output size — none showed significant interaction effects. The intergroup between-group effect values reported in the abstract (e.g., 88.9s for CPET duration, 25.9W for power output) represent TRP vs CG differences but the table format reports CG-TRP direction for intergroup comparisons. | Pass3: Added between-group CIs for strength (Tables 4) and FVC% (Table 5) from agent PDF re-read. CIs are intergroup post-test differences (TRP minus CG). Note: Power output within-TRP change=25.9W was significant but intergroup Post MD=0.9 (NS) due to baseline imbalance.

summary: A 12-week home-based telerehabilitation programme (aerobic and strength circuit training, 3 sessions/week via Zoom) was tested against usual daily activities in 120 older adults (age ~65) with post-COVID-19 syndrome in a randomised controlled trial. The primary outcome, peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak), increased in both the telerehabilitation and control groups with no significant difference between them; however, the telerehabilitation group showed significantly greater improvements in exercise test duration (+88.9 seconds), cycle ergometer power output (+25.9 watts), and lean/skeletal muscle mass (+1.4 kg skeletal muscle mass) compared to controls. A notable caveat is that the telerehabilitation group had more severe baseline disease (longer hospitalisation, more ICU admissions, more mechanical ventilation), which may limit direct group comparisons despite the positive physical outcomes observed.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome VO2peak showed a significant interaction effect (p=0.05) but no significant between-group difference (p>0.05); both groups improved (~3.0 vs ~1.9 mL/kg/min). Secondary outcomes showed significant between-group differences in CPET duration (mean difference 88.9s, p=0.001) and power output (25.9W, p<0.001).

Mean rehab duration was 27±6 days overall but differed significantly between groups (IHHT 29.5±6.3 days vs control 24.9±5.5 days, p<0.001). The methods state values expressed as medians/IQRs but tables present mean±SD; extraction used the table values. The EQ-5D baseline values show a dramatic imbalance (IHHT 38.3 vs control 86.7) suggesting possible data error or very different severity populations. The between-group change differences were calculated from reported change scores. The paper reports ANCOVA p-values adjusted for baseline for between-group comparisons on primary and some secondary endpoints but does not report adjusted mean differences or CIs. FAC score data excluded from between-group effects due to ceiling effect noted by authors (all near maximum of 5). FAC and timed-up-and-go between-group comparison reported as ns. Table 3 clinical/biochemical variables (BP, HR, SpO2, weight, Hb, CRP, FBS, lipids) were extracted only as key outcomes above to manage output size; full data available in Table 3 of the paper. summary: This controlled pilot trial tested intermittent hypoxic-hyperoxic training (IHHT) — alternating cycles of low-oxygen (10-12% O2) and high-oxygen (30-35% O2) breathing — added to standard inpatient rehabilitation in 145 long COVID patients (74% female, mean age 53) at a German rehabilitation centre. The primary outcome, 6-minute walk test distance, improved by 91.7 m in the IHHT group versus 32.6 m in the control group (a 2.8-fold difference, p<0.001), well above the 35 m threshold for clinical meaningfulness. The study was non-randomised and open-label, with the IHHT group being on average 5 years younger and having fewer comorbidities (less coronary artery disease and COPD), which limits causal conclusions despite baseline-adjusted analysis; no adverse events were recorded.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6MWT improved 91.7 ± 50.1 m (IHHT) vs 32.6 ± 54.2 m (control), ANCOVA p<0.001, exceeding the 35 m minimum clinically important difference threshold.

summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial tested 4 g/day of creatine monohydrate for 6 months in 12 adults with post-COVID-19 fatigue syndrome. The primary outcome — change in vastus medialis muscle creatine levels — was significantly higher in the creatine group than placebo (30.6 ± 3.4 mM vs. 21.9 ± 4.4 mM at 6 months, p < .01), and creatine also raised levels in brain white matter regions. Creatine reduced general fatigue at 3 months and improved several symptom scores (ageusia, breathing difficulties, body aches, headache, concentration difficulties) at 6 months compared to baseline. The trial is very small (n=6 per arm) and the lead investigator holds a patent on creatine products and received funding from the creatine manufacturer, which are significant conflicts of interest.

summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial tested 3 months of a synbiotic mixture (L. rhamnosus DSM 32550, L. plantarum DSM 34532, B. lactis DSM 32269, B. longum DSM 32946, fructooligosaccharides, and zinc) versus maltodextrin placebo in 26 adults with post-COVID-19 ME/CFS. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Major limitations for meta-analysis: (1) Only medians reported for intervention group pre-post (Table 4); no means, SDs, or IQRs reported for any cognitive outcome in either arm. Raw values stated to be available on request. (2) Control group per-arm values not reported at all - only interaction F-statistics and main effects from mixed ANOVAs are provided (Table 5). (3) BDI-II data only collected for intervention group, not control; BDI-II scores appear only in a figure (Fig. 4) with Greenhouse-Geisser F(109, 10.91) = 12.33, p = .004 reported. (4) Between-group effects are reported as interaction F-statistics from mixed ANOVAs rather than mean differences or SMDs. Effect sizes reported as rank-sum coefficient r for within-group pre-post comparisons and partial r for ANOVA effects. (5) The ~16-week total follow-up is calculated from the mean 113.87 days between assessments in the intervention group. (6) The study is explicitly described as exploratory and non-randomized. Groups were not matched for age or gender. (7) All 19 cognitive outcomes extracted; 3 showed significant time x group interactions: Story Memory (SM), Story Recall (SR), and Figure Copy (FC).

summary: This non-randomized feasibility trial tested an 8-week weekly group intervention combining computer-based cognitive training (Fresh Minder 2 software) and CBT-based group psychotherapy in 15 long COVID patients with cognitive complaints at LMU Munich. The intervention group showed significant pre-post improvements across most cognitive domains (attention, memory, executive function) with medium-to-large effect sizes, but when compared against a 15-patient control group who received no intervention, only 3 of 19 cognitive variables showed a statistically significant group-by-time interaction: story memory (p=0.046, r=0.37), story recall (p=0.030, r=0.40), and visuospatial construction (p=0.003, r=0.52). The dominant finding was that both groups improved over approximately 4 months, strongly suggesting spontaneous recovery over time accounts for most cognitive gains; the intervention showed no harmful effects and was rated as helpful by 96% of participants.

trial_rating.result_basis: Only 3 of 19 primary cognitive outcomes showed significant group-by-time interactions: story memory p=0.046 r=0.37, story recall p=0.030 r=0.40, figure copy p=0.003 r=0.52; the remaining 16 variables showed significant time effects in both groups, indicating spontaneous recovery rather than intervention effect.

PedsQL and fatigue outcomes are reported from a linear mixed-effects model intercept (overall, not per-arm), so arm_id=0 is used to indicate pooled/overall estimates. The study design is a waitlist-controlled trial where the 6-week group served as control for the first 6 weeks then received 6 weeks of intervention; both groups received IOET but at different durations and start times. The 95% CIs in figure captions for visit 4 (follow-up) appear to describe visit 4 values, not visit 3 post-intervention values, creating some ambiguity. Cohen's d values at visit 3 were reported in figure captions. Per-arm data for PedsQL subscales, visit 2 (6-week) timepoint data, and visit 4 follow-up values for primary outcomes were referenced as available in supplement tables but not extractable from the main text. summary: This small exploratory randomized controlled trial tested individualized online exercise therapy (IOET), delivered twice weekly via telemedicine, in 14 children and adolescents (ages 9–17) with long COVID and a median symptom duration of 21 months. The primary outcome was physical performance: in the 12-week group, walking distance on the 6-minute walk test increased by 220 meters (from 396 m to 616 m), handgrip strength rose by 10.5 kg, and sit-to-stand repetitions increased by 7.2; the 6-week group showed comparable gains. School attendance rose from 58% to 97% across both groups, and quality-of-life scores improved substantially, with no adverse events or post-exertional symptom worsening observed in any participant. The trial was exploratory and very small, with no no-intervention control group, so results cannot be generalized but justify a larger confirmatory trial.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6MWT increased by 220.3 m (95% CI 98.2–342.4) in the 12-week group and 172.6 m (95% CI 64.7–280.6) in the 6-week group; no between-group difference was statistically significant, but within-group improvements exceeded minimal clinically important differences with CIs excluding zero.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a non-randomized quasi-experimental pilot study (prospective observational), not an RCT. Group allocation was based on participant preference/convenience, not randomization. All outcome data are reported as medians with 25th-75th percentiles (not means and SDs), limiting meta-analytic pooling. The ANOVA-derived interaction p-values and simple main effect change scores (means with 95% CIs for TMT-B and FAB) come from the mixed-factors ANOVA which uses means, but per-arm means and SDs were not reported in tables. The 6MWT column header says 's' (seconds) but likely represents meters based on the values reported (520-671 range). Treatment duration of 20 sessions at 2x/week = approximately 10 weeks. SICI and ICF TMS sub-outcomes reported only as medians in Table 3 and are included in the RMT outcome note but not extracted as separate outcomes to manage output size. No primary outcome was explicitly designated; no adverse events were reported. The paper describes the protocol as 'safe' in the conclusions but provides no specific AE data.

summary: This pilot study tested a dual-task augmented reality rehabilitation protocol — combining active physical exercises with concurrent cognitive tasks over 20 one-hour sessions — in 10 non-hospitalized adults with long COVID brain fog and fatigue, compared to 10 similar patients who received no rehabilitation. The primary cognitive outcomes showed significant improvement only in the treatment group: Trail Making Test-B execution time decreased by 15.9 seconds (95% CI 7.6–24.1, p=0.001) and Frontal Assessment Battery score improved by 1.9 points (95% CI 0.8–2.9, p=0.002), indicating better executive function. Fatigue and physical performance measures (six-minute walk test, handgrip strength, fatigue severity scale) improved similarly in both groups with no treatment-specific benefit, and the study was unrandomized with only 10 participants per group, limiting generalisability.

trial_rating.result_basis: TMT-B execution time decreased by 15.9 s (95% CI 7.6–24.1, p=0.001) and FAB score improved by 1.9 points (95% CI 0.8–2.9, p=0.002) in the dual-task group only, with effect sizes pη²=0.275 and pη²=0.306 respectively.

No primary outcome was formally designated; all outcomes treated as exploratory. The paper states 3-month treatment duration but reports assessments at 4 and 12 weeks. RMSSD values in Table 3 are labeled 'Median (IQR)' but the ± notation in the table header is ambiguous — IQR values are reported in parentheses without explicit low/high bounds. The 10Hz arm BFI baseline SD of 4.5 appears unusually large compared to other arms (1.4-1.6), possibly a data entry issue in the original paper. The RMSSD per-arm values in Table 3 use parenthetical values without ± symbol for individual groups, suggesting those are IQR values, but the total column uses ± notation. summary: This pilot RCT tested transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) delivered via a home TENS device at three frequencies (10Hz, 25Hz, and 2Hz as a low-dose control) in 35 women with long COVID over 12 weeks. Across all groups, fatigue scores (Brief Fatigue Inventory) fell from a mean of 5.5 to 4.5 points, dyspnea (Borg scale) dropped from a median of 3 to 2 points, and health-related quality of life (SF-36 physical component) improved from 32 to 36 points — but the study used only descriptive statistics with no formal significance testing or placebo comparison. The intervention was generally safe with no serious adverse events, though mild side effects such as ear pain, insomnia, and headaches were reported in roughly one-third of participants; a key caveat is that spontaneous symptom improvement over time cannot be ruled out as the 2Hz 'control' group showed similar gains to the active groups.

trial_rating.result_basis: BFI mean decreased from 5.5 to 4.5 across all groups; no inferential statistics or p-values reported, and no significant between-group differences detected; the 2Hz control group showed comparable improvement, preventing attribution of effects to active stimulation.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a post-hoc analysis of a primary RCT (NCT05047952) that focused on cognitive deficits. Depressive symptoms (QIDS-SR-16) were a secondary outcome in the parent trial. The between-group mean difference of -5.41 and within-group changes are from the adjusted GEE model (adjusted for age, sex, education, CRP, TG-HDL, BMI, confirmed COVID diagnosis, IPAQ, nicotine use). In the unadjusted model, time (p=0.776) and treatment (p=0.079) effects were NOT significant, raising concerns about robustness. Endpoint QIDS-SR-16 scores at week 8 are not reported directly (only change scores from GEE). Adverse events not reported in this post-hoc paper. Figure 1 contains LS mean trajectories at baseline, weeks 2, 4, and 8 but numeric values at intermediate timepoints are not provided in text or tables. The TG-HDL SD in the vortioxetine arm (17.19) is very large relative to the mean (5.81), suggesting possible outliers or skewed data. 53 of 200 consented participants were lost before randomization.

summary: This 8-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial tested vortioxetine (5–20 mg/day) against placebo in 147 Canadian adults with WHO-defined post-COVID-19 condition (PCC) who had depressive symptoms. The primary outcome was change in self-reported depression score (QIDS-SR-16) from baseline to 8 weeks; vortioxetine produced a mean reduction of 4.93 points versus 0.41 points for placebo, a between-group difference of 5.41 points (p<0.001). Participants with higher baseline inflammation (CRP), metabolic disruption (TG-HDL ratio), and elevated BMI showed a more pronounced response to vortioxetine. A key caveat is that this is a post-hoc secondary analysis of a trial primarily designed to assess cognitive outcomes, meaning the depressive symptom analysis was not pre-specified as a primary endpoint.

trial_rating.result_basis: Between-group mean difference in QIDS-SR-16 at 8 weeks: -5.41 points (SEM=1.335, p<0.001); vortioxetine within-group change -4.93 vs placebo -0.41 points.

The CFQ-11 was scored using Likert (0,1,2,3) for change analysis but dichotomous (0,0,1,1) for eligibility screening. The change score of -4.6 and -2.9 are reported in the abstract and Table 3 but the SD of the change scores is not reported, only endpoint SDs. The p=0.01 is from a paired t-test comparing change scores. Table 3 reports multiple conditional analyses (e.g., baseline values for 3-month completers, baseline values for 6-month completers, and 3-month values for those completing both 3- and 6-month follow-ups with N=27). The between-group mean difference of -1.7 was calculated from the change scores (-4.6 minus -2.9). The 6-month comparison is not a controlled comparison as the wait-list group received the intervention after 3 months. SF-12 and EQ-5D-5L were collected but no quantitative results are reported for these outcomes. The paper states no SAR/Es were reported during the 12-week intervention use, reported as a combined statement not per-arm.

summary: This feasibility randomized controlled trial tested a self-administered version of the Perrin Technique — a daily routine of lymphatic drainage massage, spinal mobility and breathing exercises, and alternating hot/cold packs to the upper spine — in 100 adults with long COVID-related fatigue recruited via UK general practice and an NHS research volunteer database. The primary aim was feasibility (recruitment and retention), not efficacy; however, Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire (CFQ-11) scores at 3 months improved by 4.6 points in the intervention group versus 2.9 points in the wait-list control group (p=0.01). The study was not powered for efficacy, the wait-list design inflates apparent effect sizes, and dropout was higher in the intervention arm (30.6%) than in controls (11.8%), limiting conclusions about real-world effectiveness.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. No primary outcome was explicitly designated; the study is described as an exploratory pilot study focused on feasibility and acceptance. No inferential statistics (p-values) were reported due to acknowledged limited statistical power. Many outcomes reported as medians with IQR (non-normally distributed) rather than means with SDs, limiting meta-analytic utility. IQR values are reported as single values (range width) rather than Q1-Q3, so iqr_low/iqr_high could not be derived. The abstract reports age as mean±SD (45±9 and 39±23) but Table 1 reports median(IQR); these are likely medians with IQR despite abstract notation. The 6MWT control group T1 value of 199.1m appears anomalously low (down from 448.8m at baseline), likely reflecting imputation of very poor values for the 3 dropouts who worsened. Additional SF-36 subscales (PF, RP, BP, GH, VT, SF, RE, MH) and MFI subscales (Reduced Motivation, Mental Fatigue) and PCFS were reported as median(IQR) in Table 2 but omitted from outcome objects to manage output size.

summary: This randomized, single-blinded, placebo-controlled pilot study tested pulsed electromagnetic field therapy (PEMF) — 10 sessions of 30 minutes each over 5 weeks using a Papimi Delta device — in 20 adults with post-COVID fatigue syndrome. The intervention group showed clinically meaningful improvements in walking distance on the 6-minute walk test (increase of 55m at end of treatment, 79m at 5-week follow-up, both exceeding the 35m minimal clinically important difference), and in total fatigue scores on the Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory (improvement of 20.5 units vs a 14.3-unit threshold for clinical relevance), alongside gains in sleep quality, work ability, and quality of life. The study is a small pilot with only 10 participants per arm and no inferential statistics were reported, making it insufficient to draw conclusions about efficacy; three placebo patients dropped out due to worsening fatigue while none in the PEMF group did, which may reflect natural disease progression or a sham-arm bias.

trial_rating.result_basis: No inferential statistics (p-values or confidence intervals) were reported due to small sample size; 6MWT improved by 55m (T1) and 79m (T2) in the intervention group vs a decline of 246m (T1) and recovery of 40m (T2) in controls, but these are descriptive figures only with no significance testing.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a quasi-experimental study, NOT an RCT. Groups were assigned based on performance/clinical severity, not randomization. The between-group comparisons (Table 1, Table 2) are baseline cross-sectional comparisons between the two non-randomized groups. The longitudinal CPET data (Table 3) is a within-group pre-post comparison of the intervention group only at 2-month vs 3-month follow-up — no control group CPET data exists. CPET was not performed at baseline, so no baseline-to-follow-up comparison is possible. All Table 1 data are medians with IQR (non-parametric). EQ-5D data in Table 2 are means with SD. BMI baseline data were reported as medians with IQR in Table 1: PR median 28.87 (26.48-33.49), OPC median 28.75 (25.22-33.11). Additional baseline variables from Table 1 not extracted as separate outcomes: KLCO (L), DLCO (L), DLCO (%), PEmax (kPa), PImax (kPa). Comorbidity percentages (cardiovascular 70%, respiratory 30%) appear to be for the overall study population, not specified per arm.

summary: A 2-week supervised outpatient cardiopulmonary rehabilitation program was tested in 100 adults with long COVID syndrome (mean age 56.7 years) at Semmelweis University, compared against 100 age-matched controls who received a single check-up. The primary finding was that maximal oxygen consumption (VO2max) continued to improve significantly between 2-month and 3-month follow-up in the rehabilitation group, rising from a median of 1,276 to 1,429.5 ml/min (p=0.033), with weight-adjusted VO2 also improving from 14.6 to 16.0 ml/min/kg (p=0.021). Key caveats include the absence of a control-arm CPET, no baseline CPET measurement, and substantial follow-up dropout: only 73 of 100 participants returned at 2 months and 38 at 3 months, limiting confidence in the long-term estimates.

trial_rating.result_basis: VO2max increased from median 1,276 to 1,429.5 ml/min between 2- and 3-month follow-up (p=0.033); VO2/kg improved from 14.6 to 16.0 ml/min/kg (p=0.021), but these are within-group comparisons only, with 62% dropout by 3 months and no CPET control arm.

summary: This randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial tested 20 daily sessions of bilateral prefrontal transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) combined with online cognitive training (BrainHQ) versus sham tDCS plus cognitive training in 60 long COVID (PASC) patients at the University of São Paulo. The primary outcome was quality of life measured by the WHOQOL-BREF scale; active tDCS produced a statistically significant improvement in the psychological domain compared to sham at end of treatment (p=0.04), but this advantage did not persist at 6 or 12 months. Both groups improved on quality of life immediately and at 6 months (p<0.001 each), suggesting cognitive training alone drives much of the benefit, with the tDCS advantage fading without maintenance protocols.

trial_rating.result_basis: Active tDCS group showed significantly greater improvement in the WHOQOL-BREF psychological domain at end of treatment vs sham (p=0.04), but no significant between-group difference at 6 months or 12 months (p=0.21 at 12 months).

summary: A randomized controlled trial tested an 8-week Pain Informed Movement (PIM) program — combining group pain neuroscience education, individual functional exercise, and relaxation techniques — against usual care plus an educational booklet in 57 adults with long COVID who had developed new-onset persistent pain. The primary outcome, pain intensity (Brief Pain Inventory), was significantly reduced in the PIM group compared to controls, with a mean between-group difference of 2.84 points (p<0.001), exceeding the minimum clinically important difference of 2.0 points; pain interference, catastrophizing, fear of movement, and overall function also improved significantly. The trial was single-blind with a small sample, and a per-protocol rather than intention-to-treat analysis was used, which may overestimate treatment effects.

trial_rating.result_basis: Pain intensity mean between-group difference 2.84 ± 0.62 points (p<0.001, Cohen's d=1.21), exceeding the pre-specified MCID of 2.0 on the Brief Pain Inventory.

summary: This randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial tested 10 sessions of High-Definition transcranial Direct Current Stimulation (HD-tDCS) at 3 mA targeting the left motor cortex, combined with a tailored rehabilitation program, in 70 adults with long COVID-related fatigue (3–12 months post-infection). Active HD-tDCS produced a significantly greater reduction in total fatigue scores than sham (mean MFIS reduction 22.11 vs 10.34 points; group difference 14.03 points, effect size 1.2, p<0.001), with the largest gains in cognitive and psychosocial fatigue domains; physical fatigue did not differ between groups. Active stimulation also reduced anxiety and improved quality of life versus sham, while pain did not change; the only notable adverse event was more skin redness in the active group (37 vs 13 occurrences), with no serious adverse events.

trial_rating.result_basis: Total MFIS group difference 14.03 points, effect size 1.2, 95% CI 7.78–20.28, p<0.001; clinical response rate 77.14% active vs 45.71% sham, NNT=3.

summary: This 12-week randomized controlled trial compared aerobic exercise (AE), resistance exercise (RE), and combined AE/RE (each added to diaphragmatic breathing) against diaphragmatic breathing alone in 80 men aged 40–60 with chronic post-COVID pulmonary fibrosis. The primary outcomes were forced vital capacity (FVC) and diffusing capacity (DLCO): AE improved FVC by 5.1 percentage points more than the control group (p=0.001, Cohen's d=1.1) and DLCO by 4.6 percentage points more (p=0.001, d=0.8), with AE/RE producing similar gains; resistance exercise alone did not significantly improve FVC or DLCO compared to control. The trial was restricted to men at a single Egyptian centre, and some assessors were unblinded, limiting generalisability.

trial_rating.result_basis: AE vs control: FVC MD=5.1% (95% CI 1.1–9.1, p=0.001, d=1.1); DLCO MD=4.6% (95% CI 0.4–9.7, p=0.001, d=0.8); FVC improvement exceeds the 3% MCID but DLCO improvement does not exceed its 11% MCID.

summary: This feasibility trial tested FLEX, an online Cognitive Bias Modification for Interpretations (CBM-I) intervention, in 131 adults with long-term conditions including post-COVID condition, chronic fatigue syndrome, multiple sclerosis, and cancer, all experiencing high levels of fatigue. The primary feasibility outcomes were met: 84% recruitment rate, 70% retention at four months, and 77% full adherence to training sessions. On the key mechanistic outcome—fatigue-related interpretation bias—FLEX produced a large effect versus control at post-intervention (Hedges' g = 0.834, 95% CI [0.472, 1.196]), with small effects on self-reported fatigue and depression but negligible effects on anxiety. This was a feasibility study not powered for significance testing, so symptom effect sizes are exploratory only.

trial_rating.result_basis: Self-reported fatigue (Chalder Fatigue Scale) showed a small, non-significant effect at the primary post-intervention timepoint: adjusted mean difference 1.481 (SE 1.05), Hedges' g = 0.234 (95% CI -0.160 to 0.628); the study was not powered for significance testing.

summary: This double-blind randomised pilot trial tested 12 days of sulphur thermal water (STW) inhalations versus sterile distilled water (placebo) in 30 adults with long COVID and pulmonary sequelae. STW recipients walked 15.9% further in the 6-minute walk test at 3-month follow-up (402.8m to 466.9m, p<0.005), reported a 36.4% reduction in total St George Respiratory Questionnaire score, and showed statistically significant reductions in serum IL-6 (44.6%), IL-1β (48.5%), ACE (93.5%), and S100B (59.5%) compared to no meaningful change in the placebo group. The trial was small (n=15 per arm) and conducted at a single spa facility, limiting generalisability, though no adverse events occurred across the full 3-month follow-up including one pregnant participant.

summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (ACTIV-2) tested the monoclonal antibody combination amubarvimab/romlusevimab versus placebo in 780 high-risk, non-hospitalized adults with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 within 10 days of symptom onset, enrolled January–July 2021. The primary composite outcome—long COVID at 36 weeks or hospitalization/death by 36 weeks—favored treatment (17% vs 24%, weighted risk ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.53–0.93), but this difference was driven entirely by fewer hospitalizations and deaths (4% vs 13%), not by any reduction in long COVID. Among participants who completed the symptom diary, long COVID prevalence was nearly identical: 16% in the treatment arm versus 14% in the placebo arm (weighted risk ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.64–1.27, p=0.55), with no differences in symptom counts, severity, or quality of life at 36 weeks.

trial_rating.result_basis: The primary long COVID-specific outcome (death or long COVID composite) showed wRR=0.90, 95% CI 0.64–1.27, p=0.55; long COVID prevalence was 16% (treatment) vs 14% (placebo), a null result.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Treatment effect values in Table 3 represent baseline-adjusted between-group differences from linear mixed models, not raw per-arm endpoint means at d28. The SD column in Table 3 is the standard error of the treatment effect estimate, not the SD of the score. Post-baseline per-arm means at d28 are not reported in text or tables; scores are depicted only in Figure 2 (box plots). The t-value column in Table 3 appears to represent the test statistic from the linear mixed model. Non-significant outcomes (Chalder, DSQ-PEM, 6MWT, Borg scales, SF-36 physical function, physical role function, emotional role functioning, emotional well-being, physical pain, physical component summary) had no between-group effect estimates reported. Cross-over results also reported in Table 3 but represent within-participant differences, not parallel-group RCT effects. summary: A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase IIa trial tested a single intravenous infusion of rovunaptabin (1350 mg), a DNA aptamer that neutralises autoantibodies against G-protein coupled receptors, in 30 long COVID patients who tested positive for these autoantibodies and had fatigue as a major symptom persisting for at least 3 months. The primary outcome was safety, measured by treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) to day 28: 9 TEAEs occurred in the rovunaptabin group versus 5 in the placebo group, a non-significant difference (p=0.1299). Secondary outcomes showed significant improvements in fatigue and quality of life, including on the FACIT Fatigue Scale (mean improvement 2.91 points, p=0.0378), Bell score (7.54 points, p=0.0004), and Fatigue Severity Scale (-0.43 points, p=0.0088), though a separate phase II trial by the drug's manufacturer was reported to have failed its primary endpoint.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary endpoint (TEAE frequency to day 28) was not statistically significant: 9 events in rovunaptabin group vs 5 in placebo, p=0.1299, CI -14.80% to 63.02%.

summary: This pilot randomized controlled trial tested home-based intranasal and transcranial photobiomodulation (near-infrared light therapy via the Vielight Neuro RX Gamma device, used 20 minutes daily for 8 weeks) in 41 adults with long COVID cognitive dysfunction lasting at least 12 weeks. The primary outcome — composite cognitive score improvement at Day 56 — did not reach statistical significance overall (mean difference 0.043, 95% CI -0.007 to 0.092, p=0.088), though a prespecified exploratory subgroup of participants under 45 years showed a significant improvement over sham (p=0.028, Cohen's d ≈ 0.44). No serious adverse events occurred, but subjective outcomes including fatigue and mobility favored the sham group, and the trial was funded and largely designed by the device manufacturer, Vielight Inc.

summary: This 24-week double-blind randomized controlled trial tested nicotinamide riboside (NR) at 2000 mg/day against placebo in 58 adults with long COVID who had persistent cognitive difficulties and at least two ongoing neurological or physical symptoms. NR reliably raised blood NAD+ levels by 2.6- to 3.1-fold within 5 weeks, but did not significantly improve the primary outcomes of cognitive function (ECog, RBANS, TMT-B; p-values 0.47–0.74) or secondary outcomes of fatigue, sleep quality, depression, or anxiety compared to placebo. Exploratory post-hoc within-group analyses combining all participants during their first 10 weeks on NR showed modest improvements in executive functioning, fatigue (FSS −3.77 points), sleep (PSQI −0.74 points), and depression (BDI −1.67 points), but these are hypothesis-generating only given the absence of placebo-controlled significance and the high dropout rate (51% in the NR arm by 20 weeks).

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary cognitive outcomes showed no significant between-group differences: ECog β=0.08 (p=0.49), RBANS β=6.08 (p=0.47), TMT-B β=−1.83 (p=0.74).

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested a combination of Liu Zi Jue Qigong exercise and acupressure (QARP) added to standard care versus standard care alone in 128 patients hospitalized with severe COVID-19, following them for 28 months after discharge. At 14 months post-discharge, the QARP group showed significantly greater reductions in breathlessness scores compared to controls (mMRC difference: -0.4, 95% CI -0.6 to -0.2, p<0.001; Borg dyspnea difference: -0.6, 95% CI -0.9 to -0.3, p<0.001), and the Borg dyspnea advantage persisted at 28 months (-0.4, 95% CI -0.7 to -0.1, p=0.024). Benefits were confined to patients aged 20-59; no significant differences appeared in elderly patients or on depression or daily living scores at either timepoint.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary Borg dyspnea score (MBS) difference at 14 months: -0.6 (95% CI -0.9 to -0.3, p<0.001); mMRC difference: -0.4 (95% CI -0.6 to -0.2, p<0.001); both exceeding pre-specified minimal clinically important differences of -0.5 and -1.0 respectively.

summary: REGENECYTE, an allogeneic cord blood-derived hematopoietic progenitor cell therapy, was tested in 30 adults (aged 18-65, 70% female) with post-COVID syndrome lasting 6-18 months in a phase IIa randomized placebo-controlled trial. Participants received three intravenous infusions over 6 weeks (20:10 treatment:placebo ratio); the primary endpoint was safety, while the key secondary endpoint was change in fatigue measured by the Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire (CFQ-11). REGENECYTE produced a large, sustained reduction in fatigue: CFQ-11 Bimodal scores fell from 6.75 to 1.00 in the treatment group versus 7.70 to 5.20 in placebo by week 26 (p<0.001), with physical fatigue showing the greatest benefit; safety was favorable, with only 2 of 20 treated patients (10%) experiencing mild, treatment-related adverse events and no serious adverse events. The trial is small, single-site, single-blind, and funded entirely by the manufacturer, all of which limit confidence in the findings.

trial_rating.result_basis: CFQ-11 Bimodal score at week 26: 1.00 ± 2.22 (REGENECYTE) vs 5.20 ± 3.16 (placebo), p<0.001; Likert score 10.60 vs 15.90, p=0.001.

summary: This French multicentre RCT tested structured exercise training rehabilitation (ETR) — including high-intensity endurance cycling and progressive strength training, 2 x 60-minute sessions per week for 90 days — against standard physiotherapy (SP, 2 x 30-minute sessions per week) in 60 adults who had survived COVID-19-related acute respiratory distress syndrome requiring mechanical ventilation and still had significant breathlessness at least 3 months after ICU discharge. At 6 months, significantly more participants in the SIM01 group had alleviation of fatigue (63% vs 43%, OR 2.27), memory loss (42% vs 27%, OR 1.97), difficulty in concentration (62% vs 39%, OR 2.64), gastrointestinal upset (70% vs 54%, OR 2.00), and general unwellness (77% vs 59%, OR 2.36) compared to placebo, all surpassing the Bonferroni-corrected significance threshold. summary: This paper reports supplementary methods and crossover results from an early-phase randomized controlled trial testing Constraint-Induced Cognitive Therapy (CICT) — an intensive, structured cognitive rehabilitation program — in adults with long COVID brain fog. summary: The ReDIRECT trial tested the Counterweight-Plus remotely delivered weight management programme (dietitian-supported total diet replacement followed by food reintroduction and maintenance) in 234 UK adults with long COVID and overweight or obesity. This paper reports the economic evaluation alongside the trial: from an NHS perspective, the intervention cost £14,754 per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gained — well below the NICE £30,000/QALY threshold — with an 89% probability of being cost-effective at that threshold. summary: This 6-month randomised controlled trial tested the 'Pace Me' smartphone app combined with a Fitbit activity tracker — delivering just-in-time alerts when participants reached 50%, 75%, and 100% of their personalised daily activity allowance — against a control app with no energy management support, in 250 non-hospitalised adults with long COVID and post-exertional malaise (PEM). The primary outcome was PEM severity and frequency measured by the DePaul Symptom Questionnaire-PEM (DSQ-PEM); the intervention produced no meaningful benefit over control, with a DSQ-PEM sum score of 46 (95% CI 41–51) in the intervention group versus 44 (95% CI 39–49) in controls at follow-up (interaction effect p=0.614, partial eta-squared=0.002, trivial). Both groups improved over time, likely reflecting natural recovery from long COVID rather than any treatment effect, and no adverse events were reported in the intervention group.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary DSQ-PEM sum score interaction effect p=0.614, partial eta-squared=0.002 (trivial); ITT mixed-effects model also showed no interaction (p=0.621).

summary: The ReDIRECT trial tested a remotely delivered structured weight management program (12 weeks of total diet replacement at 850 kcal/day, followed by food reintroduction and maintenance support) in 234 UK adults with long COVID symptoms lasting over 12 weeks and a BMI above 27 kg/m². Each participant nominated the single long COVID symptom they most wanted to improve (54% chose fatigue), and that symptom score served as the primary outcome; at 6 months, the intervention group showed a statistically significant but modest improvement over controls (treatment effect -0.34 standard deviation units, 95% CI -0.67 to -0.01, p=0.047), alongside a mean weight loss of 10.3 kg versus 0.7 kg in controls. Secondary outcomes showed meaningful improvements in fatigue (-3.64 points, p<0.0001), breathlessness, depression, and quality of life, with no excess serious adverse events in the intervention group.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome treatment effect was -0.34 SD units (95% CI -0.67 to -0.01, p=0.047), below the pre-specified detectable difference of 0.5 SD units, indicating a statistically significant but small and marginal effect.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested the ReCOVery APP, a multidomain telerehabilitation mobile application covering exercise, respiratory physiotherapy, cognitive stimulation, nutrition, sleep, and community participation, as an add-on to usual GP care in 100 adults with long COVID (symptoms persisting beyond 12 weeks) recruited from primary care in Aragon, Spain. The primary outcome was quality of life measured by the SF-36, and the intervention produced no significant improvement over usual care alone: the between-group difference in physical health score change was 4.56 vs 8.02 points (p=0.234) and mental health 5.07 vs 3.20 points (p=0.615). Only 25% of intervention participants met the pre-defined threshold for meaningful app use, and secondary regression analyses found that greater app use time predicted small improvements in physical function and community social support, while gains in self-efficacy and health literacy predicted cognitive improvement and symptom reduction respectively.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary SF-36 physical health score change: intervention 4.56 vs control 8.02 points (p=0.234, CI -9.20 to 2.28); SF-36 mental health change: 5.07 vs 3.20 points (p=0.615, CI -5.49 to 9.23) — no significant between-group difference on either primary outcome component.

summary: This randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial tested hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) — 40 sessions of 100% oxygen at 2 atmospheres — against a sham procedure in 60 long COVID patients (average age ~47) with persistent symptoms for at least 3 months after confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection. The primary outcome was global longitudinal strain (GLS), a sensitive echocardiographic measure of heart muscle function; in the full cohort, HBOT improved GLS but the group-by-time interaction did not reach significance (p=0.237). In a pre-specified subgroup of 29 patients who had abnormally reduced GLS at baseline, HBOT produced a significant improvement (GLS changed from -17.8 to -20.2% vs. -17.8 to -19.1% in sham, p=0.041 for interaction), though this subgroup analysis was post-hoc and the overall trial was underpowered with only 30 patients per arm.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome (GLS in full cohort) group-by-time interaction p=0.237 (non-significant); significant result only in post-hoc reduced-GLS subgroup (p=0.041, N=29).

summary: This double-blind, sham-controlled randomised trial tested 20 sessions of prefrontal transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) over four weeks in 33 adults with long COVID neuropsychiatric symptoms, primarily chronic fatigue (Fatigue Impact Scale score ≥40). Active tDCS targeting the medial prefrontal cortex (2 mA, 30 min/session) was no better than sham on the primary outcome of fatigue reduction: the between-group difference in FIS total score at week 4 was 11.7 points in favour of sham (95% CI -11.1 to 34.5, p=0.6), with the sham group showing a larger within-group improvement. No significant differences were found for anxiety, depression, quality of life, or cognitive performance, and a Bayesian factor (BF10=0.163) provided moderate-to-strong evidence for the null hypothesis.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome FIS total score between-group difference was 11.7 points favouring sham (95% CI -11.1 to 34.5, p=0.6); BF10=0.163 indicating data ~6x more likely under null hypothesis.

summary: This randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial tested hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) — 40 sessions of 100% oxygen at 2 atmospheres — in 73 adults with post-COVID condition persisting for at least 3 months after confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection. The primary outcome was cognitive function: HBOT produced a statistically significant improvement in global cognitive score compared to sham (Cohen's d = 0.495, p = 0.038), with specific gains in executive function (d = 0.477, p = 0.045) and attention (d = 0.463, p = 0.052). Secondary outcomes also improved significantly, including energy, sleep, psychiatric symptoms, and pain interference, and brain MRI showed increased perfusion and microstructural changes in regions associated with cognition and emotion. Three authors have financial ties to a hyperbaric medicine company, and the sample size was small (37 per arm) with follow-up only 1–3 weeks post-treatment, leaving long-term durability unknown.

trial_rating.result_basis: Global cognitive score improved by 5.8 points in HBOT vs 2.4 points in sham (Cohen's d = 0.495, p = 0.038).

summary: This 10-week randomized crossover trial tested two intermittent fasting regimens in 58 adults with long COVID (mean symptom duration 24.6 months, average 20.5 symptoms at baseline): an intense fasting protocol (daily 16:8 time-restricted eating plus one 23–60 hour water-only fast per week, combined with a no-added-sugar diet) versus mild time-restricted eating (daily 10–12 hour eating window with the same no-sugar diet). The intense fasting regimen reduced the composite long COVID symptom severity score by 10.2 points versus 2.8 points for mild TRE (p=0.008), and cut the number of symptoms by 5.0 versus 1.4 (p=0.002); across the full 10 weeks, mean symptom severity fell 51.8% and symptom count fell 40.6%. Ninety percent of participants experienced at least one symptom flare-up, with 58% of flare-ups during the fasting period attributed to the fasting treatment, though no participants withdrew due to adverse events and only one hospitalization was possibly fasting-related.

trial_rating.result_basis: LC-Score decreased by 10.2 points (fasting) vs 2.8 points (TRE), p=0.008; number of symptoms decreased by 5.0 vs 1.4, p=0.002; 10-week overall LC-Score reduction 51.8%, p<0.0001.

summary: This randomized trial tested transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) over two brain targets — the primary motor cortex (M1) or the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) — each combined with 15 sessions of adaptive computerized cognitive training, in 63 long COVID patients with confirmed fatigue (average symptom duration 32 months, 81% female). Both groups showed significant reductions in physical fatigue on the Fatigue Severity Scale (mean improvement of approximately 6 points from baseline, p<0.001), with improvements in cognition, depression, anxiety, pain, and quality of life also observed in both arms and sustained at one-month follow-up. M1 stimulation showed a marginal advantage over DLPFC stimulation for fatigue reduction and sleep quality, but no statistically significant group difference was found on the primary FSS outcome. The trial lacked a sham control group, so placebo effects cannot be excluded, and follow-up was limited to one month.

trial_rating.result_basis: FSS improved by a mean of 5.984 points from baseline to post-treatment (p_bonf<0.001) in both groups combined, but the time-by-group interaction was non-significant (F=1.784, p=0.172), meaning no significant difference between the two active arms; no sham group prevents attribution of effect size to active stimulation.

summary: This pilot randomized controlled trial tested high-dose versus low-dose transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) worn daily for 4 weeks in 25 long-COVID patients experiencing chronic widespread pain, fatigue, and gait impairment resembling fibromyalgia. High-dose TENS produced a significantly greater reduction in pain interference scores (BPI-I mean difference = 2.61 points, p = 0.008, Cohen's d = 1.12) compared to low-dose TENS, and improved gait measures including cadence (5.6–9.5% depending on task) and stride time (4–8%) from baseline. Among the subset of 5 participants meeting formal fibromyalgia criteria, high-dose TENS also significantly improved fatigue scores (GFI improvement of 6.08 points, p = 0.005). The trial was small, unblinded at 4 weeks with high subsequent dropout, and the intervention group had lower baseline pain severity than controls, limiting interpretation of the between-group comparison.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome BPI-I between-group mean difference = 2.61 points favouring high-dose TENS, p = 0.008, Cohen's d = 1.12.

summary: This RCT tested a brief 'awe intervention' — four weekly one-hour online sessions teaching long COVID patients to deliberately notice and cultivate moments of awe in daily life — against a waitlist control group in 68 US adults meeting CDC long COVID criteria. The primary outcomes were stress, anxiety, depression, and well-being; the awe group showed significant reductions in depression symptoms (17% decrease vs. 2% increase in controls, d=0.96), stress (12% decrease vs. 2% increase, d=0.78), and a 16% increase in well-being, all with medium-to-large effect sizes. Anxiety did not improve significantly. The trial is small (N=30 intervention, N=38 control), used a waitlist rather than active control, and was conducted at a single time point in April 2023, limiting generalisability and ruling out placebo effects.

trial_rating.result_basis: Depression symptoms decreased by 17% in the awe group vs. +2% in controls (t(62.73)=-3.15, p=0.002, d=0.96); well-being increased 16% vs. -8% (t(61.91)=3.88, p<0.001, d=0.96); stress decreased 12% vs. +2% (t(65.82)=-3.34, p=0.001, d=0.78).

summary: This 10-week randomized controlled trial tested a symptom-titrated, individualized concurrent resistance and aerobic exercise program in 118 adults with post-COVID condition who had persistent fatigue (at least 12 weeks) and were largely inactive. Training load was adjusted before each session based on daily fatigue scores, with exercise contraindicated on days of maximum fatigue. Fatigue severity (the primary outcome, measured by the Fatigue Severity Scale) improved significantly more in the exercise group than the control group: from 5.67 to 4.51 vs. 5.49 to 5.29, a between-group difference of 0.93 points (p<0.001). The exercise group also showed significant improvements in handgrip strength, endurance capacity, and both mental and physical quality of life; no worsening of post-exertional malaise was recorded, though dropout was substantial at 34.8% in the intervention arm.

summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial tested heat-treated Lacticaseibacillus paracasei PS23 (HT-PS23, 20 billion cells/day for 6 weeks) in 31 adults (mean age 23) with long COVID symptoms persisting at least 2 months after confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection. The trial had no single pre-specified primary outcome; across multiple secondary endpoints, HT-PS23 produced statistically significant reductions in blood cortisol (p=0.006), executive function errors on the Color Trails Test 2 (p=0.018), self-reported breathing difficulty (p=0.016), and appetite loss (p=0.030) compared to placebo, while measures of depression, anxiety, sleep, quality of life, and inflammatory blood markers did not differ significantly between groups. The intervention was well-tolerated with no adverse events reported, but the small sample (14 vs 17 completers), young homogeneous population, lack of a single primary outcome, and multiple comparisons substantially limit the conclusions that can be drawn.

summary: This small exploratory randomised controlled trial tested leronlimab, a monoclonal antibody that blocks the CCR5 immune receptor, versus saline placebo in 55 adults with long COVID, administered weekly by subcutaneous injection for 8 weeks. The primary outcome — composite symptom score change from baseline — did not reach statistical significance: leronlimab reduced scores by -16.0 points versus -12.0 for placebo, with an adjusted mean difference of -1.0 (not significant). An exploratory finding showed that leronlimab-treated participants had significantly increased cell surface CCR5 expression by week 8 (p<0.0001), particularly among symptom responders, suggesting a possible immune downmodulation mechanism in some long COVID patients. The study was funded entirely by CytoDyn, the drug's manufacturer, and most authors report financial conflicts of interest, which substantially limits confidence in the interpretation of exploratory findings.

summary: This double-blind, sham-controlled pilot trial tested transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) applied to the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex — 2 mA for 20 minutes per day over 8 sessions — in 47 long COVID patients with chronic fatigue (average symptom duration ~21 months). The primary outcome, total fatigue score on the Modified Fatigue Impact Scale, did not show a statistically significant difference between active and sham stimulation groups; however, the physical fatigue subscale did improve significantly in the active group compared to sham, with a large effect size (Cohen's d = 1.032 at end of treatment). Adverse events were mild, transient, and equally distributed between groups, but the null result on the primary endpoint and the small pilot sample size mean these findings should be treated as preliminary.

summary: This pilot randomized controlled trial tested a 12-week home-based asynchronous telerehabilitation program (delivered via smartphone app with exercise videos and therapeutic education) versus a booklet-based rehabilitation program in 35 adults recently discharged from hospital after COVID-19, average age 58, with significant fatigue and psychological distress. summary: This small crossover trial tested a CBD-rich, full-spectrum hemp oil (Formula C, containing 40.7 mg/mL CBD plus terpenes) against a placebo in 31 adults with post-acute COVID-19 syndrome (long COVID), with 24 completing the study. The active treatment group showed statistically significant improvements in dyspnea (p=0.013), anxiety (p=0.006), and sleep disturbance (p=0.041) after 28 days; however, the placebo group also improved across most outcomes because the placebo (hempseed oil) was found to contain unexpected therapeutic concentrations of terpenes, eliminating the validity of the control arm. The trial is effectively uninterpretable as a placebo-controlled study, and its conclusions are further limited by small sample size, single-blind design, and the fact that it was funded by and included equity holders from the product manufacturer.

trial_rating.result_basis: Active group reached significance for anxiety (p=0.006), dyspnea (p=0.013), and sleep disturbance (p=0.041) at day 28, but the placebo arm showed similar improvements and was confirmed to contain therapeutic terpene levels, invalidating the control comparison; between-group differences were not statistically significant.

summary: This Belgian randomized controlled trial tested two brief psychoeducational interventions — one targeting cognitive strategies (metacognition, compensatory techniques) and one targeting affective symptoms (stress management, behavioural activation, CBT techniques) — in 122 long COVID patients with documented cognitive complaints and objective cognitive deficits. Both interventions consisted of four 90-minute in-person sessions; the primary outcome was subjective cognitive complaints at 2 months post-intervention. Both groups showed statistically significant reductions in executive/attention complaints (BRIEF-A) and memory complaints (MMQ) over time, but the cognitive intervention was not superior to the affective intervention — there was no group-by-time interaction for either primary outcome. Improvements were modest (small-to-moderate effect sizes), and despite gains, the majority of patients remained above clinical thresholds for fatigue (85%), sleep difficulties (79%), and psychological distress (56%) at follow-up, indicating limited clinical meaningfulness from a brief 6-hour intervention.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome group-by-time interaction for BRIEF-A: F=0.2, p=0.68; for MMQ composite: F=0.03, p=0.85 — no significant difference between cognitive and affective intervention arms, the pre-specified comparison.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested intermittent hypoxic-hyperoxic training (IHHT) — alternating low-oxygen and high-oxygen breathing sessions — added to standard inpatient rehabilitation in 145 post-COVID patients at a single German rehabilitation clinic. The primary outcome, six-minute walk distance, improved by 91.7 metres in the IHHT group versus 32.5 metres in controls (p<0.001), a difference of approximately 59 metres that exceeds the accepted minimal clinically important difference for the 6MWT. Secondary outcomes all favoured IHHT, including quality of life (EQ5D change +31.3 vs +2.9), fatigue (FAS change -8.9 vs +3.6), and stair climbing time (-1.9 vs -0.5 seconds), with no safety concerns reported.

Dichotomous outcome denominators inferred from text-stated missing data counts and may differ slightly by outcome. summary: This randomized controlled trial tested a 17-week cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) program called 'Fit after COVID' against care as usual (CAU) in 114 adults with severe fatigue 3-12 months after confirmed COVID-19, the majority of whom had not been hospitalized. CBT significantly reduced fatigue severity compared to CAU, with an overall mean difference of -8.8 points on the CIS-fatigue scale (95% CI: -11.9 to -5.8, p<0.001), representing a medium effect size (Cohen's d=0.69), and this benefit was sustained at 6-month follow-up. At post-treatment, 59% of CBT patients were no longer severely fatigued versus 26% in CAU; CBT also improved physical functioning, social functioning, somatic symptoms, and concentration. The sample was predominantly self-referred, which may limit generalizability to broader clinical populations.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome CIS-fatigue mean difference CBT vs CAU: -8.8 points (95% CI -11.9 to -5.8, p<0.001), Cohen's d=0.69 (medium effect size), sustained at both T1 (-9.3 points) and T2 (-8.4 points).

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested an 8-week supervised cardiopulmonary rehabilitation programme — combining aerobic exercise, resistance training, and respiratory exercises three times per week — in 40 adults (mean age 53) with long COVID who had persistent breathlessness or fatigue. The primary cognitive outcome showed no significant difference between the rehabilitation and control groups on any neuropsychological measure, including executive function, memory, and processing speed. However, the rehabilitation group showed significant reductions in perceived stress (PSS adjusted mean change: −2.46 vs. +3.26 in controls, p=0.002) and depression symptoms (GDS adjusted mean change: −2.39 vs. +2.68 in controls, p=0.015). The trial was underpowered for cognitive outcomes as sample size was calculated for a cardiorespiratory primary outcome, and the study was conducted at a single centre with only 32 participants completing the protocol.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary cognitive outcomes showed no significant group differences on any neuropsychological composite score (all ANCOVA p-values ranged from p=0.17 to p=0.65); secondary psychological outcomes were significant but were not the pre-specified primary endpoint.

summary: A 3-month cardiopulmonary rehabilitation program was tested in 30 convalescent COVID-19 patients, compared to 10 who received no rehabilitation, to assess recovery of right ventricular function and right ventricular-pulmonary artery coupling. Patients who completed rehabilitation showed significant improvements in right ventricular global longitudinal strain (RVGLS: -23.1% to -24.3%, p<0.001), pulmonary artery systolic pressure (28 to 27 mmHg, p=0.016), and right ventricular-arterial coupling (-0.86 to -0.93 %/mmHg, p<0.001), while the control group showed no significant change in any of these measures. The control group was very small (n=10) and patients were not randomised, limiting confidence in the findings.

summary: A 3-month cardiopulmonary rehabilitation program was tested in 60 patients one month after recovery from acute COVID-19, randomized equally to rehabilitation or no intervention. Arterial stiffness (carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity) improved significantly in the rehabilitation group (8.2 to 6.6 m/s, p<0.001) but not in controls (8.9 to 8.8 m/s, p=0.74), and left ventricular global longitudinal strain also improved only in the rehabilitation group (-19.6% to -21.3%, p<0.001). Patients with lower baseline inflammation (IL-1β below 8.4 pg/ml) showed greater benefit in ventricular-arterial coupling improvement than those with higher inflammation (0.14 vs 0.09 m/s%, p=0.04).

summary: This randomised controlled trial tested a 4-week, twice-weekly pulmonary telerehabilitation (PTR) program delivered via videoconference against usual medical care in 50 adults with persistent respiratory symptoms after COVID-19 (mostly non-hospitalised, average age 54). The primary outcome was the 1-minute sit-to-stand test: the PTR group improved by 2.1 repetitions versus 1.3 in the control group, a between-group difference of only 0.8 repetitions (95% CI -3.0 to 4.6, p=0.563), which was not statistically significant. No secondary outcomes — including fatigue, anxiety, depression, cognitive function, or quality of life — showed significant between-group differences, leading the authors to conclude that longer programs or alternative interventions should be evaluated.

summary: This randomised controlled trial tested whether a 3-month course of supervised endurance training rehabilitation (ETR, two one-hour sessions per week) reduced breathlessness in 60 adults who had been mechanically ventilated for COVID-19-related acute respiratory distress syndrome and remained dyspnoeic at least 3 months after ICU discharge, compared to standard physiotherapy (SP). trial_rating.result_basis: Primary MDP total score: ETR 26.2 vs SP 44.8 at 90 days; mean difference -18.6 (95% CI -27.8 to -9.4), p<0.0001.

summary: This pilot randomized controlled trial tested whether adding a weekly evidence-based eHealth education tool (six one-hour telehealth sessions covering COVID-19 pathology, pain neuroscience, breathing exercises, and self-management) to a six-week in-person pulmonary rehabilitation program improved outcomes in 12 post-COVID-19 patients with musculoskeletal symptoms. The only statistically significant between-group difference was in kinesiophobia (fear of movement), with the eHealth group scoring lower on the Tampa Scale of Kinesiophobia-11 after treatment (16.0 vs 23.2 points, p=0.048, effect size R=0.812). No significant differences were found between groups in pain scores, functional independence (Barthel index), or six-minute walk test distance. The trial is severely underpowered with only six participants per arm, limiting the reliability of all findings.

VSL#3 produced a statistically significant reduction in fatigue on the Chalder Fatigue Scale compared to placebo (-24% median change vs -4.4%, p=0.0079), with the benefit persisting 4 weeks after treatment ended; overall gastrointestinal symptoms also improved (SAGIS total -22.84% vs 0%, p=0.043). summary: This feasibility randomised controlled trial tested the Long COVID Optimal Health Programme (LC-OHP), a structured psychoeducational self-management intervention delivered in 6+ weekly one-on-one sessions, in 60 UK adults diagnosed with long COVID, comparing it to usual care over 6 months. As a feasibility study, the primary outcomes were recruitment and retention rates rather than clinical efficacy: the trial successfully recruited its target of 60 participants within 9 months, achieved an 83% overall completion rate, and 68% of intervention participants completed all sessions. Trends in secondary outcomes (depression, anxiety, fatigue, quality of life, and self-efficacy) favoured the LC-OHP group at both 3 and 6 months, but no inferential statistics were reported for between-group comparisons, and the control group also showed some improvements, making it impossible to draw conclusions about efficacy.

trial_rating.result_basis: No between-group p-values or effect sizes reported for clinical outcomes; the intervention group showed directional improvement across all outcomes at 3 and 6 months, but this was a feasibility trial with N=28 intervention and N=32 control, and descriptive trends only were presented.

summary: This randomized trial tested Qingjin Yiqi granules (QJYQ), a 16-herb traditional Chinese medicine formula, added to standard rehabilitation (respiratory training and Baduanjin exercise) versus standard rehabilitation alone in 388 adults recovering from COVID-19 in China. Over 14 days, patients receiving QJYQ showed statistically significant improvements in breathlessness (mMRC scale: β = −0.626, p = 0.010) and perceived fatigue (Borg scale: β = −0.395, p = 0.026) compared to controls, though overall symptom scores and 6-minute walking distance did not differ between groups. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a health economic evaluation paper (cost-utility analysis) accompanying the LISTEN RCT clinical paper. It does not report the full clinical outcomes data (e.g., fatigue, cognitive, other secondary outcomes from the main trial); those are reported in a separate clinical paper (reference 19 in this paper). The Ox-PAQ usual care arm 95% CI was not extractable from the garbled Table 5; mean of 52.17 was recovered. Table 3 had significant cell-merging and parsing difficulties; values reconstructed from text and table context. SDs are not reported for any outcome measure — only 95% CIs are available. The median age of 50 years and demographic proportions (72% female, 92% white) are reported for the overall sample only, not per arm. ICER (NHS/PSS) = £95,304/QALY gained; ICER (routine setting scenario) = £26,058/QALY gained; societal perspective: LISTEN dominates usual care. NMB at £20,000/QALY: -£378 (NHS/PSS), +£1,058 (societal). Probability cost-effective at £20,000: 3.99% (NHS/PSS), 95.40% (societal). Intervention cost: £846/participant (n=237 who received ≥1 session). Omitted from outcomes due to space: medication costs, tests costs, private healthcare costs, travel costs (all extractable from Table 2 with same structure as outcomes 7-10 above).

summary: The LISTEN trial tested a personalised self-management support intervention — up to six one-to-one sessions with a trained practitioner plus a co-designed handbook — in 544 non-hospitalised adults with long COVID symptoms lasting 12 weeks or more, recruited across 16 NHS and non-NHS sites in England and Wales. The primary health economic outcome was quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) over 3 months: participants in the LISTEN group gained a mean of 0.005 more QALYs than usual care (95% CI -0.004 to 0.014), a non-significant difference equivalent to roughly 11 additional hours of full health. From an NHS/PSS perspective the intervention cost £491 more per participant and was not cost-effective (ICER £95,304/QALY; only 4% probability of cost-effectiveness at the £20,000 threshold), but from a societal perspective — accounting for lost work, informal care, and out-of-pocket costs — the intervention dominated usual care, with a 95% probability of cost-effectiveness at £20,000/QALY.

trial_rating.result_basis: Adjusted mean QALY difference 0.005 (95% CI -0.004 to 0.014), crossing zero; ICER £95,304/QALY from NHS/PSS perspective with 3.99% probability of cost-effectiveness at £20,000 threshold.

summary: This pilot feasibility trial tested an 8-week personalised health behaviour support programme — comprising weekly one-to-one remote coaching sessions and daily physical activity and symptom diaries — in 32 adults with post-COVID syndrome (symptoms persisting ≥12 weeks). The primary outcome was feasibility of recruitment and randomisation, which was met: 67% of those screened were eligible and all 32 consented participants accepted randomisation, with 84% completing follow-up. Preliminary secondary data showed the intervention group gained 1,240 more steps/day than usual care (95% CI: 555–1,926) and reduced respiratory symptom scores (CAT) by 4 points more than controls, though the trial was not powered to confirm efficacy. No adverse events or symptom exacerbations were reported.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome was feasibility (not efficacy); the trial was explicitly underpowered for clinical endpoints. The between-group step count difference was +1,240 steps/day (95% CI: 555–1,926) but no inferential statistics were reported for this as a primary endpoint, and the study was a 32-participant pilot with no formal hypothesis test on clinical outcomes.
