summary: This Romanian RCT tested whether adding daily 20-minute progressive muscle relaxation (PMR) sessions to a standard 21-day pulmonary rehabilitation (PR) program improved outcomes in 61 long COVID patients (aged 54–74) with persistent dyspnea and fatigue. The primary finding was that the PR+PMR group showed significantly greater improvements in mental health, anxiety, and sleep quality compared to PR alone: GAD-7 anxiety scores dropped by approximately 5 points (to a mean of 4.96 vs. 8.23 in the PR-only group, p<0.001), and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index scores fell by 4.74 points (median 4 vs. 7, p<0.001), crossing the threshold from poor to good sleep quality. Exercise capacity (6-minute walk test) improved in both groups but did not differ significantly between them (366.60 m vs. 391.54 m, p=0.171). The study is limited by its small sample, short 21-day follow-up with no post-intervention monitoring, and a predominantly older male population from a single centre.

trial_rating.result_basis: GAD-7 post-intervention: PR+PMR group mean 4.96 vs. PR-only mean 8.23 (p<0.001); PSQI median 4 vs. 7 (p<0.001); PSQI reduction of 4.74 points exceeds the 3-point MCID threshold.

Per-arm means and SDs are also not reported for HADS, GAD-7, or PHQ-9 continuous scores — only Cohen's d effect sizes within each group are reported. Between-group effect sizes (Cohen's d) are reported only as within-group comparisons, NOT as between-group differences. No between-group p-values are reported for continuous outcomes except for HADS Anxiety binary outcome at 8 weeks (p<0.01, stated as '**'). Symptom duration reported as mean 51 (SD 27) weeks for rehabilitation group and 58 (SD 31) weeks for waiting list — converted to months as approximately 11.8 (SD 6.3) and 13.4 (SD 7.2) months respectively. The paper reports Cohen's d within the rehabilitation group for SF-36 outcomes (8 weeks): physical functioning=0.5, role physical=0.4, bodily pain=0.5, vitality=0.7, social functioning=0.6, role emotional=0.3, mental health=0.9, PCS=0.3, MCS=0.7. At 6 months: physical functioning=0.6, role physical=0.5, bodily pain=0.4, vitality=0.6, social functioning=0.6, role emotional=0.3, mental health=0.9, PCS=0.4, MCS=0.6. Waiting list within-group Cohen's d (8 weeks): physical functioning=0.5, social functioning=0.4, mental health=0.4. At 6 months: physical functioning=0.6, vitality=0.6, mental health=0.8. HADS within-group Cohen's d (TR): anxiety d=0.4 (p<0.01) at 8 weeks, d=0.6-0.7 (p<0.001) at 6 months; depression d=0.6-0.7 (p<0.001) at 8 weeks, 6 months. WL: depression only d=0.5-0.6 at 8 weeks (p<0.01) and 6 months (p<0.05). GAD-7 within-group TR: d=0.4 (p<0.01) at 8 weeks, d=0.3 (p<0.05) at 6 months; WL no improvement. PHQ-9 within-group TR: d=0.8 (p<0.001) at 8 weeks, d=0.5 (p<0.001) at 6 months; WL: d=0.6 (p<0.05) at 6 months only. ICF pain-related b-categories data presented only in Figure 3 as percentages — no extractable numeric means/SDs. SF-36 General Health showed no significant improvement in either group. summary: An 8-week multidisciplinary telerehabilitation programme delivered via Microsoft Teams was tested in 67 adults with long COVID (mean age 43, 78% women) who had persistent symptoms for at least 12 weeks after mild SARS-CoV-2 infection, compared against 42 people on a waiting list. summary: This Phase II feasibility trial tested heart rate variability biofeedback (HRV-BF) — 10 sessions over 5 weeks using the HeartMath emWave system — added to standard care (analgesics and antidepressants) versus standard care alone in 18 adults with long COVID who met diagnostic criteria for CFS/ME. summary: This randomized controlled trial tested an 8-week gym-based resistance training program (twice weekly, 70% of 1-repetition maximum, seven machine exercises) in 46 adults aged 65 and older with long COVID symptoms including muscle weakness and exercise intolerance. The primary functional outcome was the Chair Stand Test: the intervention group significantly improved both speed (5-repetition sit-to-stand improved from ~9.1s to 6.7s in men and 8.8s to 7.0s in women) and number of repetitions in 30 seconds (men: 15 to 24; women: 18 to 25), while the control group showed no change. Isometric strength improved significantly across most muscle groups in both sexes, with the largest gains in trunk extensors (~22% in men, ~23% in women); however, isokinetic torque improvements did not reach significance for the group-by-session interaction. The program was safe and well-tolerated, with a 93% average attendance rate and only two dropouts due to unrelated musculoskeletal pain.

summary: A single 45-minute session of osteopathic manipulative treatment (OMT) was tested against a sham treatment in 42 long COVID patients (mean age 51 years) with persistent fatigue lasting at least 12 weeks. The primary outcome was heart rate variability (HRV); immediately after OMT, RMSSD increased from 17.8 ms to 21.6 ms (Hedges' g = 0.82), SDNN rose from 19.6 ms to 26.0 ms (g = 0.80), mean heart rate dropped from 67.3 to 62.3 bpm (g = -1.10), and the Baevsky stress index fell significantly — all indicating a short-term shift toward parasympathetic dominance. These gains fully reversed within 48 hours, and no long-term or clinically meaningful benefit was demonstrated from a single session.

trial_rating.result_basis: RMSSD increased from 17.8 ms to 21.6 ms immediately post-treatment (Hedges' g = 0.82, 95% CI [0.19, 1.40], p < 0.01), but returned to baseline by 48-hour follow-up (17.4 ms), indicating only a transient effect with no sustained benefit.

No explicit reporting of dropouts or missing data; all enrolled patients appear to have completed assessments, but no CONSORT-style flow data for attrition is reported.
Objective outcomes (CPET, 6MWT, muscle strength) are well-standardized. Patient-reported outcomes (FACIT, mMRC, CAT, HADS) are validated instruments, but assessors were not described as blinded.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1) This is a non-randomized quasi-experimental study (propensity-matched), not a true RCT; allocation to PR vs UC was based on patients' ability to attend supervised sessions. 2) Per-arm baseline and endpoint values for 6MWT, quadriceps force, handgrip strength, SPPB, and 60s sit-to-stand were reported only as change scores or in figures without explicit per-arm pre/post means+SDs in tabular form — 6MWT, QF, and handgrip extracted as change_from_baseline only. 3) WRpeak SD for change from baseline listed in abstract as 10W (PR group: +19±10W); Table 2 shows pre 94±46 and post 113±50, consistent. Abstract also states 19±10W change. 4) VE and Vt in Table 2 show slight discrepancy with Table 3 (peak pre values): VE 56.7 vs 55.2 and Vt 1.63 vs 1.587 — likely rounding or slightly different subsets; both extracted as reported. 5) HR in Table 2: PR group pre 127±19 (Table 2) vs 127±18 (Table 3) — minor rounding, both extracted. 6) SPPB total score and components (balance score, 4m walk test, 5-rep sit-to-stand) data appear only in Figure 3 without tabular values — not extracted numerically. 7) The p-values reported as 0.001 in text are likely p<0.001 displayed as exact; flagged as p_value_exact=false where stated as 0.001 throughout. 8) Omitted from detailed extraction (data in figures only): SPPB total score and individual components. 9) WR%predicted and VO2%predicted extracted in Table 2 but not separately included as outcome objects to manage JSON size; key data: PR pre WR%pred=70±26, post=86±29; UC pre=75±29, post=78±30; PR pre VO2%pred=66±17, post=75±18; UC pre=65±20, post=62±19.

summary: A 12-week hybrid pulmonary rehabilitation (PR) programme — comprising 8 supervised outpatient sessions followed by 24 home-based walking sessions — was tested in 27 previously hospitalised long COVID patients (mean age 57, average 140 days post-discharge) with severe fatigue, compared to 15 usual care controls. Peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak) increased by 2.4 mL/kg/min (15%) and peak work rate by 19 watts (20%) in the PR group, with no improvement in either measure in the usual care group; 6-minute walk distance also improved by 72 metres, exceeding the minimum clinically important difference. The study was non-randomised and underpowered relative to its own sample size calculation, which limits the strength of conclusions.

trial_rating.result_basis: VO2peak improved by 2.4 mL/kg/min in the PR group vs no change in usual care (p=0.001); peak work rate improved by 19 watts (p=0.001); 6MWT improved by 72 metres (p=0.001).

Baseline per-arm means and SDs for outcome measures are NOT reported in text or tables — only in figures. The p-values stated for MFIS physical (p<0.001) and psychosocial (p<0.001) in the abstract appear to refer to post-intervention between-group comparisons, not the ANOVA interaction (which shows p=0.187 and p=0.014 respectively); this inconsistency is noted. summary: A 12-week supervised plank-based core stabilisation program (MORETA methodology, 2 sessions/week) was tested in 39 women with long COVID (mean symptom duration ~20 months) in a non-randomised pilot trial in Madrid. The primary outcomes were fatigue (Modified Fatigue Impact Scale, MFIS) and health-related quality of life (EQ-5D-5L and EQ-VAS): the intervention group improved physical fatigue domain scores by 39.1% vs 16.7% in controls, and EQ-VAS self-rated health by 19.6% vs 1.1% in controls, with a statistically significant group-by-time interaction for EQ-VAS (F=4.347, p=0.046) and psychosocial fatigue domain (p=0.014), though the total MFIS interaction was not significant; no post-exertional symptom exacerbation was reported. The non-randomised design with self-selected group allocation and small sample size (n=20 intervention, n=19 control) introduce substantial risk of selection bias, limiting causal inference.

trial_rating.result_basis: EQ-VAS group×time interaction F=4.347, p=0.046 (intervention +19.6% vs control +1.1%); psychosocial MFIS interaction p=0.014; total MFIS group×time interaction p=0.551 (non-significant).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a quasi-experimental before-after study, not an RCT; there is no randomization and the two groups (COVID-19 patients vs. healthy controls) are not randomized comparators but rather separate cohorts each serving as their own pre-post controls. Between-group effect sizes in this extraction reflect pre-vs-post within-arm differences (paired comparisons), not between-arm comparisons, as that is the primary analysis structure used. The study reports only acute effects from a single 20-minute scTS session assessed 15 minutes post-intervention; there is no extended follow-up. FVC % predicted values are reported per individual in Table 1 (mean 68±3% predicted). Blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen saturation, and VAS pain were monitored as safety measures but no numeric results were reported for these. Time since infection reported as 59±48 days (mean±SD); converted to months as 1.97±1.60 months. All spirometry data (PIF, PEF, tPIF, tPEF, FVC) are reported as mean±SD in text; no figures-only data were extracted.

summary: A single 20-minute session of transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation (scTS) applied over the T5 and T10 thoracic spinal segments was tested in 10 adults with post-acute COVID-19 respiratory deficits (mean age 55, all with FVC around 68% predicted). Peak inspiratory flow increased from 94 to 134 L/min (p=0.040) and peak expiratory flow increased from 88 to 109 L/min (p=0.049) immediately after stimulation, with faster time-to-peak for both measures, indicating improved neuromuscular activation of respiratory muscles. Total lung capacity (FVC) was unchanged, suggesting the effect is neural rather than structural. The study is very small, unblinded, uncontrolled, and used a single session design with unmatched healthy controls, so results are exploratory only.

trial_rating.result_basis: PIF increased from 93.99 to 133.67 L/min (p=0.040) and PEF from 87.84 to 108.85 L/min (p=0.049) in n=10 patients with no control arm for the COVID group.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested a four-week neuro-meditation program (Rebalance®, combining sound therapy, coach-guided meditation, and light stimulation) in 34 long COVID patients with confirmed cognitive and psychological impairment. The intervention group (n=17) completed ten 30-minute sessions and showed significantly faster reaction times on three cognitive tasks compared to the untreated control group: choice reaction time improved by 12.1% (593ms to 521ms, p<0.001), pattern comparison by 13.3% (1244ms to 1079ms, p<0.001), and Simon task by 8.4% (539ms to 494ms, p<0.01). Subjective measures also improved significantly, including large reductions in physical fatigue (-13 points), mental fatigue (-7.7 points), depression (-5.2 points), and anxiety (-3.6 points), all p<0.001; however, the study is small (17 per arm), lacked a placebo or active control, and the Rebalance® device is a commercial product of an institution connected to the authors.

trial_rating.result_basis: Choice reaction time: 593ms baseline vs 521ms post-intervention (p<0.001); physical fatigue reduced by 13.0 points vs -0.6 in controls (p<0.001); n=17 per arm.

summary: This single-blind randomized controlled trial tested twice-daily oral supplementation of 1.66 g L-arginine plus 500 mg liposomal vitamin C against placebo for 28 days in 46 adults (median age 51, 65% women) with long COVID and persistent fatigue. The primary outcome, 6-minute walk test distance, improved by a median of 30 m in the treatment group versus 0 m in the placebo group (mean difference 50 m, 95% CI 20–80 m, p=0.001), exceeding the 35 m minimal clinically important difference threshold. Secondary outcomes also favored the supplement: handgrip strength increased by 3.4 kg versus 1.0 kg (p=0.03), flow-mediated dilation reached 14.3% versus 9.4% (p=0.03), and fatigue persisted in only 9% of the treatment group versus 80% of the placebo group at day 28. The trial was small (23 per arm, single center) and single-blind rather than double-blind, limiting the strength of conclusions.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6-minute walk distance improved by median 30 m (treatment) vs 0 m (placebo), mean difference 50 m, 95% CI 20–80 m, p=0.001, exceeding the 35 m minimal clinically important difference.

summary: This randomised trial tested whether 1-methylnicotinamide (1-MNA), a niacin metabolite with anti-inflammatory and antithrombotic properties, could improve exercise tolerance and fatigue in 50 non-hospitalised adults with persistent post-COVID-19 symptoms. After one month of daily 58 mg 1-MNA supplementation, participants in the treatment group walked a mean of 42 m further in the 6-minute walk test compared to a 13 m improvement in the unsupplemented control group (p=0.0016), and 92% of treated patients improved versus 60% of controls. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This study is NOT an RCT; it is an open-label two-cohort observational study where both cohorts (PCIBS n=16 and IBS-control n=28) received the same intervention (Curcuma + Boswellia + low-FODMAP diet). The 'arm_id=1' is the long COVID (PCIBS) group and 'arm_id=2' is the IBS-without-COVID control group. There is no placebo or untreated control arm. Between-group effect direction convention: control minus PCIBS (arm2 minus arm1) as reported in Table 2. The 'n_lost_to_followup' for PCIBS arm represents screened (28) minus completed (16)=12 excluded at screening; similarly control screened 35 minus completed 28=7 excluded at screening — these are screening exclusions, not post-enrollment dropouts. GAE data: PCIBS — grade 1: n=1 (6.3%), grade 2: n=2 (12.5%), grade 3: n=8 (50.0%), grade 4: n=5 (31.3%); Control — grade 1: n=0 (0%), grade 2: n=2 (7.1%), grade 3: n=9 (32.1%), grade 4: n=17 (60.7%). Grade ≥3 response: PCIBS 81.3%, Control 92.8%, p>0.05. Table 2 CI for abdominal pain in PCIBS: lower bound listed as '-5.593' and '-5.008' in the extracted table — based on the table structure, PCIBS delta change CI 95% is (-7.560; -5.008) and Control delta change CI 95% is (-7.511; -5.593). The between-group difference for pain CI is (-1.879; 1.373). Adverse events reported as 'No adverse effects related to the supplementation were reported during the study' — applies to all participants combined, not broken down per arm.

summary: This pilot study tested 30 days of supplementation with lecithin-based formulations of Curcuma longa (500 mg twice daily) and Boswellia serrata (150 mg twice daily), combined with a low-FODMAP diet, in 16 adults with post-COVID-19 irritable bowel syndrome (IBS-like symptoms 60–120 days after infection) compared to 28 adults with IBS who had no prior COVID-19 infection. Both groups showed statistically significant reductions in abdominal bloating (the primary outcome), but the effect was smaller in the post-COVID group (score change: −1.950) than in the IBS-only group (−2.850), with the between-group difference reaching significance (p=0.001). A key caveat is that gut dysbiosis, measured by urinary indican, improved significantly only in the IBS-only group (−36.2 units) and not in the post-COVID group (+7.9 units, i.e., no improvement), suggesting that post-COVID dysbiosis may require different treatment strategies; the study had no placebo arm, was open-label, and enrolled very small numbers.

trial_rating.result_basis: Abdominal bloating (primary outcome) decreased significantly within the post-COVID group (intra-group Δ −1.950, CI95% −2.238 to −1.662), but the between-cohort comparison showed the post-COVID group improved less than the IBS-only group (difference −0.899, CI95% −1.270 to −0.528, p=0.001); no placebo control was included.

summary: This pilot randomized controlled trial tested whether drinking hydrogen-rich water (HRW, 500 mL twice daily for 14 days) reduced fatigue and breathlessness in 32 long COVID patients with self-reported fatigue and dyspnea. The primary fatigue outcome (Fatigue Severity Scale) showed a significantly greater percent reduction in the HRW group compared to placebo (p=0.046, Cohen's d=0.696), and HRW also improved six-minute walk distance, chair stand test performance, and sleep quality. However, dyspnea scores (mMRC) did not improve significantly with HRW versus placebo (p=0.556), and no improvements in mood or anxiety were detected.

trial_rating.result_basis: FSS percent change was significantly greater in HRW vs placebo (p=0.046, 95% CI -20.607 to -0.198, d=0.696), but this was a secondary percent-change analysis; the primary mixed-effects model showed no significant group effect (p=0.122) or interaction (p=0.184), and the primary dyspnea outcome was null (p=0.556).

summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial tested a five-strain probiotic (OMNi-BiOTiC Pro-Vi 5, taken twice daily for six months) in 21 adults who had experienced severe COVID-19 roughly 10 months earlier, comparing them to 10 mild-disease controls. The probiotic significantly increased gut microbial richness at 3 months (p=0.047) and 6 months (p=0.014), reduced fatigue scores on the ARTIQ questionnaire at 3 months (p=0.014), improved psychological burden (p=0.022), increased stool butyrate at 6 months, and reduced neutrophil ROS production and CD4+ TEMRA cells at 3 months; however, increased intestinal permeability and the reorganization of Ruminococcaceae and Lachnospiraceae remained unaffected. The trial was small (8 probiotic completers vs 13 placebo) with a notable 38% dropout rate in the probiotic arm, making all findings preliminary and hypothesis-generating.

trial_rating.result_basis: Microbial richness improved in the probiotic group at 6 months (p=0.014); fatigue reduction at 3 months (p=0.014); these are secondary/exploratory endpoints and the trial was not powered for a single primary outcome, with only 8 completers in the probiotic arm.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. This is a 4-arm trial stratified by COVID severity (severe vs moderate), with a healthy donor control group (n=25, arm_id 5) that was not included in randomized arms as it received no intervention. 2. All cytokine biomarker data (IL-6, IL-8, IL-17A, IFN-gamma), nitrate/nitrite ratio, antioxidant activity (AOA), PMN ATP levels, and phagocytosis index quantitative data appear ONLY in figures (Figure 1, Figure 2, and referenced additional figures) with no tabulated numeric values extractable from text — these outcomes were noted as significant but numeric means/SDs were not reported in text. Outcomes omitted due to data-only-in-figures: IL-6, IL-8, IL-17A, IFN-gamma plasma levels, plasma nitrate/nitrite ratio, antioxidant activity, PMN ATP content, phagocytosis index (%), intracellular bacterial killing (%). 3. The Borg scale is labeled 1-10 but Group 3 baseline values (10.8) exceed this range — likely the scale used differs or values represent a different metric (possibly a modified Borg or dyspnea visual analogue scale); values extracted as reported verbatim. 4. Table 2 had extensive merged/duplicate rows with the same values appearing for multiple answer score levels (e.g., '2-great' and '1-moderate' rows show identical means); only one set of values per question item was extracted. 5. ECG data reported as counts at two time points (30-40 days and 50-60 days post-discharge), corresponding to baseline and end-of-trial respectively. 6. No primary outcome was designated; paper lacks trial registration. 7. Oral-nasal-pharyngeal microbiota data not tabulated quantitatively. 8. A 5th group (healthy donors, n=25) served as a normative reference and was not randomized; excluded from arm-level extraction. 9. The Borg score for severe COVID groups is presented such that improvement = score increases (counterintuitive direction); values extracted verbatim. Higher Borg score in this paper's context may indicate improved exercise tolerance rather than worse dyspnea — this is ambiguous from text; higher_is_better set to false as Borg score conventionally measures dyspnea/exertion.

summary: This randomized placebo-controlled trial tested daily oral supplementation with 28g of fermented Carica papaya and Morinda citrifolia syrups (BioRex Papaya and BioRex Noni) added to standard rehabilitation care in 188 adults recovering from moderate or severe COVID-19 (primarily the delta variant). After 20 days, patients receiving the fermented fruit supplements showed significantly greater reductions in plasma IL-6 and IL-8 levels, normalization of elevated nitrite/nitrate levels, improved immune cell function (phagocytosis restored toward normal range in severe COVID survivors), and greater improvement in self-reported symptoms including weakness, physical and mental working capacity, heart pain, arrhythmia, and tachycardia compared to placebo. The study has notable limitations: it was single-center with no pre-registration, blinding adequacy is unclear, several co-authors have commercial ties to the tested products, and the placebo (diluted honey water) may not have been inert.

trial_rating.result_basis: Total average symptom score decreased from 1.2±0.2 to 0.5±0.1 in FFS group vs 0.9±0.1 in placebo (severe COVID, p<0.05); IL-6 normalized in FFS groups vs remained significantly elevated in placebo groups (p<0.01); oxygen desaturation during 6-minute walk test occurred in 53.3% of FFS patients vs 71.4% of placebo patients.

summary: This 12-week open-label randomized controlled trial tested vitamin D replacement therapy guidance (25 µg daily vitamin D3 supplement plus dietary counseling, sun exposure, and exercise) versus alfacalcidol (active vitamin D preparation) alone in 85 adults with ME/CFS developing after COVID-19 infection or vaccination who had vitamin D insufficiency or deficiency (serum 25(OH)D <30 ng/mL). The intervention group reduced their ME/CFS symptom count by a mean of 6.7 symptoms versus 1.2 in the control group (between-group difference -5.6; 95% CI: -7.2 to -3.9; p<0.001), and 16 of 42 intervention participants versus 1 of 38 controls no longer met ME/CFS diagnostic criteria at 12 weeks. Key caveats are the open-label design (no blinding), 83.5% of participants enrolled from a single clinic, and the use of a simple symptom count rather than validated quality-of-life measures as the primary endpoint.

trial_rating.result_basis: Mean symptom reduction -6.7 (intervention) vs -1.2 (control), between-group difference -5.6 (95% CI: -7.2, -3.9; p<0.001); 38% of intervention participants vs 3% of controls no longer met ME/CFS diagnostic criteria.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. Baseline LC Research Index was reported as median (IQR): K2/D3 arm 11 (6,17) vs SOC 16 (8,22), p=0.01 — this significant baseline imbalance is a notable methodological concern. 2. For outcome 2 (binary LC index >=12), week-24 percentages were back-calculated from baseline percentages and reported directional changes: K2/D3 baseline 42.9% minus 7.1% = ~35.8%; SOC baseline 54.7% plus 7.2% = ~61.9% — these are approximate calculated values. 3. Between-group changes for oxLDL, sTNF-RI, sCD163, and BDG were reported as change-from-baseline in each arm with p-values but no formal between-group difference estimate or CI was provided in the text; p-values are from the longitudinal mixed models. 4. Longitudinal data at week 12 exists (visits at weeks 0, 12, 24) but no week-12 numeric values were reported for any outcome in text or tables. 5. Figure data (Figures 2, 3, 4) contain additional timepoint information but no extractable numeric values were provided; noted as 'data only in figures' for intermediate timepoints. 6. Total AE counts by severity grade (Grade 1=159, Grade 2=49, Grade 3=4, Grade 4=1) were reported for the combined sample but not broken down per arm. 7. HOMA-IR, LDL, HDL, non-HDL, triglycerides baseline data extracted but no statistically significant between-group changes were reported for these metabolic markers at follow-up beyond glucose. 8. The note about 19.2% vs 8.6% with 25(OH)D <20 ng/mL 'p=0.8' appears to be from Supplementary Table S1 which was not fully available.

summary: This 24-week randomized controlled trial tested daily supplementation with 2000 IU vitamin D3 and 240 µg vitamin K2 (MK-7 form) against standard of care in 151 adults with established long COVID (at least 2 moderate symptoms persisting 3+ months after confirmed infection). The vitamin K2/D3 group showed a 7.1% decrease in the proportion meeting the RECOVER Long COVID Research Index threshold of ≥12, compared to a 7.2% increase in the standard-of-care group (p=0.01); in adjusted models, the LC Research Index was 3.2 points lower in the treatment arm (p=0.04), and the treatment group had nearly 2 fewer total symptoms (-1.7, 95% CI -3.2 to -0.1, p=0.02). The trial lacked a placebo control, which is a meaningful limitation, though vitamin D levels rose only in the treatment arm, supporting adherence; no adverse events were attributed to the intervention.

trial_rating.result_basis: LC Research Index 3.2 points lower in K2/D3 arm vs SOC in adjusted model (p=0.04); total symptom count -1.7 (95% CI -3.2, -0.1, p=0.02); proportion with index ≥12 decreased 7.1% vs increased 7.2% in SOC (p=0.01).

Between-group p-values for mMRC, SpO2, and Adaptation Potential are reported as U=0 in the table (Mann-Whitney U=0 implies p very small but exact value not given beyond p<0.05); only FAS (p=0.0002) and Carlisle HR (p=0.0003) have explicit p-values for between-group comparison. The intergroup comparison rows show absolute difference in post-intervention means and percent improvement ratio relative to control group change — these are not standard effect sizes. Between-group mean differences for mMRC, SpO2, and AP were calculated from post-intervention means. summary: This trial tested individually dosed hypoxi-hyperoxic therapy (IDHHT), alternating cycles of low-oxygen (FiO2 ~11-13%) and high-oxygen (FiO2 ~35-40%) breathing using the Oxyterra device, added to a standard physical therapy programme in 40 middle-aged adults (45-59 years) with confirmed post-COVID syndrome. After 3 weeks, the IDHHT group showed significantly greater improvements than the physical-therapy-only control group across all measured outcomes: fatigue (FAS score) fell by 41.5% vs 25.1%, oxygen saturation rose by 3.3% vs 1.4%, dyspnea (mMRC) improved by 55.3% vs 34.0%, and cardiovascular adaptation potential improved by 23.7% vs 13.8%. No adverse effects were reported in the IDHHT group.

trial_rating.result_basis: FAS fatigue score decreased by 11.99 points (41.5%) in the IDHHT group vs 7.15 points (25.1%) in controls; between-group difference 4.84 points, p=0.0002 (Mann-Whitney U test).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. Most outcome data over time (severity scores for fatigue, headache, respiration problems, organoleptic disorders, hair loss, cough, pain, sweatiness, anxiety, depression, cognitive performance) are presented only in figures (Figures S1-S13 in Supplement 2) with no tabulated per-arm means and SDs at intermediate or final timepoints — only baseline values are in Table 1. Workout time data is similarly only in figures. The IL-6 end-of-study values (Day 21) for each arm were extracted from narrative text in the Discussion section (4.730±0.329 pg/mL for ADAPT-232 and 5.981±0.530 pg/mL for placebo), where ± appears to indicate SEM not SD. The workout (daily walk time) baseline values in Table 1 appear to use SEM not SD given the very small values (0.0628 and 0.0757). Note that baseline 'Physical activity (daily walk) min' values of 5.534 and 5.162 minutes appear unusually low and may represent log-transformed or differently scaled data. The p=0.0148 for workout interaction and p<0.0001 for between-group comparison are from figure captions only. Creatinine between-group p=0.0012 is from Figure 2 caption. Omitted from outcomes due to data only in figures: fatigue severity score over time, headache severity score, respiration severity score, organoleptic severity score, hair loss severity score, cough severity score, pain severity score, sweatiness severity score, HAM-A score change over time, HADS score change over time, d2 test change over time. summary: This randomized, quadruple-blind, placebo-controlled trial tested Chisan®/ADAPT-232 — an oral combination of Rhodiola, Eleutherococcus, and Schisandra extracts — in 100 adults with long COVID symptoms (mean age 49) who had been discharged from hospital, ICU, or isolation and had at least three persistent symptoms. The primary outcomes showed mixed results: ADAPT-232 reduced the duration of fatigue by one day and pain by two days in 50% of patients, with significantly fewer patients still experiencing pain on Day 9 (39% vs. 57%, p=0.0019) and fatigue on Day 11 (28% vs. 43%, p=0.0157), and it significantly increased daily workout time compared to placebo (p<0.0001); however, overall symptom severity scores did not significantly differ between groups for most measures. ADAPT-232 also significantly reduced blood creatinine compared to placebo (p=0.0012), suggesting a possible kidney-protective effect, though the study was small, funded by the manufacturer of the test product, and described by the authors as a pilot trial.

trial_rating.result_basis: Fewer patients had pain on Day 9 (39% ADAPT-232 vs. 57% placebo, p=0.0019) and fatigue on Day 11 (28% vs. 43%, p=0.0157); workout time difference p<0.0001; but overall symptom severity showed no significant between-group difference for most endpoints.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Paper is primarily in Russian with parallel English abstract. Age and sex per-arm breakdown not provided; only overall age range (43-68 years) stated. CRP units reported as mg/mL in the paper (likely mg/L clinically — extracted as stated). VAS for general health status: higher score = worse health (symptom severity scale), so higher_is_better=false. Between-group p-values reported only as p<0.05 threshold with symbols (* and #); no exact p-values given. HIF-1alpha between-group difference at endpoint was not statistically significant (p>0.05 stated). Calculated mean differences at endpoint: HIF-1alpha arm1-arm2 = 61.38-58.31 = 3.07 pg/mL; CRP arm1-arm2 = 2.39-5.23 = -2.84 mg/mL; VAS arm1-arm2 = 27.57-44.3 = -16.73 points. The paper states CRP decreased >2-fold in intervention group (p<0.05) and VAS decreased ~2-fold in intervention group (p<0.05), both significantly different from control group. No exact between-group effect sizes or CIs were provided. Unequal randomization (27:15) is not explained. Study duration described as 1 year (April 2021-May 2022) refers to enrollment period, not follow-up duration.

summary: This single-centre Russian RCT tested intermittent hypoxia-hyperoxia therapy (ReOxy) — 8–10 sessions alternating low-oxygen (12–15% FiO2) and high-oxygen (up to 40% FiO2) breathing, individually dosed via biofeedback — added to standard rehabilitation in 42 patients aged 43–68 with post-COVID syndrome plus osteoarthritis and hypertension. The primary outcome was change in C-reactive protein (CRP) and HIF-1α; CRP fell by more than 50% in the treatment group (from 5.82 to 2.39 mg/mL, p<0.05) versus only 21% in the placebo group, while self-reported wellbeing on a visual analogue scale halved in the treatment group compared to a 1.3-fold improvement in controls. HIF-1α rose 17% in the treatment group but this difference was not statistically significant, and no adverse events were recorded. The study is substantially limited by small sample sizes (n=27 active, n=15 placebo) and high within-group variability in HIF-1α, making the biomarker findings difficult to interpret.

trial_rating.result_basis: CRP decreased from 5.82±2.27 to 2.39±1.24 mg/mL in the treatment group (p<0.05 vs baseline and vs placebo), representing a >50% reduction; VAS wellbeing score fell from 54.33±14.56 to 27.57±5.07 (p<0.05 vs baseline and vs placebo).

SF-36 and ESS numeric data appear only in figures (Figures 1-4) — no tabular values reported; result_source set to not_reported for these outcomes. Neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, platelets, creatinine, eGFR, azotemia, and albuminuria from Table 1 are not extracted as separate outcome objects due to output size constraints — all were non-significant. summary: A double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial tested an oral food supplement (OFS) containing Echinacea angustifolia, rosehip, propolis, royal jelly, and zinc (2 capsules/day for 8 weeks) in 33 long COVID patients at a single Italian centre. The primary finding was a significant reduction in fatigue severity scale (FSS) scores during the OFS period compared to baseline (36 ± 6.06 vs. 25 ± 4.13, p=0.0001), alongside significant reductions in inflammatory markers CRP (p=0.0145), neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (p=0.0455), and monocyte-to-lymphocyte ratio (p=0.0005). The trial is limited by a very small sample size (n=33), a single centre, and the absence of monitored zinc and vitamin C serum levels during the study.

trial_rating.result_basis: FSS score decreased from 36 ± 6.06 to 25 ± 4.13 during the OFS period (p=0.0001), representing an 11-point reduction on a 9–63 scale.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested whether replacing 45 minutes of standard neurological rehabilitation with EMG-driven robotic upper-limb exercises (using the Luna EMG robot) produced better outcomes than 120 minutes of standard rehabilitation alone in 81 patients transferred from ICUs with post-COVID-19 fatigue syndrome. summary: This randomised open-label trial from Uzbekistan tested four rehabilitation programmes in 166 adults (average age 46) with neuropsychological symptoms of long COVID, including fatigue, sleep disturbance, anxiety, depression, cognitive impairment, and anosmia. The main group (n=46) received acupuncture combined with therapeutic exercise incorporating yoga elements and small-group psychotherapy; comparator groups received massage plus physiotherapy, acupuncture alone, or home exercise only. The combined acupuncture-plus-exercise group showed the largest improvements across all outcomes: the six-minute walk test distance increased by 18% (from ~364m to ~430m), dyspnoea on the Borg scale fell by 53%, depression severity on the HADS fell by 66.7%, and quality-of-life scores (EQ-5D) rose from ~57 to ~87 points (+53%), all significantly better than comparator groups (p<0.05). The study had no blinding, no placebo control, and outcomes were self-reported, which limits confidence in the findings.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested the addition of audiovisual stimulation (binaural brainwave entrainment shifting from beta to theta activity over 22-minute sessions) and cognitive behavioral therapy (5 sessions of 40 minutes each) to standard rehabilitation in 59 long COVID patients with emotional disturbances 1–6 months post-infection, mean age ~60 years. In the intervention group (n=29), anxiety and depression scores on the HADS improved significantly compared to the control group receiving standard rehabilitation alone, with 93.1% of treated patients showing no signs of anxiety or depression after treatment versus 64% in controls; situational anxiety on the Spielberger-Khanin scale dropped from a median of 46 to 42 points (p<0.001), and high-level situational anxiety was eliminated in all 21 patients who had it at baseline (p<0.001 between groups). trial_rating.result_basis: Situational anxiety median fell from 46 to 42 in the intervention group vs unchanged (45.5 to 45.5) in controls (p<0.001 between groups); 93.1% of intervention patients had no anxiety/depression post-treatment vs 64% in controls (p<0.05).

summary: This single-blind randomized controlled trial tested an 8-week calisthenics exercise program (jumping jacks, burpees, squats, planks, and related movements) in 176 adults with post-COVID syndrome, comparing therapist-supervised sessions against a home-based program. summary: This randomized controlled trial tested acupuncture added to a standard multi-modal rehabilitation program versus rehabilitation alone in 160 post-COVID-19 patients (average age 61, 76% women) hospitalized at a rehabilitation center in Kazakhstan. summary: This randomised controlled trial tested a rehabilitation programme combining robotic mechanotherapy with biofeedback (Con-Trex lower-limb trainer), interactive balance therapy (Stabilan 01-2), and virtual reality training (Nirvana system) against a standard rehabilitation programme (therapeutic gymnastics, low-intensity laser, speleotherapy, chest massage) in 120 adults aged 40-70 with post-COVID syndrome assessed 1-6 months after infection. The experimental group showed significantly greater gains in cardiorespiratory fitness: maximum work performed increased by 12.9% versus 3.0% in controls (post-rehabilitation difference 25.3% higher, p=0.006), oxygen consumption at the first ventilatory threshold rose 6.3% versus 5.0% (p=0.016 between groups), and diastolic blood pressure at peak exercise fell by a mean of 7 mmHg (p=0.003). Dyspnoea severity also improved more in the experimental group: the proportion with moderate-to-severe dyspnoea fell from 78.3% to 13.3%, and 86% had mild or no dyspnoea after treatment, compared with 58.3% in the control group. No safety concerns were reported, but notable conflicts of interest exist: four authors hold a patent on the intervention tested.

trial_rating.result_basis: Maximum work performed increased 12.9% in the intervention group vs 3.0% in controls, with post-rehabilitation values 25.3% higher in the intervention group (p=0.006); diastolic BP at peak load fell by 7 mmHg (p=0.003); proportion with mild or no dyspnoea reached 86% vs 58.3% in controls (p<0.001 for mild dyspnoea category).

summary: This randomized trial tested whether adding personalized normobaric interval hypoxic-hyperoxic therapy (NBIHHT) — alternating breathing of low-oxygen (10–15% O2) and high-oxygen (up to 40% O2) gas mixtures, individually dosed via real-time pulse oximetry feedback — to a standard rehabilitation program improved outcomes in 120 adults (mean age 62) with persistent symptoms more than 12 weeks after moderate COVID-19 pneumonia. Patients in the NBIHHT group (n=60) showed significantly greater improvements than the standard rehabilitation group (n=60) across all primary outcomes: six-minute walk distance increased by 19.9% vs 12.0%, vital lung capacity by 12.8% vs 8.1%, breath-hold time on inspiration by 51.2% vs 24.1%, resting heart rate fell by 13.3% vs 7.3%, and anxiety and depression scores dropped by ~64% and ~61% vs ~52% and ~43% respectively (all p<0.001). Quality-of-life gains were sustained at 3 months in the NBIHHT group and stable at 6 months, whereas the control group showed a declining trend by 6 months; no safety concerns were reported, though the trial lacked a sham-control arm and did not pre-register.

trial_rating.result_basis: Six-minute walk test improved by 19.87% in the NBIHHT group vs 12.01% in controls (p=0.000 within group; between-group p=0.051 at endpoint), with breath-hold time improving 51.15% vs 24.14% (p=0.000 and p=0.006 respectively).

summary: This small Russian trial tested 18 sessions of EEG-based neurofeedback training (alpha-rhythm stimulation at 8-14 Hz using the 'Neuro V' device) in 24 COVID-19 survivors with emotional disturbances, compared to 16 controls who received no intervention. The primary outcomes were validated measures of stress, anxiety, and depression: the treatment group showed large reductions in stress (PSM-25: 138.1 to 59.8), state anxiety (56.4 to 39.0), trait anxiety (58.1 to 41.8), and depression scores (86.9 to 58.4), all significantly better than controls (p<0.05). The study has no randomisation or blinding described, a very small sample, and the control group was not matched for setting — both groups stayed at a resort hotel, which confounds the results.

trial_rating.result_basis: Stress score dropped from 138.1 to 59.8 in the treatment group vs 115.7 to 88.6 in controls (p<0.05); depression score dropped from 86.9 to 58.4 vs 74.3 to 65.1 in controls (p<0.05).

summary: This study tested 16-18 days of mountain spa rehabilitation with or without ubiquinol (reduced coenzyme Q10, 200 mg/day) in 36 non-vaccinated post-COVID-19 patients (3-6 months after hospitalization) at a high-altitude sanatorium in Slovakia. The primary biochemical finding was that ubiquinol supplementation markedly raised CoQ10 levels in platelets (+68%), whole blood (+194%), and plasma (+232%), while CoQ10 remained unchanged in the rehabilitation-only group. Clinically, the ubiquinol group showed greater symptom reduction across multiple domains: for example, overall fatigue fell from 85% to 35% of patients and shortness of breath from 65% to 30%, compared to more modest improvements without supplementation. The study had no placebo control or blinding, was small and unrandomized, and lacked a statistical comparison of clinical symptom outcomes between the two arms.

trial_rating.result_basis: CoQ10 in platelets increased from 97.5 to 163.7 pmol/10^9 PLT in the ubiquinol group (p<0.0001 vs baseline and vs control); clinical symptom comparisons between arms were not statistically tested.

summary: The EXER-COVID trial tested a 6-week supervised muscle power resistance training program (two sessions per week, 50–70% of daily 1RM, performed at maximum speed) in 100 adults with long COVID (mean age 48, 68% women) in a randomized crossover design conducted in Spain. The primary outcome, peak VO2, improved by 2.10 mL/kg/min (95% CI 1.25–2.94, p<0.001) compared to usual care. The program also increased upper and lower body strength, reduced psychological distress, improved quality of life and cognitive performance, and reduced 7 of 22 long COVID symptoms including dyspnea (RR=0.56, 95% CI 0.39–0.82) and weakness (RR=0.75, 95% CI 0.59–0.95), with no notable safety signals reported.

trial_rating.result_basis: Peak VO2 improved by 2.10 mL/kg/min (95% CI 1.25 to 2.94, p<0.001) in the exercise vs. usual care condition; per-protocol analysis showed 2.40 mL/kg/min (95% CI 1.56 to 3.25, p<0.001).

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested an 8-week program of slow deep breathing exercises (30 minutes/day, 5 days/week) versus usual activity in 60 older adults (aged 60–82) with long COVID in Thailand. The exercise group showed significant improvements across multiple outcomes: the 6-minute walk test improved significantly (F=22.56, p<0.001), blood pressure fell (systolic and diastolic, p<0.001), lung function measures including FVC and FEV1 increased, and oxidative stress markers improved (MDA decreased, SOD and catalase increased). The study was single-blinded with no dropout, but lacked objective adherence monitoring and did not assess longer-term durability of effects.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6-minute walk test showed significant group-time interaction (F=16.49, p<0.001) with exercise group outperforming controls at both weeks 4 and 8 (p<0.001); systolic blood pressure group-time interaction F=23.17, p<0.001.

The paper reports a chi-squared statistic of 8.712 with p=0.003 in the text for the primary outcome but the table shows p=0.004; both values extracted, p=0.004 used as primary (from table). 3. Percentages in Table 1 appear to have minor rounding inconsistencies (e.g., arm 1: 34.2+48.5+17.3=100.0%; arm 2: 22.8+34.1+43.1=100.0%; but 29/35=82.86% rounded to 82.7%). 4. IBS-SSS within-group t-statistics reported (arm 1: t=11.12, p<0.001; arm 2: t=13.20, p<0.001) but no between-group test statistic for IBS-SSS or IBS-QOL continuous outcomes. 6. summary: This Russian trial tested whether adding the probiotic Bifiform (containing Bifidobacterium longum BB-46 and Enterococcus faecium ENCfa-68, 3 capsules daily for 2 weeks) to standard IBS treatment improved outcomes in 70 adults who developed irritable bowel syndrome following COVID-19 infection. The primary outcome was overall treatment effectiveness: 82.7% of patients in the probiotic group responded, compared to 56.9% in the control group (p=0.004). Both groups showed statistically significant improvements in IBS symptom severity (IBS-SSS) and quality of life (IBS-QOL) scores, but improvements were larger in the probiotic group; however, the trial was open-label with no blinding, limiting confidence in the results.

summary: This pilot RCT tested individualized homeopathic treatment versus placebo in 77 adults with long COVID (mean symptom duration ~9 months, 80% female) over 12 weeks via telemedicine. The primary outcomes — Fatigue Assessment Scale (FAS), and the physical and mental composite scores of the SF-36 — showed no significant difference between the homeopathy and placebo groups at any time point (4, 8, or 12 weeks). Repeated-measures ANOVA found a statistically significant interaction favoring placebo over verum for fatigue (FAS: F(3,210)=3.3, p=0.021) and physical health (PCS: F(3,210)=3.28, p=0.022), meaning the placebo group improved earlier; both groups improved overall, likely reflecting natural recovery. The verum group reported nearly twice as many transient symptom worsening events (19 vs. 10), which the authors attribute to a homeopathic aggravation effect.

trial_rating.result_basis: No significant between-group difference at any time point for FAS, PCS, or MCS; the only significant ANOVA interaction (FAS p=0.021, PCS p=0.022) favored placebo over verum.

summary: This prospective study tested nintedanib (a tyrosine kinase inhibitor used in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis) added to standard treatment versus standard treatment alone in 50 adults who developed CT-confirmed lung fibrosis after recovering from COVID-19. After 90 days, the nintedanib group showed significantly greater improvement across all lung function measures: FVC rose from 54.5% to 65.6% predicted, FEV1 rose from 28.1% to 41.7% predicted, and PEFR% rose from 30.1% to 34.4% predicted, all with p<0.05 versus both baseline and the control group. The main caveat is the very small sample size (25 per group), non-randomised allocation, single-centre design, and absence of blinding, which substantially limits confidence in the findings.

trial_rating.result_basis: FVC% improved from 54.45 to 65.55 in the nintedanib group vs unchanged 52.45 in controls (p=0.001); FEV1% improved from 28.05 to 41.65 vs 28.33 in controls (p=0.002).

summary: This Indonesian experimental study tested structured cardiopulmonary exercise training (12 supervised sessions at moderate or high intensity) in 30 healthcare workers with post-COVID-19 syndrome, compared against a 10-person no-exercise control group. Functional capacity, measured by VO2 (ml/kg/min), increased significantly in all exercise groups versus controls: the younger moderate-intensity group gained +2.27 ml/kg/min (p=0.021), the younger high-intensity group gained +2.98 ml/kg/min (p=0.003), and the older moderate-intensity group gained +2.45 ml/kg/min (p=0.002). summary: A 3-month hybrid integrated care program combining 8 outpatient pulmonary rehabilitation sessions with 24 home-based ICT-supported sessions was tested in 27 long COVID patients with significant fatigue (mean FACIT score 26), compared to 15 patients receiving usual care. The primary outcome of exercise tolerance improved substantially in the rehabilitation group: peak work rate increased by 19±10 watts, 6-minute walk distance by 72±63 meters, and FACIT fatigue score by 15±9 points (all p=0.001), while the usual care group showed improvement only in breathlessness (mMRC). Patient compliance with the home-based program was 95%, supporting feasibility, though the study is limited by its small, non-randomised design and conference abstract format with no pre-registration or blinding details reported.

summary: This study tested osteopathic manual treatment (sessions every two weeks for 10–12 weeks) in 20 adults with post-COVID fatigue and autonomic symptoms (astheno-neurotic syndrome), compared against 20 untreated controls. The primary outcome was severity of asthenia on the Scale of Asthenic State (SAS): the treated group improved by 4.7 points versus 0.8 points in the control group. Treated patients also showed normalization of autonomic balance (Kerdo index moving from −3.29 to −0.35) and improvements in mental health and general health on the SF-36. summary: This randomized controlled trial tested an 8-week circuit training program combining aerobic, strength, and breathing exercises (50 minutes, three times per week, at 65-75% maximum heart rate) in 60 Indonesian women with post-COVID-19 syndrome. The exercise group showed significantly greater improvements than controls in FEV1 (forced expiratory volume; interaction p=0.010, effect size d=-0.66), FEV1/FVC ratio (interaction p=0.006), peak expiratory flow (interaction p=0.009, effect size d=-0.67), and oxygen saturation (interaction p=0.041), while FVC and maximum voluntary ventilation improved in both groups equally. The FEV1/FVC ratio actually declined in the control group over the 8 weeks, underscoring the value of the exercise program, though the study was limited to women only and lacked long-term follow-up beyond the intervention period.

summary: This randomized controlled trial compared physiotherapist-supervised synchronous telerehabilitation (STR) against unsupervised asynchronous telerehabilitation (ATR) in 31 Brazilian adults with post-COVID syndrome, using an 8-week progressive exercise program including aerobic, strengthening, and breathing exercises. The primary outcome—lower limb functional strength measured by the Five Times Sit-to-Stand Test—improved significantly within the STR group (from 11.02s to 9.63s at 8 weeks, p=0.03) and showed a statistically significant between-group difference (p=0.027, Cohen's d=0.52), though post-hoc testing did not confirm this between-group difference. STR also produced significant within-group improvements in dyspnea, fatigue, stress, and quality of life, while ATR improved only fatigue and anxiety; notably, dropout was substantially higher in the ATR group (13 of 21 lost by 20-week follow-up vs. 8 of 23 in STR), limiting the reliability of comparisons.

trial_rating.result_basis: Between-group difference in FTSTS was p=0.027 (Cohen's d=0.52), but post-hoc testing did not confirm this difference; within-group improvement in STR was from 11.02s to 9.63s (p=0.029, 95% CI 0.10–2.40).

summary: This randomized trial tested daily home-based transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS), delivered via a standard TENS device clipped to the left ear tragus, in 114 adults with post-COVID fatigue. Among the 24 participants in the active treatment arm who met minimum adherence (at least 1 hour/day on at least 50% of days), fatigue measured on a Visual Analogue Scale improved by 11.9 points (±17.8) after 8 weeks, compared to non-significant reductions of 8.0 points in both the sham and placebo groups; the active group also showed significant improvement across all domains of the Fatigue Impact Scale and in an objective measure of peripheral muscle fatigue. A major caveat is that this is a per-protocol subgroup analysis of adherent participants only — one-third of the 114 enrolled did not meet minimum usage — and the main between-group intention-to-treat analysis is reported separately; the experimenter was also not blinded after randomization.

trial_rating.result_basis: VAS fatigue score improved by 11.9 ± 17.8 points in the active nVNS group (p=0.003, Cohen's d=0.939, N=24), versus non-significant reductions in sham (p=0.018) and placebo (p=0.141) groups; this is a per-protocol subgroup analysis, not the pre-specified primary analysis.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. The paper does not report baseline (pre-MBSR) outcome scores — all reported values are from 6-month and 12-month post-MBSR timepoints. No baseline means/SDs available for BPI-SF, HADS, or ISI. Weeks_from_randomization for the two timepoints are estimated as ~32 weeks (8 weeks treatment + ~6 months follow-up) and ~58 weeks (8 weeks treatment + ~12 months follow-up). 2. HADS anxiety and depression mean scores are reported in text/Figure 3 but SDs are not provided for these continuous scores. ISI continuous means (9, 13.6 at 6 months; 9.1, 11.1 at 12 months) are also reported without SDs. T-statistics are given for HADS-A (t=-3.636, t=-5.167) and HADS-D (t=-2.823, t=-2.458) and ISI (t=-8.801, t=-3.569) but not CIs. 3. The insomnia categorical outcome (absence of insomnia 53.2% vs 30.4%) was reported with chi-square statistic (x=4.944, p=.026) — this appears to be the chi-square value not the ISI mean score as stated in the abstract. 4. The abstract states insomnia score '53.2 vs 30.4' which matches the categorical percentages in Table 2 (not ISI continuous scores), suggesting the abstract conflated percentage data with score data. 5. Control group n at 12 months is 43 per Table 2 (not 46), consistent with 3 additional dropouts noted in limitations. 6. Baseline demographic table shows n=93 for analyzed population but randomization was 105 total (52 IG + 53 CG). The 12 missing patients (5 IG + 7 CG) are the dropouts. 7. The paper uses 'psychoeducation' as the label for the MBSR intervention in the abstract methods section but the intervention is clearly MBSR throughout.

summary: This Italian RCT tested an 8-week Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) program (2 hours per week in small groups) added to usual drug therapy versus usual care alone in 105 COVID-19 survivors who had been admitted to intensive care and developed new-onset chronic pain, anxiety, depression, or insomnia. The primary outcome was chronic pain assessed by the Brief Pain Inventory; the MBSR group showed statistically significant reductions in 'least pain in the last 24 hours' at 6 months (0.91 vs 1.43, p=0.035) and 12 months (2.20 vs 2.83, p=0.012), alongside significant improvements in anxiety (HADS score 11.28 vs 13.15, p<0.001), depression (9.95 vs 11.23, p=0.007), and insomnia at 6 months (53.2% vs 30.4% absence of insomnia, p=0.026). The authors themselves noted that the pain reductions, while statistically significant, appeared clinically small, and the study was single-centre with a sample size below its original target of 125.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome (least pain in last 24h) improved by 0.52 points at 6 months (0.91 vs 1.43, p=0.035) and 0.63 points at 12 months (2.20 vs 2.83, p=0.012); authors themselves characterised these reductions as statistically but not clinically significant.

summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT tested CCSA (a coordination complex of ethylmethylhydroxypyridine succinate and meldonium, brand name Brainmax), given as 10 daily intramuscular injections, in 30 adults with post-COVID fatigue and cognitive symptoms persisting more than 12 weeks. The primary outcome, fatigue severity on the MFI-20 scale, improved significantly more with CCSA than placebo: a median reduction of 20 points versus 12 points (p=0.043). Cognitive function on the MoCA also improved more with CCSA (median +2 points vs +1 point, p=0.023), and resting-state fMRI showed increased connectivity between the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and temporal regions after CCSA. Key limitations include very small sample size (15 per arm), single centre, short follow-up with no post-treatment assessment, industry funding with author financial ties to the manufacturer, and a possible learning effect on the MoCA in younger patients.

trial_rating.result_basis: MFI-20 median reduction -20.0 points (CCSA) vs -12.0 points (placebo), p=0.043; MoCA median improvement +2 vs +1 points, p=0.023.

summary: A 6-week outpatient cardiopulmonary rehabilitation program — combining respiratory muscle training, inspiratory muscle training, upper limb resistance exercises, and treadmill aerobic training — was tested against an educational control in 33 adults with post-COVID-19 syndrome in Brazil. The rehabilitation group walked 100.5 m further on the 6-minute walk test than controls (95% CI: 7.4–193 m, p=0.002), a clinically meaningful improvement in functional capacity. Dyspnea also improved significantly (mMRC inter-group difference: −1.45, 95% CI: −1.98 to −0.92), and upper limb muscle mass increased by 0.63 kg more than controls; fatigue scores did not differ significantly between groups. The trial was small (n=33) and unblinded to participants, limiting generalizability.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6MWT inter-group difference of 100.46 m (95% CI: 7.40–193 m, p=0.002), exceeding the commonly cited minimal clinically important difference of ~25–54 m.

All outcome arm_results and between_group_effects are null/empty because the trial had not yet reported results at time of publication. The baseline PROMIS-29 score of 42 (SD 8) is from a personal communication cited in the power calculation, not from trial data. summary: The PAX LC trial is a Phase 2, double-blind, placebo-controlled decentralized trial testing 15 days of nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (Paxlovid) versus placebo/ritonavir in 100 highly symptomatic US adults with long COVID, with the primary outcome being change in PROMIS-29 Physical Health Summary Score from baseline to Day 28. This paper describes the trial protocol only — no efficacy or safety results are reported, as the study was ongoing at time of publication. The trial is notable for its fully decentralized design, including at-home blood draws, direct drug shipment, and electronic health record integration, and includes deep immunophenotyping to identify potential biomarkers of treatment response.

trial_rating.result_basis: No results reported; this is a protocol/methods paper. Primary endpoint (PROMIS-29 Physical Health Summary Score change at Day 28) was powered to detect a 5-point difference (SD=8, 80% power, N=100), but no outcome data are available.

summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot RCT tested 14 days of beetroot juice supplementation (200 mL/day, ~600 mg nitrate) versus placebo in 25 adults with long COVID aged 20–60 years who reported persistent fatigue. The primary outcome—change in fatigue resistance—improved significantly within both groups over 14 days (+21.8 s overall, p<0.001), but there was no significant difference between beetroot juice and placebo (median change +26.6 s vs +15.0 s; mean difference 1.3 s, 95% CI −13.5 to 19.6 s; p=0.92). Beetroot juice did produce beneficial changes in gut microbiota composition (increased Akkermansia, Oscillospira, Prevotella, Roseburia, Ruminococcaceae) and inflammatory markers (IFN-γ and MIP-1β) compared to placebo, though the clinical significance of these biological changes is unclear.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome (fatigue resistance) showed no significant between-group difference: mean difference 1.3 s, 95% CI −13.5 to 19.6 s, p=0.92.

summary: This uncontrolled pilot study assessed three intravenous infusions of human umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stem cells (UC-MSCs, 1×10⁶ cells/kg on days 0, 7, and 14) in 10 long COVID patients with persistent symptoms and lung lesions. At 1 month, most patients reported symptom improvement (e.g., sleep difficulties 89% to 11%, anxiety/depression 78% to 22%), and quality-of-life score improved from 64.6 to 80.0 (p=0.01); CT severity scores significantly improved by month 6 (median score 4.0 at baseline vs. 3.0 at month 6, p<0.05). summary: A six-week course of heart rate variability and temperature biofeedback (six one-hour sessions) was tested in 20 adults with long COVID recruited from a UCLA specialty clinic. In this uncontrolled single-arm trial, participants reported significant improvements across somatic symptoms (PHQ-15: 14.7 to 10.1 at 3 months, d=1.04), anxiety (GAD-7: 9.0 to 4.1, d=1.42), depression (PHQ-9: 10.5 to 6.5, d=0.99), sleep quality (PSQI: 10.6 to 8.9, d=0.72), and number of bad days per month (19.7 to 7.8, d=1.90), with gains sustained at three-month follow-up. summary: This open-label randomized controlled trial tested oral thiamine (vitamin B1, 600 mg/day for 8 weeks) plus supportive therapy versus supportive therapy alone in 66 long COVID patients in Tehran, Iran. The primary finding was that thiamine significantly accelerated symptom resolution: by week 7, 67% of the thiamine group had resolved symptoms versus 33% of controls, and by week 8, recovery rates were 87% versus 40%. Multiple individual symptoms including fatigue, anosmia, myalgia, anorexia, dyspnea, palpitations, skin rash, and hair loss showed significantly greater improvement in the thiamine group by week 6 (p<0.05 to p<0.0001). Key limitations include open-label design (no blinding), significant baseline imbalances between groups (symptom onset interval, CRP, neutrophil/lymphocyte percentages), small sample size, and reliance on subjective patient-reported symptom scores.

trial_rating.result_basis: Recovery rate 87% thiamine vs 40% control at week 8; multiple symptoms significantly improved at week 6 (e.g. fatigue: 1.33±0.52 vs 2.31±0.62, p=0.001; anosmia: 2.29±1.11 vs 3.60±0.70, p=0.009; dyspnea: 0.00 vs 0.50±0.21, p<0.0001).

summary: This pilot RCT tested major ozone autohemotherapy (O3-MAH) added to conventional treatment versus conventional treatment alone in 73 Chinese patients with post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC), most of whom were elderly (median age ~70) with symptoms persisting for ~20 weeks after Omicron infection. The primary outcomes favored O3-MAH: 71% of O3-MAH patients achieved ≥50% symptom score reduction versus 45% of controls (p=0.0325), with significantly better 6-minute walk distance (6MWD %predicted, p=0.0032) and tidal volume (p=0.0374). O3-MAH also improved inflammatory markers (CRP, SAA, PCT) and cellular immunity markers (lymphocyte, CD3, CD4 counts), with no adverse events reported. Key limitations include inability to blind participants to treatment allocation and imbalanced baseline severity between groups, which may have inflated apparent benefits.

trial_rating.result_basis: 71% response rate (≥50% symptom reduction) in O3-MAH vs 45% controls (p=0.0325); 6MWD %predicted significantly higher in O3-MAH group post-treatment (p=0.0032); tidal volume p=0.0374.

summary: This 8-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial tested vortioxetine (5–20 mg/day) versus placebo in 149 Canadian adults with WHO-defined post-COVID-19 condition, focusing on cognitive function, depressive symptoms, and quality of life. The primary outcome — change in Digit Symbol Substitution Test (DSST) score — showed no significant between-group difference (mean difference 0.157, 95% CI −0.179 to 0.492, P=0.361), though a subgroup with elevated baseline CRP showed significant cognitive improvement with vortioxetine (P=0.045). Vortioxetine significantly outperformed placebo on depressive symptoms (QIDS-SR-16 mean difference −1.52, 95% CI −2.85 to −0.19, P=0.026) and health-related quality of life (WHO-5 mean difference 2.36, 95% CI 0.77 to 3.94, P=0.004); adverse event rates were similar between groups (26.8% vortioxetine vs 22.1% placebo).

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary DSST outcome: mean difference 0.157, 95% CI (−0.179, 0.492), P=0.361 — not statistically significant.

summary: This feasibility study tested Energy Management Education (EME), a 7-session occupational therapy group intervention teaching energy conservation and pacing strategies, in 17 adults with long COVID-related fatigue at a Swiss rehabilitation centre. The primary feasibility objectives were met, with 57% recruitment, 0% dropout, and 70-77% follow-up rates. On secondary clinical outcomes, self-efficacy in energy management strategies improved significantly from baseline to post-intervention (SEPECSA mean 5.66 to 7.40, partial η²=0.636), and fatigue impact (MFIS) and daily activity competency also improved with large effect sizes. The study had no control group and EME was delivered alongside other interdisciplinary rehabilitation, so effects cannot be attributed to EME alone.

trial_rating.result_basis: SEPECSA self-efficacy score improved by 1.73 points (BL 5.66 to T1 7.40, p<0.001, partial η²=0.636); MFIS fatigue impact improved by 10.69 points at follow-up (p=0.030, partial η²=0.254); no control group.

summary: Eight weeks of home-based inspiratory muscle training (IMT) was tested in adults with long COVID (PASC, n=7 completers) and mild-to-moderate ME/CFS (n=9 completers), compared to healthy controls (n=9). Across all groups, IMT significantly improved inspiratory muscle strength, 6-minute walk distance (p=0.002), resting heart rate (p=0.037), heart rate variability parameters (HF power, RMSSD, pRR50; all p<0.05), and sleep symptoms (p=0.009); in the ME/CFS group only, autonomic function scores on the COMPASS 31 also improved (vasomotor p=0.001, secretomotor p=0.023, weighted score p=0.005). This was an uncontrolled pilot study with no sham or waitlist control arm and very small group sizes, so natural symptom recovery cannot be excluded; the authors urge caution given post-exertional malaise risk.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6-minute walk distance improved across all groups (main effect p=0.002); HRV parameters improved (LF p=0.035, HF p=0.034, RMSSD p=0.034, pRR50 p=0.035); no control arm and n=7-9 per group limits causal inference.

summary: This bicentric randomized feasibility study tested singing-based respiratory training (SBRT) in 47 adults with post-COVID syndrome and respiratory symptoms at a university outpatient clinic and inpatient rehabilitation center in Germany. The primary outcome was feasibility, measured by compliance and adherence: 96% of participants completed all supervised sessions, and dropout was 15%. Across all participants, pre-post improvements reached medium effect sizes for physical health-related quality of life (VR-12 physical component, Cohen's d=0.52), anxiety (GAD-7, d=0.55), and depression (PHQ-9, d=0.50), though there was no control group so these changes cannot be attributed to SBRT alone. The study found no advantage for SBRT targeting a respiratory rate of 6 breaths/minute compared to standard SBRT, and lung function parameters showed only small, non-significant improvements.

trial_rating.result_basis: No control group; all pre-post effects are uncontrolled. Strongest finding is Cohen's d=0.55 (95% CI 0.11 to 0.98) for GAD-7, but this is a within-group pre-post change with no comparator arm, making attribution to the intervention impossible.

summary: This randomized single-blind trial tested a 6-week lifestyle adjustment program (12 individual sessions combining cognitive restructuring, disorder education, relaxation, goal-setting, and motor imagery) versus an information leaflet plus standard care in 54 long COVID patients in Spain. The primary outcomes were quality of life (EQ-5D-5L) and disability (WHODAS 2.0); the intervention group showed significant between-group improvements in EQ-5D self-care (p=0.004) and anxiety/depression (p=0.009) dimensions, and in the WHODAS self-care subscale (p=0.014), though most other between-group comparisons were non-significant. Within the intervention group, total WHODAS disability score improved by 11.97 points (p=0.001) and the EQ-5D VAS improved by 12.57 points (p=0.003), but no follow-up data were collected to assess durability.

trial_rating.result_basis: Between-group significance reached only for EQ-5D self-care (p=0.004) and anxiety/depression (p=0.009) dimensions and WHODAS self-care subscale (p=0.014); most other between-group comparisons were non-significant including total WHODAS (p=0.492) and total WSAS (p=0.197).

summary: This RCT tested intermittent hypoxia exposure (IHE) — alternating 5-minute cycles of hypoxic air (10–12% oxygen) and normal air, repeated five times per session for a median of 10 days — versus normoxia exposure (NE) as a control, both added to routine respiratory therapy, in 95 long COVID patients with persistent dyspnea and fatigue (symptoms ≥12 weeks). IHE produced significantly greater improvements in 6-minute walk distance (+47m vs +23.5m, p=0.001), FVC %predicted (+6.1% vs +3.2%, p=0.001), and fatigue scores (FAS reduction: 15.5 vs 6.0 points, p=0.001) compared to NE. summary: This uncontrolled before-after study tested Anvifen (aminophenylbutyric acid, a GABAergic anxiolytic) at 500 mg three times daily for 21 days in 92 long COVID patients aged 18–50 with persistent brain fog at least 12 weeks after PCR-confirmed COVID-19. Across all measured outcomes, statistically significant improvements were seen after treatment: cognitive scores improved (MoCA median 22 to 25, TMT-B 281 to 231 seconds), anxiety fell (HADS anxiety 10.5 to 7), fatigue decreased (FAS 27 to 20), sleep quality improved (15 to 25 out of 30), and quality of life scores rose on both physical and mental SF-36 components. However, the study had no control group and no placebo arm, making it impossible to distinguish drug effects from natural recovery or regression to the mean.

trial_rating.result_basis: MoCA improved from median 22 to 25 (p=0.00001), HADS anxiety from 10.5 to 7 (p=0.000025), TMT-B from 281 to 231 seconds (p=0.00001); all within-group comparisons, no control arm.

Per-arm means and SDs for individual outcomes at baseline and follow-up are NOT reported in this paper — only between-group mean differences with 95% CrI (Bayesian credible intervals, not frequentist CIs) and SD differences are provided. The CrI values have been placed in ci_95_low/ci_95_high fields as the closest equivalent, though they are 95% credible intervals not confidence intervals. The SMIP between-group mean difference upper bound (42.7) appears to be a typographical error in the paper (Table 3 states '141.2 (68.0 to 42.7)'); the lower bound 68.0 is clearly correct and 42.7 is likely a formatting error — the true upper CI is not determinable from the text. Outcome data for MIP and SMIP appears primarily in figures (Figure 3) with distribution shapes shown but no tabular per-arm means/SDs. The primary RCT data (McNarry et al. 2022) would need to be consulted for per-arm baseline and endpoint values. Proportion of response estimates extracted: MIP 0.84 (95% CrI 0.63-1.0), SMIP 0.95 (95% CrI 0.76-1.0). Table 4 dose-response beta coefficients extracted in subgroup_analyses section. BDI baseline values: IMT group 5.8 (SD 2.5), Control group 5.4 (SD 2.9) — these are baseline dyspnea index scores, not outcome change scores.

summary: This secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial examined whether individuals with long COVID respond differently to 8 weeks of home-based inspiratory muscle training (IMT), using data from 111 IMT participants and 36 usual-care controls. The primary finding was strong heterogeneity in inspiratory muscle strength responses: mean improvements of 26.6 cmH2O for maximal inspiratory pressure (MIP) and 141.2 pressure time units for sustained MIP, with the intervention group showing substantially greater variability than controls (Bayes factor >100 for both). Greater training dose was the strongest predictor of improvement, with each standard deviation increase in cumulative power associated with a 10.9 cmH2O gain in MIP; however, no evidence of heterogeneous treatment effects was found for perceived dyspnea or health-related quality of life.

trial_rating.result_basis: MIP improved by 26.6 cmH2O (95% CrI 10.5–42.7) in IMT vs control; SD difference 22.8 cmH2O (75% CrI 4.7–37.7), Bayes factor >100; ~84% of IMT participants estimated to show some MIP improvement.

summary: This Turkish RCT tested 6 weeks of supervised telerehabilitation (via video call, 3×/week) versus unsupervised home exercise versus patient education alone in 36 long COVID patients with persistent dyspnea (mMRC ≥2). At week 6, the telerehabilitation group showed significantly greater reductions in dyspnea (mMRC 2.58→0.42) and fatigue (Chalder total 20.91→7.25) compared to controls (p=0.001 and p=0.003), and also improved exercise capacity (6MWT +66m, p=0.001) and respiratory muscle strength (MIP 96.8→135.4%, p<0.001), while the home exercise group improved only dyspnea and fatigue. By week 12, between-group differences were no longer significant, as control group dyspnea also improved spontaneously, suggesting partial natural resolution of symptoms regardless of intervention.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome mMRC dyspnea improved from 2.58 to 0.42 in telerehabilitation vs 1.17 in controls at week 6 (group×time interaction p=0.001, Cohen's d=4.24); Chalder fatigue total 20.91→7.25 vs 18.83→16.17 (p=0.003).

summary: This Egyptian RCT tested whether adding laser acupuncture (3 sessions/week for 4 weeks) to a pedometer-based home walking program (3,000 steps/day) improved quality of life in 60 post-COVID-19 patients aged 35–48 compared to walking alone. Both groups improved significantly on all outcomes, but the combined group outperformed walking alone on the SF-36 quality-of-life score (78.15 vs. 73.51, p<0.0001), fatigue (FAS 25.07 vs. 29.57, p<0.0001), six-minute walk test (396m vs. 386m, p=0.002), and inflammatory markers including CRP (4.15 vs. 5.13 mg/L, p=0.001). The study is small and single-centre, recruited from one Egyptian outpatient clinic, excluded patients with common comorbidities, and did not include a sham-laser control, making it impossible to rule out placebo effects from the additional clinic contact.

trial_rating.result_basis: Combined group SF-36 post-treatment 78.15 vs. 73.51 in walking-only group (p<0.0001); FAS 25.07 vs. 29.57 (p<0.0001); no sham control to isolate laser-specific effects.

summary: This Danish randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial tested high-dose coenzyme Q10 (500 mg/day for 6 weeks) against placebo in 119 long COVID patients recruited from specialist outpatient clinics. The primary outcome — change in a PCC-specific symptom score and EQ-5D health index — showed no significant difference between CoQ10 and placebo: symptom score mean difference −1.18 points (95% CI: −3.54 to 1.17, p=0.32) and EQ-5D health index difference 0.01 (95% CI: −0.02 to 0.04, p=0.40). Both groups improved over time, likely reflecting spontaneous recovery or a placebo effect. CoQ10 was well tolerated, with treatment-related adverse events in only 11% of participants, all grade 1 or 2.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary PCC symptom score mean difference CoQ10 vs placebo: −1.18 points (95% CI: −3.54 to 1.17, p=0.32); EQ-5D health index difference: 0.01 (95% CI: −0.02 to 0.04, p=0.40). Both null results.

summary: This Russian RCT tested whether adding transcranial electrical stimulation (TES) to Cortexin pharmacotherapy improved outcomes compared to Cortexin alone in 150 long COVID patients (aged 18-45) with chronic fatigue and cognitive impairment. After 15 days, the TES+pharmacotherapy group showed 74.6% reduction in fatigue scores (MFI-20) versus 60.3% in the pharmacotherapy-only group, a 36.9% between-group difference (p=0.001), and 93.3% of TES patients achieved full symptom remission versus 64.0% in controls (p=0.002). TES also produced significantly greater reductions in pro-inflammatory cytokines TNF-α (41% greater reduction, p=0.002), IL-1β (35% greater, p=0.020), and IL-6 (37% greater, p=0.011) compared to pharmacotherapy alone. No adverse events were recorded in either group.

trial_rating.result_basis: MFI-20 fatigue score reduced 74.6% in TES group vs 60.3% in pharmacotherapy group, 36.9% between-group difference (p=0.001); CGI-S full remission 93.3% vs 64.0% (p=0.002).

summary: This double-blind, sham-controlled pilot RCT tested transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) targeting the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in 47 long COVID patients with persistent fatigue (mean illness duration ~21 months). Active tDCS (2 mA, 20 min/day for 8 sessions over 2 weeks) produced a statistically significant improvement in physical fatigue compared to sham, with a significant time-by-group interaction on the MFIS-physical subscale (F=3.517, p=0.034), though no significant effect was found for the total MFIS score or cognitive fatigue. The treatment was well-tolerated with only mild, transient adverse events and no between-group differences in safety; however, this is an unpublished preprint, the sample is small, and the primary total fatigue outcome did not reach significance.

trial_rating.result_basis: MFIS-total time-by-group interaction was not significant (F=1.730, p=0.184); MFIS-physical subscale showed significant time-by-group interaction (F=3.517, p=0.034), with active group improving from T0 to T1 (mean log difference 0.105, p<0.001) while sham did not (p=1.0).
