summary: This single-arm pilot clinical trial enrolled 14 adults with long COVID in a 10-week supervised aerobic exercise training program (cycle ergometer and treadmill, twice weekly). The primary biomarker finding was that exercise training enabled a significant acute exercise-induced response in serum extracellular vesicle RNA, with 53 differentially expressed genes (predominantly downregulated, including immune/inflammation-related genes MYL9, NRGN, B2M, CCL5) identified at peak exercise after training but not before, and no SARS-CoV-2 RNA was detected in EVs at any timepoint. Clinically, peak VO2 increased significantly by 7.4% (1.88 to 2.03 L/min, p<0.05) and peak work rate increased 16% (139 to 155 W, p<0.05) after training, though absence of a control group prevents attribution to exercise versus spontaneous recovery.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm study (no randomization, no control group) so between_group_effects are reported as pre-vs-post comparisons within the single arm, not between treatment and control arms. The primary outcomes of this paper are transcriptomic (EV RNA sequencing), not clinical; clinical outcomes (VO2, work rate) are secondary and were published in a prior companion paper (Abbasi et al., J Clin Med 2024). The paper reports clinical improvements in the companion paper of 60-63% improvement in fatigue, -42% depression, -29% anxiety, -10% dyspnea but does not provide raw means/SDs for these in the current paper. VO2 post-training SD appears to be a transcription error (0.07 vs 0.69 pre-training); extracted as reported. Immune cell counts analyzed by 2-way repeated-measures ANOVA (acute exercise x training); main effect p<0.001 for acute exercise but no significant training effect. Pathway analysis results (z-scores, number of pathways) are qualitative summaries without per-arm quantitative values extractable into the outcomes schema; these are described in extractor_notes only. 21 enrolled, 14 completed (7 did not complete all exercise trials).

summary: This single-arm feasibility trial enrolled 26 adults with post-COVID-19 condition (PCC) and comorbid POTS at Karolinska University Hospital, Sweden, who underwent 12 weeks of individually tailored endurance and strength exercise with weekly physiotherapist support. The primary aim was to evaluate feasibility, which was demonstrated with 76% exercise adherence and 96% protocol completion rate, no serious adverse events, and acceptable data completion across questionnaires and accelerometry. summary: This single-arm before-and-after feasibility study examined 8 weeks of home-based personalized computerized cognitive training (CogniFit CCT) in 73 adults with long COVID-related cognitive dysfunction (brain fog), most of whom had been symptomatic for over a year. summary: The Solidarity Finland trial randomized 156 hospitalized COVID-19 patients at 15 Finnish hospitals to oral imatinib 400 mg/day (up to 14 days) plus standard of care versus standard of care alone, with 1-year follow-up of mortality, recovery, quality of life, and long COVID symptoms. Imatinib showed no benefit on 30-day mortality (HR 1.09, 95% CI 0.23–5.07) or 1-year mortality (HR 1.34, 95% CI 0.46–3.88), and no significant difference in self-reported recovery (79% vs 88.3%, RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.78–1.06) or any EQ-5D-5L or symptom domain at 1 year. A meta-analysis of 4 trials (n=732) yielded a pooled mortality RR of 0.73 (95% CI 0.32–1.63), raising serious doubts about imatinib's benefit in hospitalized COVID-19 patients.

summary: This single-arm interventional cohort study (n=23) tested Psychophysiologic Symptom Relief Therapy (PSRT), a 13-week group-based mind-body program combining psychophysiologic education, desensitization, and MBSR, in adults with long COVID (PASC) without objective organ injury. The primary outcome, SSS-8 somatic symptom score, decreased by a mean of 10.9 points (55% reduction) from baseline to 13 weeks (p<0.001; 95% CI: -13.5 to -8.3). Statistically significant improvements were also observed across all secondary outcomes including fatigue (FSS-9), dyspnea (MDP), pain (BPI), pain anxiety (PASS-20), physical functioning (PROMIS-29), and brain fog at all three follow-up timepoints; however, the absence of a control arm limits causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is a single-arm pre-post study (not an RCT); all 'between_group_effects' represent within-arm pre-vs-post comparisons using paired tests. RoB2 is not strictly applicable to non-randomized designs but has been applied to highlight the absence of randomization as the primary bias concern. The PROMIS-29 physical function subscale used here is scored 0-16 with higher=worse (difficulty), so 'higher_is_better' is false. The paper notes 1/23 (4%) missing values for pain interference at 4 and 8 weeks (n_analyzed=22 for those timepoints). The brain fog instrument is not externally validated. Adverse events were not formally reported. The median symptom duration at baseline was 267 days (IQR: 144, 460); time since infection in months was not directly reported. Individual SSS-8 component data (Supplementary Table 2) and visualization test data (Supplemental Table 3) were not available in the main text. The FSS-9 exercise worsens symptoms item (ordinal, not continuous) was reported separately but not as a standalone extracted outcome here; key finding was 57% strongly agreed at baseline vs 4% at 13 weeks.

summary: This pilot RCT (n=14 completers) tested Constraint-Induced Cognitive Therapy (CICT) — combining Speed of Processing Training with behavior change techniques — versus treatment-as-usual in adults with long COVID brain fog and IADL impairment. CICT produced very large improvements over TAU in daily-life cognitive task performance (COPM Performance MD=3.7, 95% CI 2.5–4.9, p<0.001, d=2.6) and brain fog (MCS MD=−4.0, 95% CI −5.3 to −2.6, p<0.001, d=−3.1), as well as a significant return-to-work advantage (80% vs. 0%, p=0.048). Results support feasibility and provisional efficacy, warranting a larger blinded RCT with an active comparator.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. summary: This single-arm open-label feasibility trial enrolled 12 adults with clinically diagnosed long COVID in Yorkshire, UK, to receive up to 150 mg/day CBD (MediCabilis 5% CBD Oil) orally for 21 weeks. The primary feasibility aims were recruitment rate, tolerability, and safety: recruitment fell well short of target (12 of 30 planned participants in 6 months), but retention was 100%, there were no serious adverse events, and the drug was well-tolerated with mild side effects (most commonly dry mouth, increased appetite, dry/itchy eyes). Secondary outcome data (PHQ-9, GAD-7, PSQI, FSS, BPI-SF, EQ-5D-5L, C19-YRS, Fitbit measures) were reported only in figures without numeric values in the text, making quantitative extraction impossible; the authors noted only speculative trends toward improvement in anxiety, depression, and sleep without statistical testing due to the absence of a control group.

This is a single-arm study with no control arm, so between_group_effects arrays are empty throughout. The n_randomized field is null because this was not a randomized trial — participants were enrolled into a single arm. summary: This was a prospective open-label pilot study in South Korea testing three traditional Korean herbal medicines — Bojungikgi-tang (BIT), Kyungok-go (KOG), and Cheonwangbosim-dan (CBD) — in 45 long COVID patients with fatigue or cognitive dysfunction, allocated by clinician syndrome differentiation (no randomization or control group). Cognitive dysfunction outcomes showed little significant improvement across arms, with the exception of K-MoCA in the KOG group and CFQ in the CBD group at later timepoints; no adverse events were causally related to the medications, confirming feasibility but not efficacy.

summary: This was a prospective, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover phase IIa trial (reCOVer) evaluating BC007 (Rovunaptabin, 1350 mg IV single infusion), a GPCR functional autoantibody (GPCR-fAAb) neutraliser, in 30 PCS patients with confirmed GPCR-fAAb positivity and prominent fatigue at a single German centre. The intervention was well tolerated with no serious adverse events.

summary: This single-arm feasibility study tested a 6-week theatre-based wellness programme (including breathing, movement, voice, and drama exercises) delivered to 20 adults with diagnosed long COVID either in-person or online. summary: This single-arm pilot study enrolled 13 adults with neurologic long COVID (PASC) symptoms and reduced glucagon-stimulated GH secretion (<10 ng/mL) and treated them with daily subcutaneous recombinant human growth hormone (somatropin) for 9 months, followed by 3 months of off-treatment observation. GH treatment was associated with significant improvements in fatigue (BFI, MFSI-SF), quality of life (QoL-AGHDA), mood (POMS), and depression (BDI-II), but not sleep quality (PSQI) or cognition (MoCA). Improvements in submaximal physical performance (walk distance at 25% and 50% effort, isometric/isokinetic torque at 25% effort) were also significant, but maximum-effort measures and body composition did not change; critically, symptoms largely returned after GH was discontinued, suggesting symptomatic but non-curative benefit.

summary: This Norwegian pilot study tested a 3-4 day concentrated micro-choice based interdisciplinary group rehabilitation program in 241 patients with chronic low back pain, long COVID, or type 2 diabetes using a single-arm pre-post design with 3-month follow-up. summary: This pilot RCT (n=14 completers) compared two 8-week virtual pulmonary rehabilitation approaches in adults with post-COVID syndrome: physiotherapist-led group video conference sessions (PR_VC, n=8) versus self-directed pre-recorded video sessions (PR_SD, n=6), both delivered 3x/week. The PR_VC group showed significantly greater improvement in sit-to-stand capacity (median change +3 vs -3.5 repetitions, p=0.012, Cohen's r=0.67), while the PR_SD group showed significantly greater worsening in fatigue, neurocognitive, and autonomic symptoms on the DSQ-SF. Both approaches were feasible and safe with 83% session completion, high satisfaction, and no adverse events.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a pilot feasibility study — not powered for efficacy; between-group effect values (mean differences) not reported, only p-values and Cohen's r effect sizes. All outcome data reported as median change scores (post minus pre) with IQR and 95% CI of median using non-parametric Mann-Whitney tests. EQ-5D-5L and EQ-VAS domain scores (pre/post) shown only in radar plots and box plots (Fig. 2) — absolute endpoint values not extractable from text; only change scores reported in Table 3. Additional DSQ-SF items not included as separate outcomes but all change score data extracted in Table 3: next day soreness (p=0.789), tiredness after minimum exercise (p=0.232), feeling unrefreshed (p=0.691), muscle pain (p=0.548), bloating (p=0.694), problems remembering things (p=0.051), irritable bowel (p=0.351), feeling unsteady (p=0.407), cold limbs (p=0.791), flu-like symptoms (p=0.940), smells/chemicals make you feel sick (p=0.224) — all non-significant and omitted as separate outcome objects to manage output size.

summary: This single-arm open-label pilot study (N=45) tested the Muse-S EEG wearable brain-sensing headband with guided meditation app as an adjunct treatment in long COVID patients over 90 days, with follow-up to 180 days. Statistically significant within-group improvements were observed at end of treatment (day 90) in perceived stress (PSS-10: -5.0±5.3, p<0.001), emotional distress (PROMIS: -4.5±5.5, p<0.001), sleep, cognitive function, self-efficacy, and quality of life, with improvements persisting at day 180. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm pre-post study with no control group; all between_group_effects arrays are empty as there is no comparator arm. No randomization was performed. The paper labels itself as an 'open-label clinical trial' but functions as an uncontrolled pre-post feasibility pilot. STAI score is labelled in Table 4 as significantly associated with usage (p=0.028) but Table 3 shows no significant within-group change at any timepoint by paired t-test — this discrepancy is noted. PHQ-2 (depression) and Fitbit wearable data (heart rate, steps, SpO2) were collected but no quantitative results were reported in the paper text or tables; these outcomes are omitted. PROMIS Cognitive Function Abilities Short Form 4a results were not separately reported from the main Cognitive Function form. The LASA-6 baseline mean of 5.0 (SD 2.1) appears to be a per-item score (0-10) not the total (0-60).

summary: This single-arm, uncontrolled expanded access program enrolled 10 adults with post-COVID-19 syndrome who received 5 intravenous infusions of autologous adipose-derived mesenchymal stem cells (2×10^8 cells each) over 14 weeks, with follow-up to 40 weeks. The primary outcomes — total VAS symptom severity and Fatigue Assessment Scale scores — both improved significantly from baseline to end of study (VAS: median 37.6 to 4.90, p=0.0039, ES=0.91; FAS: median 33.0 to 15.0, p=0.0039, ES=0.91). All eight SF-36 quality-of-life subscales also improved significantly (p=0.0039–0.0078), and the treatment was well tolerated with 40 mild-to-moderate AEs and no serious adverse events; however, the absence of a control group makes it impossible to rule out natural disease course or placebo effects as explanations for the improvements.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm expanded access study (no randomization, no control group), not an RCT; RoB2 domains are assessed accordingly. The FAS total baseline median is reported as 32.5 in the abstract text but as 33.0 in Table 2; 33.0 (from Table 2) was used as primary source. The VAS IQR at EOS is reported as '1.26-9.81' in Table 2 but '1.3-9.8' in the text; Table 2 values were used. Intermediate VAS and FAS timepoint data (weeks 2, 6, 10, 14, 18) appear only in Fig. 2 with no numeric values extractable. SF-36 intermediate timepoint data (week 6) also appears only in Fig. 3 without numeric values. 'Between_group_effects' fields for all outcomes reflect within-arm baseline-vs-EOS comparisons (Wilcoxon signed-rank test), not true between-group comparisons, as this is a single-arm study. summary: This open-label single-arm pilot study evaluated 4 weeks of oral paraprobiotics (Abiprol + Brexibiol, 1.92 g/day total of inactivated bacterial strains) in 6 long-COVID patients followed for >12 months at a Swiss university hospital. Improvements in multiple clinical measures (dysautonomia, fatigue, depression, daily steps) were observed in 30%–80% of measurements per patient, but no quantitative effect sizes or p-values for clinical outcomes were reported, limiting interpretation. Significant immunological changes included reduced HLA-DR expression on B cells and NK T cells, reduced CD40 on nonclassical monocytes, and reduced TLR2 expression on CD4+, CD8+, and NK T cells (all p<0.05 by paired Wilcoxon test), suggesting paraprobiotics may modulate immune activation; however the uncontrolled design and very small sample size preclude causal conclusions.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is a Class IV evidence single-arm pre-post pilot study (n=6) with no control group and no randomization — it is not an RCT. Quantitative clinical outcome data (means, SDs, p-values) for all questionnaire and digital/wearable outcomes are not reported in the paper text; Figure 1 is a checkerboard visualization and eFigure 11 shows individual score values (supplementary, not in provided text). Immunological outcome data appear only in heat map figures (Figures 4–6) as percentage changes, with no actual MFI or frequency values reported in text — set result_source to 'not_reported' for all arm_results. Statistical significance for immunological outcomes (HLA-DR on B cells and NK T cells, CD40 on nonclassical monocytes, TLR2 on T cells) is stated as p<0.05 (Wilcoxon paired test) but exact p-values are not given. Between_group_effects for immunological outcomes represent pre-post within-arm comparisons, not between-group comparisons (no control arm exists). Per-arm results for all outcomes have no extractable numeric values from the main text. Adverse events not mentioned. Post-treatment follow-up data available for patient 2 only (20 days steps/fatigue, 30 days sleep quality) but not systematically for all patients. Funding included an unrestricted grant from Weltmont Laboratories (the paraprobiotic manufacturer).

summary: This single-arm prospective pilot study (n=42) tested a single 10-minute virtual pet-assisted therapy (VAT) session — interaction with a virtual dog via VR headset — in long COVID outpatients at a Japanese university hospital. Immediately after the session, the mean total symptom severity score decreased significantly by 7.2% (34.6 to 32.1, p=0.004), with significant improvements also seen in fatigue (6.3 to 5.7, p=0.004), dyspnea (2.3 to 1.9, p=0.038), memory impairment (4.8 to 4.2, p=0.015), and tinnitus (2.3 to 1.8, p=0.012), all with small effect sizes (0.13–0.22). The study lacked a control group and measured only immediate within-session changes, preventing causal conclusions.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm pre-post pilot study with no randomization and no control group; the 'between_group_effects' fields are repurposed to capture within-person pre-vs-post differences (Wilcoxon signed-rank test results). Effect sizes reported by the paper are described as Wilcoxon effect sizes (r), not Cohen's d: total=0.13, fatigue=0.22, dyspnea=0.14, memory impairment=0.19, tinnitus=0.19. Follow-up duration is effectively zero as all measurements were taken immediately before and after the single session on the same clinical visit day. The paper does not report adverse events formally; VR-related motion sickness was mentioned as a design consideration but no AE data are tabulated. Figure 6 shows total score as mean±SD bar chart but values are reported numerically in text. Design type set to quasi-experimental as there is no randomization and no comparator arm.

summary: This single-arm retrospective study from Turkey evaluated 2 months of low-dose oral methylprednisolone (total 680 mg, mean 11.3 mg/day in tapering doses) in 97 long COVID-19 patients with persistent symptoms (fatigue, dyspnea, chest discomfort, palpitation, cough) at least 4 weeks after acute SARS-CoV-2 infection. summary: This blind, randomized placebo-controlled trial (n=101 completers; 52 intervention, 49 placebo) from Uzbekistan tested whether electroacupuncture Voll (EAV) medicament testing could determine daily ribavirin dosing in long COVID patients aged 16-50, with observations over three years (2020-2023). The primary finding was that EAV-determined ribavirin doses increased over the observation period (e.g., Ne-3 meridian: 232.8 mg in 2020-21 to 607.8 mg in 2023) and were inversely correlated with electrodermal activity pre-test readings (Spearman ρ = -0.766 to -0.919, p<0.001), while the placebo group showed no normalization of EAV post-test readings. Importantly, this paper was retracted in June 2025, no clinical outcomes were measured, and the intervention is based on pseudoscientific electroacupuncture dosimetry with no demonstrated clinical benefit.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL: This paper was RETRACTED on June 6, 2025. No clinical benefit of ribavirin was assessed. Table 2 has garbled row ordering (Le-1a* pre/post-test rows appear swapped in the source). The ± values in Table 1 appear to be SDs (labeled as such in context), but Table 2 states 'means and standard errors' — SE values are used accordingly in outcomes 1-3. summary: This single-center, open-label, non-randomized interventional study in Ukraine enrolled 320 reproductive-age women with long COVID and menstrual cycle disturbances, divided by presence (n=160) or absence (n=160) of GI symptoms and further assigned to oral vs vaginal micronized progesterone (200mg twice daily x10 days) combined with vitamin D, magnesium, and valerian. At 3 months, approximately 78% of GI- and 71% of GI+ patients reported symptom relief, rising to 89% and 87% respectively at 6 months; vaginal progesterone showed 2.5–14% better outcomes than oral, with fewer side effects. No control arm, no validated outcome instruments, and no between-group statistical testing were reported, severely limiting interpretability.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Critical data quality issues: (1) No randomization described — this is NOT an RCT despite being labeled 'interventional'; design is quasi-experimental at best. (2) There is no placebo or control arm — all 4 groups received active treatment. (3) Primary outcome data (% relief) is reported only as group-level averages pooled across the 4 arms, not broken down by arm; per-arm percentages appear only in Figures 2 and 3 which were not readable. (4) No means, SDs, or validated outcome instrument scores are reported anywhere. (5) Arm allocation: paper states 'two subgroups: oral n=90 and vaginal n=90' but this is ambiguous — it likely means 90 oral and 90 vaginal within EACH of the two GI groups (total 180+180=360 or possibly 45+45+45+45=180 within 320 total). Given n_total=320 and 4 subgroups, n=80 per arm is also plausible; n=90 per subgroup stated but adds to 360 not 320. Discrepancy unresolved. (6) Baseline demographics are reported only for GI+ vs GI- groups combined, not by progesterone route. (7) Side effect data shown only in Figure 2 (not readable). (8) No p-values, CIs, or formal statistical comparisons between arms reported.

summary: This parallel-group RCT (n=27 completers) compared 8 weeks of videoconferencing-guided synchronous telerehabilitation (VCG-ST) versus mobile application-guided asynchronous telerehabilitation (MAG-AT) in COVID-19 survivors recently discharged from hospital in Turkey. Both programs (aerobic, strengthening, and pulmonary exercises, 3×/week) significantly improved resting and post-exertion oxygen saturation, physical activity (IPAQ), dyspnea, fatigue, heart rate, and 30-second sit-to-stand performance at 8-week post-treatment and 8-month long-term follow-up (p<0.05 for all within-group). VCG-ST produced significantly greater improvements in resting oxygen saturation (p=0.031) and post-exertion oxygen saturation (p=0.004) between groups; no other outcome showed a statistically significant between-group difference, though adherence was higher in the MAG-AT group (92% vs 84%).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. Tables 1–4 are referenced in the text but their numeric data were not included in the paper text provided (only table titles given). Per-arm means and SDs for all outcomes (baseline, post-treatment, and follow-up) are therefore not available for extraction — only change-from-baseline scores reported narratively in the text for oxygen saturation and IPAQ, and between-group p-values. Exact sample sizes per arm at randomization are not explicitly stated (14 completed VCG-ST, 13 completed MAG-AT, with 1 dropout each; original randomization n per arm unclear but 15 and 14 inferred from 29 total randomized). The paper notes baseline oxygen saturation was significantly lower in VCG-ST vs MAG-AT (p=0.019 at rest, p=0.008 after exertion), which complicates between-group comparisons. All between-group effect values are from repeated-measures analysis (not simple end-point comparison). IPAQ interaction p=0.013 refers to group×time interaction across all timepoints. The n_randomized per arm values are inferred as 15 and 14 based on the CONSORT flow description. Demographic data (age, sex, BMI) are stated to be in Table 1 but numeric values not provided in text. Post-treatment follow-up = 8 months minus 8 weeks treatment = approximately 24 weeks (calculated).

summary: This single-arm pre-post study examined 30 days of a 5-species Lactobacillus probiotic blend with inulin prebiotic in 126 COVID-19 patients (68% with chronic symptoms persisting >30 days, mean 120 days), recruited from a UK hospital post-COVID clinic. All three primary outcomes — cough score, fatigue (Chandler scale), and subjective well-being — improved significantly at 30 days in both early and chronic cohorts (all p<0.001), with large Cohen's d effect sizes for fatigue (d=1.36) and well-being (d=1.10). However, the absence of a control arm means these improvements cannot be causally attributed to the intervention, and the study has high risk of bias.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is a single-arm pre-post study with no control group — RoB2 is applied but most domains are high risk by design. The paper states n=126 for the whole cohort but Table 2 notes chronic cohort n=96 (not n=86 as stated in text/Table 2 header); both values appear — 86 is stated in methods ('86 (68%) in a chronic phase') but t-test df suggests n=96 (t95). The chronic cohort n used here follows the t-test df (t95 implies n=96). Fatigue analysis used t118/t119 suggesting some missing data (~7 participants). CI direction for subjective well-being in Table 1 appears reversed in paper (5.98 to -2.67) — corrected to positive change direction in extraction. No between-group effects are calculable as there is no control arm. Subgroup analysis sample sizes for the BMI subgroup (n=46+80=126) and hospitalization subgroup (n=79+47=126) are internally consistent. Bowel symptom improvement (25/31, 82%) and sleep improvement (8/10, 80%) are notable self-reported binary outcomes extracted in Table 4 but not in formal outcomes above due to no formal instrument.

summary: This single-arm pilot study tested a 10-week online singing and breathing retraining programme (SingStrong) in 21 adults with long COVID in Ireland who completed at least 50% of classes. Participants showed statistically significant pre-post improvements in all breathlessness measures (at rest p<0.001, dressing p=0.01, stairs p<0.001), fatigue (p=0.03), usual activities (p=0.04), pain/disability (p=0.03), voice quality (p=0.01), and cognition/communication (p=0.04). The proportion meeting ME/CFS diagnostic criteria also decreased, but the absence of a control group means results cannot be attributed definitively to the intervention.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm pre-post pilot study with no control group — not an RCT. All 'between_group_effects' entries represent within-arm pre-post comparisons (not between-arm comparisons). The C19-YRS scale is scored 0-10 where higher = worse (symptoms rated from 0 best to 10 worst). Some outcomes reported as mean(SD) at baseline but median(IQR) post-intervention (or vice versa) reflecting use of non-parametric tests for non-normal distributions; both are extracted as available. N=27 enrolled, N=21 analyzed (those completing ≥10/20 classes). Baseline Fukoda DSQ-SF: the text states 21/21 analyzed participants met Fukoda criteria (Table 3 confirms all 21 had pre-intervention data with all showing 'Yes' for Fukoda). The paper does not report adverse events formally. Cohen's d effect sizes are reported in Table 4 and 5 but not extracted as between-group effects per protocol rules. Airway complications and Swallowing outcomes from Table 5 omitted as data nearly all zeros with no significant change.

summary: This single-arm pre-post feasibility study assessed the acute effects of a single 45-minute session combining aerobic, strength, and breathing exercises (at 65-75% maximum heart rate) on pulmonary function and oxygen saturation in 36 women with post-COVID-19 syndrome (symptoms persisting >12 weeks). Post-exercise improvements were statistically significant for FEV1 (2.5 to 2.8 L, p<0.001), FEV1/FVC% (79.1 to 86.5%, p=0.004), PEF (3.9 to 5.03 L/s, p=0.001), MVV (51.3 to 62.1 L/min, p=0.004), MVV duration (10.6 to 11.4 s, p=0.018), SVC (decreased 3.03 to 2.7 L, p=0.030), and SpO2 (97.8 to 98.2%, p=0.005), with Cohen's d effect sizes of 0.5-0.8; FVC and MRf did not change significantly. The study lacked a control group, precluding causal inference, and was limited to the acute effects of a single exercise session.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is a single-arm pre-post feasibility study with no randomization and no control group — it does not qualify as an RCT. summary: This quasi-experimental Brazilian pilot study randomized 8 physically inactive adults with Long COVID (symptoms ≥3 months) to either traditional machine/dumbbell resistance training (TRAD, n=4) or elastic band resistance training (ELAS, n=4), both performed twice weekly for 12 weeks. No significant between-group differences were found; however, pooling all participants, the total DSQ-COVID symptom score decreased by ~45% (from 1215.6±323 to 671.8±398 AU; p=0.006, Cohen's d=1.33), handgrip strength increased by ~14% (31.2 to 35.3 kg·f; p=0.012), and systolic blood pressure decreased significantly (129.7 to 116.6 mmHg; p=0.040). Individual symptom scores for fatigue, bone/joint pain, and memory loss decreased by 53%, 48%, and 50% respectively (all non-significant but with moderate effect sizes), and no adverse events or desaturation episodes were reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. arm_id=99 used throughout to represent the pooled all-participants analysis (n=8), which was the primary statistical approach reported in Table 2. Per-arm post-intervention values for most outcomes were not reported — only baseline per-arm values (Table 1) and combined pre/post values (Table 2) were provided. The DSQ-COVID score at the 6-week intermediate timepoint was reported only in Figure 2 (no tabular values); the significant within-ELAS-group time effect (p=0.043 at 6 weeks, p=0.045 at 12 weeks) was verbally described but per-arm values at 12 weeks post were not tabulated separately. Individual symptom scores (fatigue, bone/joint pain, memory loss) at pre/post were not numerically reported — only percentage change data in Table 3; these were not extracted as separate outcomes due to absence of absolute values. Baseline body fat % discrepancy: Table 1 reports 36.6±11.8 overall but Table 2 reports 36.3±11.8 as 'Before' — both retained as reported. One participant started antihypertensive medication during the study, confounding the SBP result. 5 withdrawals occurred pre-randomization (from the initial 13 volunteers); the exact initial allocation is not stated, so n_randomized is listed as null.

summary: This single-arm service evaluation assessed a 12-week blended (6 weeks virtual, 6 weeks face-to-face) community rehabilitation programme in 601 UK adults with long COVID. The programme consisted of 3 x 45-minute exercise sessions per week plus weekly telephone support. Significant and clinically meaningful improvements were observed across all primary outcomes — dyspnea (D-12 change: -3.4, 95% CI -3.9 to -2.9), functional capacity (DASI change: +9.2, CI 8.2-10.1), mental wellbeing (WHO-5 change: +20.3, CI 18.6-22.0), and health-related quality of life (EQ-5D-5L utility change: +0.11, CI 0.10-0.13) — all p<0.001, with all CIs exceeding pre-specified MCIDs; however, the absence of a control group precludes causal inference.

summary: This single-arm feasibility study tested 8 weeks of individually tailored internet-based CBT (ICBT) with weekly asynchronous therapist support for COVID-19-related psychological symptoms in 24 Swedish adults (66.7% probable post-COVID syndrome) during the pandemic's final phase. Of 24 enrolled, 15 (62.5%) completed post-treatment assessments. Statistically significant improvements were found in depression (BDI-II, r=0.53), anxiety (GAD-7, r=0.43), health anxiety, post-traumatic stress, loneliness, and exhaustion, while stress, quality of life, cognitive failures, and financial well-being showed no significant change; insomnia paradoxically worsened on one test but not the robustness check. Without a control group, observed improvements cannot be causally attributed to the intervention.

summary: This single-arm prospective pilot study assessed 10 days of twice-daily home-based transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (t-VNS) using the Parasym device in 24 female long COVID patients (mean age 45.8 years, mean 20.2 months post-infection) with prominent cognitive symptoms. Significant improvements were observed in composite fluid cognition, attention, processing speed, episodic memory, anxiety, depression, and sleep at post-intervention and 1-month follow-up, with fatigue improvement reaching significance only at 1-month follow-up; olfactory performance did not improve. The absence of a control group precludes definitive attribution of these statistically significant improvements to the intervention, but effect sizes were moderate to large (Cohen's d 0.33–0.82; rank biserial r 0.6–0.98).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm uncontrolled pilot study — all 'between_group_effects' entries represent within-group pre-post comparisons (not true between-group effects), coded using within-group comparison labels. No per-arm means or SDs are reported in the text for any outcome; data appear only in figures (bar/box plots) not reproduced in extractable form, so all mean/SD fields are null. The Dimensional Change Card Sort Test (DCCS) showed only trending significance (p=0.07, not surviving Bonferroni correction) and is not included as a separate outcome entry but is noted here. Cognition analyses at follow-up used n=18 due to 6 out-of-state participants completing remote testing (PSM and LSWM used full n=24 at all timepoints). kNN imputation was used for 9 missing questionnaire values across anxiety (3), sleep (3), depression (2), and fatigue (1). summary: This within-subject study (n=20) tested whether a single 30 mg oral dose of pyridostigmine, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, could improve hand grip strength and orthostatic function in patients with post-infectious ME/CFS (90% post-COVID). Compared to a no-treatment control visit, maximum hand grip strength after repeated exertion (Fmax2) was approximately 1.5-fold higher with pyridostigmine (p=0.01), reversing the 32% decline seen without treatment; orthostatic heart rate increase was also significantly reduced (17 bpm vs 13 bpm, p=0.017). The study was unblinded and non-randomized with a fixed treatment order, limiting causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a within-subject non-randomized study, not an RCT — treatment order was not randomized (control visit always first). Arms here represent the two study conditions (no-PS visit vs PS visit) rather than parallel groups. Some figure data (Figure 1A course of HGS values) not fully extractable numerically. The absolute median Fmax2 values with and without PS are provided in text and extracted. No numeric mean difference or CI was given for the Fmax2 between-group comparison — only the ratio (~1.5-fold) and p-value. N=13 for passive standing test (7 declined). summary: This single-arm open-label study tested a 9-ingredient nutraceutical supplement (including beta-caryophyllene, pregnenolone, DHEA, bromelain, St. John's Wort, Boswellia serrata, quercetin, zinc, and vitamin D) in 51 long COVID patients from 18 US states over 4 weeks. All 12 assessed symptoms (fatigue, weakness, cardiac/neurological symptoms, shortness of breath, GI disorders, ageusia/anosmia, anxiety, joint pain, rash, cough, insomnia) showed statistically significant improvement at both 2 and 4 weeks compared to baseline using paired t-tests with FDR correction (p<0.01); 72-84% of participants reported improvement in each symptom. The study had no control arm, no placebo, and no randomization, making it impossible to rule out natural disease course or placebo effects; minor adverse events occurred in 7 participants.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Critical limitation: this is a single-arm, non-randomized, open-label pre-post study — NOT an RCT. No randomization occurred; between_group_effects are empty throughout as there is no comparator arm. All quantitative outcome data (per-symptom means and SDs at each timepoint) appear only in figures (Figure 3 and Figure 4) which were not reproducible from the paper text; therefore all arm_results means/SDs are null with result_source 'not_reported'. The paper reports statistical significance (p<0.01, paired t-tests with Benjamini-Krieger-Yekutiel FDR correction) for all 12 symptoms at both 2- and 4-week timepoints vs. baseline, but no exact p-values, mean scores, or SDs are provided in the text or tables. The 12-symptom severity scale is not validated or described beyond its existence. Age range (21-73 years) is reported but no mean/SD; female:male ratio stated as 'approximately 2 to 1' (percent_female estimated as ~66.7%). Prior treatment duration range reported as 3-20 months. Conflict of interest: authors own stock in NTN Enterprises LLC, which sponsored the clinical study and holds the patent on the formulation.

summary: This non-randomized experimental repeated-measures study compared three doses of individualized pulmonary rehabilitation (12, 24, or 36 sessions, twice weekly) in 60 Chilean adults with post-acute sequelae of severe COVID-19 requiring invasive mechanical ventilation, assessed at baseline, end of program, and 1-year follow-up. All three groups showed significant within-group improvements in spirometric parameters, 6-minute walk distance, handgrip strength, fatigue, dyspnea, functional status, and most quality-of-life domains; these gains were generally maintained at 1-year follow-up. Crucially, at the 1-year assessment there were no statistically significant between-group differences in most outcomes (except physical FAS, total FAS, PCFS, and bodily pain favoring the 12-session group), suggesting that a shorter personalized program may be sufficient, though the non-randomized design with substantial baseline imbalances limits causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Study is explicitly non-randomized; group allocation was by clinical criterion (ability to walk 30 minutes continuously at 12 sessions). Significant baseline imbalances existed between groups in key outcomes (6-MWD, FVC, FEV1, FAS, mMRC, PCFS, Borg), making between-group effect comparisons potentially misleading. Between-group p-values reported in Tables 5 for 1-year follow-up comparisons are from omnibus tests (not pairwise); pairwise p-values listed in table footnotes indicate specific pair(s) significant. The table note for Borg in the 36s group (Table 4) lists STST baseline as '25.22 ± 8.27' which appears to be an error (baseline was 15.22 per Table 1). Total FAS SD in 36s post-PRP is listed identically as '19.17 ± 19.17' which may be a typographic error. Treatment duration varies by arm (12s ≈ 6 weeks, 24s ≈ 12 weeks, 36s ≈ 18 weeks); total follow-up duration was approximately 1 year plus treatment duration. SF-36 subscales Role Physical, General Health, Vitality, Social Functioning, Role Emotional not fully extracted in outcomes section but all data are available in Tables 2-5; omitted to stay within output limits. FEV1 % predicted data also available in tables but omitted as secondary. Borg scale data (dyspnea during 6MWT) available in tables but omitted from outcomes section.

summary: This prospective, open-label, single-arm study tested a 16-week tele-yoga intervention (50-min daily and 25-min as-needed sessions) in 86 adults with long COVID and moderate-to-high psychological stress (PSS ≥ 14) across two centers in India. Using a mixed-model ITT approach, the intervention produced statistically significant within-group reductions in perceived stress, general health, anxiety, and insomnia at both 4 and 16 weeks (all p<0.001); depression improved significantly at 4 weeks but not at 16 weeks, and trauma distress improved at 4 weeks only. The absence of a control arm precludes causal inference, and 63% of participants dropped out by week 16, primarily due to busy schedules.

Figures 1-4 show graphical data but numeric values were extracted from tables and text where available. The study design is quasi-experimental (no randomization, no control), classified as such despite being registered as a clinical trial.

summary: This single-arm feasibility study enrolled 16 patients with obesity and post-COVID condition in a 4-week inpatient multidisciplinary rehabilitation program combining exercise therapy, nutritional intervention, psychological support, and whole-body cryostimulation (WBC; 10 sessions at -110°C). All 16 participants completed the program with no adverse events. Statistically significant pre-post improvements were observed in weight, BMI, waist circumference, TUG, VAS pain, PGWBI, CRP, LDL, total cholesterol, glucose, SBP, and HR (p<0.05); SpO2 improved significantly in the Pneumology subgroup (n=5); the 6MWT improvement (+64.4 m) did not reach significance (p=0.093). Without a control group, the contribution of WBC specifically cannot be separated from the effects of the broader rehabilitation program.

summary: This single-arm pre-post study enrolled 41 ambulatory long COVID patients in a 12-week individualized exercise program combining 15 minutes of endurance training on a Total Body Trainer with 10-15 minutes of breathing, stretching, and strengthening exercises, conducted 2-3 times per week. Statistically significant improvements were observed in FACIT-Fatigue scores (mean increase 7.41 points from baseline, 95% CI 3.81–11.02, p<0.001, Cohen's f=0.67), 1-minute sit-to-stand test repetitions (median increase from 21 to 24, p<0.001), and workload capacity (median increase from 34W to 79W, p<0.001, Kendall's w=0.76), while the Post-COVID Functional Status Scale score (median 3) remained unchanged. The absence of a control group limits causal inference, and fatigue scores remained in the clinically relevant range (mean 26.80 at 12 weeks, cutoff ≤30) despite significant improvement, suggesting longer-term treatment may be required.

summary: This open-label, non-randomized pilot study tested a 4-day oral prednisone course (30 mg/day) in 9 long COVID patients with persistent symptoms (myalgia, arthralgia, asthenia, dyspnea, and others) approximately 9 months after mild acute COVID-19. All treated patients reported complete or partial symptomatic improvement after treatment, with arthralgia improving in 86%, myalgia in 75%, and asthenia in 57% of cases, and deep immune profiling showed that pre-treatment immunological alterations (elevated cDC, Th1 skewing, reduced naïve T cells and Tregs, increased PD-1 exhaustion markers) normalized after corticosteroid treatment and were maintained at 4-month follow-up; however, the lack of a randomized control arm and very small sample size (n=9 treated) severely limits causal interpretation.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is NOT a randomized controlled trial — it is a non-randomized, open-label, single-arm pre-post pilot study with a non-treated asymptomatic post-COVID comparison group (NSP, n=5). No randomization was performed, no blinding, and no placebo control. Classified as quasi-experimental. All quantitative immunological outcome data (flow cytometry percentages/MFI values) are reported only in figures (Figures 1–2 and Supplementary Figures S1–S5) with no numeric values in the text or tables — only p-value thresholds (p<0.05, p<0.01, p<0.001) are stated. Exact numeric values for all immune biomarkers are therefore not_reported in text. Only symptom-level data (counts of patients with symptoms) are extractable from the text. The TTP+4M follow-up was conducted in only 6 of 8 treated patients. Total follow-up duration calculated as 4 months ≈ 17.7 weeks post-treatment-start (0.57 weeks treatment + 17.1 weeks post-treatment). Adverse events were not discussed or reported.

summary: This open-label, 6-arm RCT conducted at a single center in India evaluated 15 days of yogic breathing (short breathing technique [SBT] alone for active COVID-19 patients; SBT plus long-duration breathing technique [LDBT] for COVID-recovered patients and healthcare workers) versus usual care in 71 participants across three populations. The primary outcome was D-dimer: levels were significantly reduced within the COVID-recovered yoga group (p=0.002) and the HCW yoga group showed significantly lower D-dimer than controls at day 15 (p=0.01), while the active COVID groups showed no significant between-group difference. Secondary 6-minute walk test distance improved significantly in COVID-positive yoga participants (p=0.01) and HCW yoga participants (p=0.002) compared to controls, but the study is limited by very small sample sizes (n=11-12 per arm), lack of blinding, and open-label design.

summary: This quasi-experimental single-arm pre-post study evaluated a 4-week personalised digital physiotherapy programme (delivered via Physiotec software with videoconference support) in 32 long COVID patients in Andalusia, Spain. summary: This single-arm before-and-after feasibility pilot study tested 8 weeks of home-based personalized computerized cognitive training (CogniFit CCT) in 73 adults with self-reported cognitive dysfunction at least 3 months after COVID-19 infection. All five cognitive domains assessed (attention, memory, coordination, perception, reasoning) showed statistically significant improvements from baseline to post-intervention, with mean z-score changes ranging from 0.36 (reasoning) to 1.01 (coordination) and mean percentile gains of 11–18 points. However, the absence of a control group means that practice effects, natural recovery, and regression to the mean cannot be ruled out as explanations for the observed gains.

Dropout: 262 candidates enrolled, 103 completed both assessments, 73 also met the 10-session minimum. Figure 2 (relationship between minutes of training and cognitive gain) contains data only in figure form — not extractable numerically. No adverse events were reported anywhere in the paper.

summary: This single-arm pilot clinical trial enrolled 29 post-COVID-19 patients (mild, moderate, or severe) in a 2-month outpatient pulmonary and functional rehabilitation program consisting of inspiratory muscle training, aerobic exercise, and peripheral muscle strengthening, administered twice weekly for 16 planned sessions. Significant pre-post improvements were observed in 6-minute walk test distance (326 to 445 m, p<0.001), FVC (p=0.004), FEV1 (p=0.001), maximal expiratory pressure (p<0.001), handgrip strength (p<0.011), and patient-reported outcomes including mMRC, CAT, and PCFS (all p<0.001). The absence of a control group precludes causal attribution, but results suggest clinically meaningful gains in functional and respiratory capacity following structured rehabilitation.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm pre-post design with no randomization or control group; classified as quasi-experimental. All between_group_effects entries represent within-arm pre-post comparisons (not between-arm comparisons), as this is a single-arm study. FVC% and FEV1% columns in Table 2 appear to represent ratio of achieved/predicted value (not percent predicted in the usual sense), with values of 3.7 and 2.9 at baseline — these may be data entry errors in the paper or a non-standard reporting format; extracted as verbatim. The paper states sample size calculation required 42 participants but only 29 completed, indicating the study was underpowered. No adverse events were reported anywhere in the paper. Systolic BP: baseline 131.7±15.3, post 128.6±14.8, p=0.272; Diastolic BP: baseline 88.2±10.7, post 85.2±17.7, p=0.432; Oxygen saturation: 96.1±2.6 vs 96.2±2.4, p=1.000 — these vital signs outcomes were not included as separate outcome objects to stay within size limits but all data is available in Table 2.

summary: This single-center randomized trial from Mexico enrolled 54 post-COVID-19 condition patients (all with vitamin D deficiency and prior severe COVID-19 hospitalization) and compared 8 weeks of weekly bolus vs. daily oral cholecalciferol supplementation. Both regimens significantly increased GPx activity (an antioxidant biomarker), while only bolus dosing significantly reduced IL-6 levels and only daily dosing significantly improved HADS anxiety and depression scores. Neither regimen produced statistically significant improvements in cough, dyspnea, or fatigue. The absence of a placebo arm and the self-controlled design preclude causal conclusions.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. This is a self-controlled RCT with two active arms (bolus vs. daily vitamin D) — no placebo control. arm_id=1 assigned to bolus (primary intervention), arm_id=2 to daily (active comparator). 2. Within-group p-values (paired t-test) are the primary statistical results; between-group comparisons are secondary. 3. The between-group p-value for GPx at baseline (p=0.006) is noted in text — suggesting non-equivalent groups at baseline. 4. Between-group effect for HADS anxiety at post-treatment (p=0.01) is verbatim; other between-group p-values for HADS depression and IL-6 post-treatment not explicitly reported (stated only as p>0.05 or not significant). 5. Overall combined results (all 54 patients) also reported: GPx pre 182.42±78.33, post 234.12±113.76 (p=0.0001); IL-6 pre 4.92±9.59, post 2.62±6.40 (p=0.07); HADS anxiety pre 4.04±3.98, post 1.07±2.12 (p=0.0001); HADS depression pre 3.81±4.54, post 1.24±2.35 (p=0.001) — these pooled results not extracted as separate outcomes. 6. The obesity % in Table 1 for bolus group appears to contain a typographic error (42.9% listed as 26 participants out of 28, which would be ~92.9%; likely should be 42.9% = ~12 participants). 7. No intermediate 30-day biomarker results were reported numerically. 8. Trial registered at ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT06419712.

summary: This single-arm pre-post study enrolled 31 long COVID patients in Poland who underwent 15 sessions of hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) at 2.5 ATA. Significant improvements were observed across multiple domains including quality of life (EQ-5D-5L VAS: 67.8 to 83.6, p<0.001), aerobic endurance (two-minute step test: ~92 to 126 steps, p<0.001), venous lactate levels (1.35 to 1.06 mmol/L, p=0.025), working memory (p=0.015), and attention/concentration (p<0.001). However, the absence of a control group severely limits causal inference, as improvements may reflect natural recovery rather than HBOT effects.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm pre-post study with no randomization or control group — classified as quasi-experimental, not RCT. Many Fullerton test subscores (dynamometer, back scratch, sit and reach by timepoint) are reported only in supplementary Table S2 which was not available in the full text provided. Spirometry values (FEV1, FVC, FEF25-75) are described narratively and in supplementary figures/tables but specific means/SDs by timepoint were not extractable from the provided text. Anion gap change p=0.0245 is stated but no means/SDs reported for anion gap in text. Subjective symptom questionnaire results (headache, fatigue, sleep, etc.) are described as significant (p<0.001) but numeric scores are in supplementary Table S1, not available here. EQ-5D-5L domain distributions (walking, self-care, daily activities, pain, anxiety/depression) extracted as percentages reporting 'no problems' category. Follow-up duration stated as '2-24 weeks' making precise weeks_from_randomization calculation impossible. Between-group effect entries for pre-post comparisons within a single arm use 'baseline_vs_posttreatment' as the comparison label rather than arm1_vs_arm2, since there is no control arm.

summary: This prospective before-and-after interventional study evaluated an 8-week outpatient pulmonary rehabilitation program (45-min sessions, 3x/week, combining cycle ergometer and progressive resistance exercises) in 60 post-COVID-19 syndrome patients in Brazil. summary: This single-arm prospective pilot study enrolled 20 patients with long COVID or post-COVID-19 conditions who had general fatigue and were prescribed hochuekkito (a traditional Japanese Kampo herbal medicine at 7.5 g/day) for 8 weeks at a specialized outpatient clinic in Japan. The primary outcome, the Japanese version of the Fatigue Assessment Scale (FAS), decreased from a mean of 35.9 (SD 5.9) at baseline to 31.2 (SD 9.4) at 8 weeks in the 13 patients with complete data, a mean reduction of 4.7 points (95% CI: 0.5–8.9), which exceeds the minimal clinically important difference of 4 points. As a single-arm study with no control group, it is not possible to attribute this improvement to hochuekkito versus natural recovery, and the authors note a planned RCT is underway.

summary: This single-arm prospective pilot study assessed 10 sessions of hyperbaric oxygenation (100% O2 at 2.2 atm, 75 min/session, 5x/week) in 59 evaluable long COVID patients (mean age 43.9 years, 56% female) at the Medical University of Graz, Austria. summary: This single-arm pilot trial enrolled 13 post-COVID-19 patients with upper limb impairment following severe COVID-19 hospitalization to evaluate a 6-week robotic hand exoskeleton rehabilitation program (RobHand, 4 sessions/week, 45 min each). Participants showed significant improvements in hand-related functional independence (FIM self-care, transfers, locomotion subscales; p<0.05), most SF-36 quality-of-life domains, and finger range of motion (passive flexion increased by 60.4±25.7% and active flexion by 28.7±11.2%). summary: This Swiss single-arm pilot study (n=7) of ME/CFS patients with post-COVID-19 condition and elevated GPCR autoantibodies evaluated 4 sessions of therapeutic plasmapheresis plus low-dose IVIG (2g Octagam per session) over approximately 60 days, with repeated measures of psychometric outcomes (EQ-5D-5L, ISI, FSS, HADS) at baseline, after 2nd PE, and after 4th PE. The primary finding was a statistically significant negative association between β2-adrenergic receptor antibody concentration and EQ-5D-5L index score (R²=0.32, p=0.014) and between M3-muscarinic receptor antibody concentration and EQ-5D-5L index score (R²=0.46, p=0.002), though neither survived Bonferroni correction; no significant improvements in clinical outcomes over the three timepoints were detected, and autoantibody levels did not significantly change after treatment.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm, uncontrolled pilot study — there is no comparator arm. All per-arm numeric data (means, SDs) for clinical outcomes (EQ-5D-5L, ISI, FSS, HADS) are presented only in box plot figures (Figures 1 and 3) with no accompanying tables or text values; result_source set to 'not_reported' for these. Antibody concentration data similarly shown only in box plots. The main quantitative findings reported are multilevel model regression coefficients (effect of antibody concentration on EQ-5D-5L index), extracted in outcome_ids 9 and 10. The study used multiple imputation (MICE) for 2 patients who prematurely withdrew. One patient was excluded entirely for lacking all baseline and follow-up data (therefore enrolled n=8, analyzed n=7). Statistical power was only 10%. Outcomes also collected but not analyzable: 6MWT (discontinued due to PEM), Schellong test, IES-R — no numeric data extractable. β1-adrenergic and M4-muscarinic receptor antibodies showed no significant associations with any outcome (reported only as non-significant in text, no values given).

summary: This single-arm pilot study tested 10 weeks of supervised aerobic exercise training (20 sessions, twice weekly) in 14 long COVID patients at Harbor-UCLA Medical Center. Participants showed significant improvements in VO2peak (+1.55 mL/kg/min, p=0.030), peak work rate (+16W, p=0.010), depression (PHQ-9 -42%, p=0.001), dyspnea (mMRC, p=0.015), and multiple SF-36 quality-of-life domains, but no significant changes in 6-minute walk distance, physical activity levels, or anxiety. summary: This single-arm, non-randomized trial enrolled 77 post-COVID patients (mean age 59.4 years, 39% female) in a 2-week inpatient pulmonary rehabilitation program consisting of supervised respiratory muscle training, aerobic exercise, and motivational breathing therapy. Significant pre-post improvements were observed across all spirometric parameters (FVC median 75% to 78.4%, FEV1 median 78.2% to 80.5%, both p<0.001), TLC, DLCO, and arterial blood gases (PaO2 median +7.6 mmHg), alongside marked reductions in CRP (median 8.9 to 1.3 mg/dL) and D-dimer (median 1722 to 203 ng/mL). Quality of life improved significantly in physical, psychological, and environmental domains of the WHOQOL-BREF; however, the absence of a control group precludes causal attribution of these changes to the rehabilitation program.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm pre-post design with no control group; all 'between_group_effects' represent pre-post within-arm comparisons (Wilcoxon test), not true between-group comparisons — marked as 'calculated' mean differences. The post-intervention SD for TLC (51.23) and DLCO (56.62) are anomalously large relative to the means, likely due to outliers (max TLC=505.9%, max DLCO=561.5% in the post data) — these are extracted verbatim. The paper reports median as the primary summary statistic (Wilcoxon non-parametric tests used); means and SDs are also provided in Table 2 and are extracted. Adverse events not reported. No 6-minute walk test included. WBC change was not statistically significant overall (p>0.05 by Wilcoxon), though sex-stratified analysis showed significance in males. Social relationships QoL domain did not improve significantly (p>0.05). The abstract states PaO2 increased by 7.6 mmHg — this refers to median change (59.4 to 67.0 mmHg = +7.6 mmHg), consistent with Table 2.

summary: This before-after case-controlled trial (n=5) tested whether adding spinal cord transcutaneous stimulation (scTS) to respiratory training (RT) improved respiratory function in post-acute COVID-19 patients with FVC deficits. All participants first completed 10 daily sessions of RT alone, then 10 daily sessions of scTS combined with RT. Compared to RT alone, scTS+RT produced significantly greater improvements in FVC (2.28 to 2.99 L, p=0.034), percent-predicted FVC (54.4% to 69.6%, p=0.023), PEF (1.52 to 2.11 L/s, p=0.023), and tPEF (0.56 to 0.43 s, p=0.013), with an average effect size twice that of RT alone (1.46 vs 0.78), though the study's single-arm sequential design, absence of a control group, and n=5 severely limit causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-cohort sequential crossover design, not a true RCT. All 5 participants received RT first (arm_id=2 in this extraction), then scTS+RT (arm_id=1). Arm_id=2 represents the RT-alone phase (both serving as baseline context and as a comparator). The study reports paired within-subject before-after comparisons using paired t-tests and Signed Rank tests, not between-group comparisons in the traditional sense. For PIF and PEF at baseline, the paper uses Median ± MAD notation (non-normally distributed); values labeled as mean±SD in results text are actually median±MAD for these outcomes at some timepoints — noted in context. The PEF outcome at baseline shows '1.15 ± 0.37' and post-RT '1.38 ± 0.04' labeled as Median ± MAD. Pre-scTS PEF is listed as '1.52 ± 0.49' and post-scTS as '2.11 ± 0.49' with mean±SD notation; these may represent a switch to normal distribution at post-scTS timepoint or inconsistent reporting. Effect size data (Cohen's d per outcome) are shown in Figure 5 but not tabulated numerically in text beyond the averages (RT: 0.78±0.70; scTS+RT: 1.46±0.38). Blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen saturation, and VAS pain were monitored as safety outcomes but no numeric data reported. No adverse events formally reported. Conflict of interest noted: Gerasimenko holds shareholder interest in Cosyma Inc., manufacturer of the Neostim-5 device used.

summary: This single-arm Italian pilot study treated 16 vaccinated patients with phase-1 adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) developed within 4 months of COVID-19 infection using ultrasound-guided anterior rotator interval hydrodilatation (corticosteroid + lidocaine + saline) followed immediately by 10 weeks of physiotherapist-led rehabilitation (20 sessions). All outcome measures improved significantly from baseline to 10 weeks: VAS pain fell from 6.9 to 1.0, SPADI from 55.5% to 8.5%, DASH from 58 to 12, and shoulder flexion ROM from 55° to 150°, all reaching p<0.00001. summary: This Ukrainian quasi-experimental study compared one versus two daily sessions of early inpatient physical rehabilitation (positioning, verticalization, breathing exercises) in 102 severe COVID-19 ICU patients (n=51 per group). At hospital discharge, two daily sessions produced a statistically significant improvement in anxiety and depression (HADS 9.52 vs 11.33, p=0.02) but not in physical function (AM-PAC, JH-HLM) or cognition (MMSE). Post-COVID-19 Functional Status at approximately 57 days post-discharge was significantly better in the twice-daily group (PCFS 1.62 vs 2.06, p=0.02), suggesting that higher rehabilitation dosing during ICU reduces long COVID symptom burden.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Study described as forming groups 'based on number of rehabilitation sessions per day' with no mention of randomization procedure — classified as quasi-experimental/non-randomized comparative study despite being presented alongside RCT literature. The PCFS follow-up timing is ambiguous: abstract states '57 days after discharge' while methods state 'first visit or phone contact 5-7 days after discharge'; likely the PCFS tool protocol is 5-7 days but actual follow-up was ~57 days post-discharge. Baseline outcome data (pre-rehabilitation) not reported for any outcome scale. No adverse events data reported. No CI data provided for any between-group comparison.

summary: This single-arm, pre-post pilot study (n=11 post-COVID-19 patients) evaluated a 4-week home telerehabilitation program using the ARC Intellicare system (AI-powered IMU sensors, 45 min/day, 5 days/week) in people with post-COVID-19 condition and Parkinson's disease. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm pre-post study (no control group); all 'between_group_effects' entries represent within-arm pre-post changes, not between-group comparisons. Whole-sample results also available in Table 5 (N=21) but COVID-19 subgroup (N=11) data extracted here as this is the relevant population for long COVID meta-analysis. summary: This open-label, uncontrolled pilot trial tested HRG80 Red Ginseng (a hydroponically grown Panax ginseng with high rare ginsenoside content) in 188 US adults with severe chronic fatigue syndrome and/or fibromyalgia, including a subgroup (40%) with post-viral onset (including some post-COVID cases), over one month of treatment. In the full sample, all six VAS outcomes improved significantly from baseline (all p<0.001), with the primary composite score (energy + well-being + mental clarity) improving from 12.2 to 17.1 (Cohen's d=-1.04; 40% improvement), and 60.1% of participants self-reporting improvement. However, the study has no placebo control arm, is open-label, and had 25% loss to follow-up, making it impossible to distinguish treatment effects from placebo response or natural history; findings should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating only.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: IMPORTANT DESIGN NOTE: This is a single-arm pre-post study, NOT a controlled trial. All outcome arm_results are coded as arm_id=0 (overall sample) since there is no true comparator arm; 'between_group_effects' are actually pre-post within-subject differences. The two 'arms' in study_design (capsule vs. tablet) reflect a secondary formulation comparison only, not intervention vs. control. Per-arm data for capsule vs. tablet subgroups are NOT reported separately for baseline/endpoint means and SDs — only percentage improvements in Table 6 (improvers only) and interaction F-statistics in Tables 4-5. Table 6 reports percentage improvement only for improvers subsample by dose/form subgroup but does not give absolute means/SDs per subgroup. The paper reports paired t-test t-statistics and Cohen's d for all outcomes but no confidence intervals for the within-subject mean differences. Duration of illness mean 18.9 years (SD 10.6) reported for overall sample. Post-viral subgroup n=76; improvers subsample n=113. No post-study follow-up conducted. 64 participants did not return post-study questionnaires and were excluded from analysis (not included in n=188). The study received 258 applications; 6 withdrew during the study with stated reasons. Total enrolled implied ~258; 188 completed. The 'randomization' described applies only to which formulation (capsule/tablet) participants received — participants were not randomized to intervention vs. control.

summary: This single-arm, open-label, before-after study examined the effect of recombinant human IL-2 (rhIL-2; 0.5 mg subcutaneously × 3 doses over ~5 days) on NK cell phenotype and function in 29 post-COVID-19 patients (assessed 3 months after acute infection) who had low NK cell counts at baseline. After treatment, the absolute and relative count of total NK cells was restored to the level of healthy controls (n=30), and multiple NK cell subsets (CD57+, CD62L+, CD8+) showed significant increases from baseline. Clinical symptom burden also declined markedly (e.g., fatigue: 100% → 6.9%; headache: 89.7% → 3.5%), but the absence of a control arm makes it impossible to attribute these improvements specifically to rhIL-2.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm before-after study, not an RCT; there is no comparator treatment arm — a healthy control group (n=30) was used only as a reference for NK cell levels, not as a treatment comparison arm. Total NK cell percentage and absolute count data for treated patients are described as being in Figure 1 (images not extractable); exact median/IQR values for these outcomes could not be extracted from text. The treatment duration (3 injections × 48h interval) yields approximately 5 days; post-treatment assessments were done once after completing the course with no long-term follow-up described. Table data for some NK subsets contained OCR/formatting artifacts from the PDF (Table 5 especially had duplicated header rows); values were reconciled from context. CD16-CD56+ CD8+ NK subset and CD16-CD56dim CD8+ NK subset data were extracted from the garbled Table 5: CD16-CD56+ CD8+ before: median 0.05 (0.02-0.11), after: 0.04 (0.01-0.05); CD16-CD56dim CD8+ before: 0.06 (0.01-0.23), after: 0.08 (0.01-0.25) — not included as separate outcome objects to limit JSON size. summary: This single-arm pre-post study in 21 post-COVID patients (≥6-12 months after SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia) evaluated topical nasal application of a synthetic GM-CSF active site peptide (Acegram-spray, 30 mcg/day) for 10 days on immune parameters. The treatment significantly increased NBT neutrophil spontaneous activity (14.6% to 22.3%, p<0.01), induced activity (40.4% to 55.8%, p<0.01), T helper cell percentage (41.5% to 47.6%, p<0.03), and C3a complement fragment levels (104.3 to 128.0 conventional units, p<0.001), while other immune parameters showed no significant change. The authors concluded the peptide primarily modulates innate immunity and that additional immunomodulators targeting T, B, and NK cells would be needed for comprehensive post-COVID immune rehabilitation.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm pre-post study, not a true RCT. The paper describes 'two comparison groups' (before and after treatment in the same patients), not separate treatment and control arms. The abstract mentions n=21 while the Methods section states n=20 — the table uses n=21, which was used here. Values reported as M±m (mean ± standard error of mean), not SD; placed in 'se' field accordingly. P-values reported as thresholds only (p<0.01, p<0.02, p<0.03, p<0.05, p<0.001). Measured outcomes include T lymphocytes (CD3+), cytotoxic T cells (CD8+), TNK cells (CD3+CD56+), NK cells (CD3-CD56+), B lymphocytes (CD19+), activated helpers (CD4+CD25+), activated T cells (HLA-DR), IgA/IgM/IgG (total and SARS-CoV-2 specific), phagocytosis, C1q, C5a — but only the 6 statistically significant outcomes were reported with numeric values in the table; all others reported as non-significant without data.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm pre-post study (no control group, no randomization) despite being labelled a 'prospective intervention study'. The paper incorrectly uses 'quasi-experimental' framing. SF-36 Pain subscale shows a counterintuitive direction: baseline mean 84.05 is very high (lower pain burden = higher score in SF-36), dropping to 28.4 post-intervention — this is coded as pain worsening on the scale but authors describe it as improvement; the scale may be reported as a 'pain interference/limitation' subscale where lower is better (pain scales vary in direction). The change score of 55.65 is coded as positive in the paper. The 6MWT was measured in laps of a 30m corridor rather than meters, making cross-study comparison difficult. No between-group effects are calculable as there is no comparator arm.

summary: This single-arm, uncontrolled pre-post study enrolled 25 non-hospitalized patients with mild post-COVID-19 syndrome (fatigue, myalgia, cough, sore throat, shortness of breath) and treated them with iWALL Tablet, a polyherbal Ayurvedic formulation containing 9 herbs including Ashwagandha, Guduchi, and Amalaki, at 750 mg twice daily for 12 weeks. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm pre-post study, not an RCT. The SD column in Table 2 appears mislabeled — the values reported as 'S.D' (e.g., fatigue BT S.D = 0.89) are plausible SDs, but the column labeled 'S.E' (e.g., 0.18) and values labeled 't score' appear to be one-sample t-statistics (mean/SE), not two-sample between-group t-tests. The 't score at 0.01 level of significance' column likely represents t = mean/SE for each timepoint separately rather than a BT vs AT comparison t-test; no paired t-test p-value is explicitly stated. The SD field was left null and SE was populated from the paper's 'S.E' column. The '99% confidence interval' column values (e.g., 0.46 for fatigue BT) appear to be half-widths of the CI rather than full CI bounds, and represent 99% CI (not 95%), so ci_95_low/high were left null. No between-group effects are calculable as there is no control arm. Table 3 response categories: Good Response 12 (48%), Fair Response 8 (32%), Poor Response 5 (20%), No Response 0 (0%).

summary: This observational cross-sectional study compared post-COVID-19 psychiatric and somatic outcomes in 246 hospitalized COVID-19 survivors who had either received IL-6 receptor inhibitors during acute illness (tocilizumab, n=67; sarilumab, n=21) or had not (controls, n=158). summary: This prospective observational before-after study evaluated 12-day spa therapy (balneotherapy and/or inhalation crenotherapy) in 78 post-COVID-19 patients with pre-existing chronic joint, musculoskeletal, skin, or respiratory diseases at three Italian spas. Spa therapy produced statistically significant reductions in VAS scores for nearly all post-COVID-19 symptoms including chronic fatigue (-47%), muscle pain (-48%), brain fog (-41%), and persistent cough (-68%), as well as significant improvements across all eight SF-36 quality of life dimensions (all p<0.0001), with the largest gains in role limitations due to physical (+72%) and emotional (+66%) functioning. The study lacked a randomized control arm, making it impossible to distinguish treatment effects from natural recovery or placebo effects; nonetheless, improvements were consistently observed across sexes, with females tending to show greater percent improvements in QoL dimensions despite lower baseline scores.

Logistic regression results are reported in Supplementary Table S4 (summary included in text). risk_of_bias.domain_judgments: confounding:critical, selection:serious, classification:moderate, deviations:serious, missing_data:low, measurement:moderate, reporting:moderate
risk_of_bias.key_concern: Critical confounding: all 152 patients had pre-existing autonomic dysfunction and were already on autonomic therapy before COVID-19, making it impossible to separate COVID-19 effects from pre-existing disease trajectory; no comparison group of long COVID patients without pre-existing autonomic dysfunction; unblinded; proprietary device (lead author is co-founder of device manufacturer).

summary: This retrospective, hypothesis-generating, single-arm before-after study followed 152 patients with pre-existing autonomic dysfunction who had undergone P&S (parasympathetic/sympathetic) testing and treatment prior to COVID-19 infection, then were re-tested and re-treated after developing long COVID. Post-COVID-19, patients showed a significant increase in autonomic dysfunction burden (mean 2.34 to 3.67 dysfunctions, p=0.004) and symptom burden (mean 9.74 to 14.6 of 28 symptoms), with parasympathetic excess becoming the dominant dysfunction (27.0% to 46.7%) and sympathetic withdrawal decreasing in relative prevalence. Following resumed autonomic therapy (Midodrine, Alpha-Lipoic Acid, Nortriptyline, and low-intensity exercise), both autonomic dysfunction count (3.67 to 1.63, p=0.003) and symptom count (14.6 to 7.44, p=0.004) were significantly reduced, supporting the hypothesis that targeted autonomic therapy may be beneficial in long COVID, though the lack of a control group and highly selected population (pre-existing autonomic disease) severely limits causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. This study has a highly unusual and confounded design: all participants had pre-existing autonomic dysfunction and were already receiving autonomic therapy BEFORE COVID-19 infection. This is not a typical long COVID treatment trial but a retrospective outcomes study in a pre-selected clinical population. 2. The paper does not report SDs for any of the continuous outcomes (symptom counts, dysfunction counts) — only means and p-values are given, limiting meta-analytic utility. 3. The pre-COVID follow-up therapy duration was stated as 'less than 9 months' and post-COVID therapy duration as 'less than 6 months' — no exact durations are reported, making follow-up_weeks not calculable. 4. The p-values reported in Table 3 compare row to row within the pre-COVID or post-COVID phase (e.g., pre-COVID baseline vs. pre-COVID follow-up; post-COVID baseline vs. post-COVID follow-up) — not all pairwise comparisons are reported. The p-value for post-COVID vs. pre-COVID baseline for symptoms is stated in text as p<0.001 for the increase to 14.6. 5. Lead author (Colombo) has a conflict of interest as co-founder of Physio PS, Inc., manufacturer of the P&S Monitor 4.0 device used for all measurements. 6. IRB statement is non-standard (HIPPA rather than HIPAA, no formal IRB approval stated). 7. The paper states results are based on Pearson correlation and Student's t-test (SPSS v.20) but does not report test statistics or effect sizes beyond means and p-values.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Male: HR 0.697 (95% CI 0.559–0.868); Female: HR 0.879 (95% CI 0.786–0.984); both statistically significant.
Age 18–59: HR 0.765 (95% CI 0.688–0.85), significant. ≥60 years group results not explicitly stated for composite but showed no significant benefit for depression, anxiety, or insomnia individually.
<2 doses: HR 0.769 (95% CI 0.695–0.851), significant. ≥2 doses group did not show significant benefit for individual psychiatric outcomes (depression, anxiety, insomnia).
White: HR 0.832 (95% CI 0.743–0.932), significant; Non-white: HR 0.705 (95% CI 0.547–0.909), significant.

summary: This propensity-score matched retrospective cohort study used the TriNetX global health research network to investigate whether omega-3 PUFA supplementation (taken before COVID-19 diagnosis) was associated with lower risk of post-COVID-19 psychiatric sequelae in 16,962 non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients matched 1:1 to controls. Omega-3 users had a significantly lower risk of developing any psychiatric sequelae (HR 0.804, 95% CI 0.729–0.888, p<0.001), including depression (HR 0.828), anxiety (HR 0.833), and insomnia (HR 0.679) in the 90-day to 1-year follow-up window. Significant protective associations were also observed for cough and myalgia, but not for fatigue, cognitive symptoms, chest pain, or abnormal breathing, and benefits were consistent across most demographic subgroups.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per-arm event counts for individual psychiatric outcomes (depression, anxiety, insomnia) and all somatic secondary outcomes were not reported in the paper text — only composite psychiatric sequelae counts (633 omega-3, 1048 non-omega-3) were stated. All individual outcome HRs are from Table 2 and Table 3 (tables not included in full text provided). Pre-matching sample sizes reported (16,962 omega-3; 2,248,803 non-omega-3) but post-matching Ns for matched cohort not stated. Omega-3 dose, formulation, and duration of supplementation were not captured in the TriNetX database and are not reported. The study examines pre-COVID-19 omega-3 exposure as a preventive intervention rather than a long COVID treatment — the 'long COVID' framing refers to post-acute sequelae emerging 90 days to 1 year after infection.
